This treatise states: "The doctrine of causelessness (ahetuvāda) is the adherence to the view that things arise without a cause;

it is neither existent nor non-existent, for it does not exist by virtue of being either existent or non-existent. This is called 'causelessness,' and this is what is meant by the 'adherence to spontaneity' (svabhāvavāda)."

The *Pò* (Commentary) says: This is not that it does not arise without cause; because there are causes and conditions, it can indeed arise. "That which is now the text" refers to contemplation (*guan*) and wisdom (*zhi*).
"Departing from illusion" (*li huan*)—one phrase—refers to delusion (*wang*) and its objects (*jing*). Since one has departed [from them], there is no contemplating wisdom.
Since it is said to be "departing from illusion," there is no deluded mind. If one clings to object and wisdom, reckoning them as such, this constitutes attachment (*zhi*).
Now, it is further removed from [the notion of] causelessness; thus it is said: "There is no nature of causelessness," which is likewise a removal. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both together, nor without a cause. For this reason, they are said to be unarisen.

As above, these four negations of the four illusions all involve the conceptualization of the four natures—self, other, both, and neither. If these four negations were to exist [as entities], [they would again fall into the error of reification].
The first calculation: four times four is sixteen. Each of the four illusions also has four calculations, totaling another sixteen.
The four illusions and the four detachments together make thirty-two. Now, examining these thirty-two, each one lacks a root;

they all arise from the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vijñāna*). Now, looking back at this wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment, it arises from my own mind. Now, I observe myself...
The mind is itself empty; sin and merit have no master. Furthermore, contemplate that the mind is no-mind, and that dharmas do not abide in dharmas.

They do not abide in the fetters (saṃyojana), yet they do not leave the ocean of fetters. Though they are free from afflictions, they are not separate from afflictions. The four illnesses reveal their essence, and the flower of the mind shines forth. Therefore it is said:
"Attaining that which is nothing to be separated from, one immediately eliminates all illusions" (the following provides a metaphor).
For example, when drilling for fire, fire arises from the mutual friction of two pieces of wood; once the wood is exhausted, the ashes fly away and the smoke is extinguished.
By drilling wood with wood, fire is produced; by cultivating illusion with illusion, illusion is extinguished. Now, it is said that two pieces of wood depend upon each other.

The wood that serves as the object of dependence is a metaphor for the mind of false attachment, which is precisely the perceived object (*ālambana*). The wood that serves as the agent of dependence is a metaphor for...
Contemplation (*guan*) is itself illusory wisdom; it is the contemplation that is capable of observing. Subject and object are mutually identical; the objective realm and the contemplation merge.

As the realm and the contemplation are mutually refined, the ignorance, the aggregates, and the delusions within the interim are finally exhausted. Furthermore, the two middle pieces of wood may be used as a metaphor for the anvil and the mallet.
The wood that serves as the cause is called the "anvil," which is the objective realm. The wood that serves as the instrument is called the "mallet," which is the contemplation. Anvil and mallet—

The self as subject and object, with ignorance and delusion in between, are themselves the very substance [of reality]. Once the furnace has been ignited and the hammer and anvil appear before one, there is no place for the deluded mind in the interim to escape;
it cannot help but be dissolved. This is the point where the deluded mind is extinguished.
The wondrous clarity of true awakening manifests. The two pieces of wood are mutually dependent: one piece represents the distancing [of the subject], which is the observing consciousness;
the other piece represents the objective realm of the aggregates (*skandha*), which is the observed object. Therefore, it is said that all are illusory, transformative, and false realms.
The "shadows" (skandhas) are extinguished; these constitute the divisions of the single layer of subject and object. Regarding "the fire emerges and the wood is exhausted":

the fire is a metaphor for the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which can destroy all phenomena and empty all appearances. As the Sūtra says: "Because of maintaining firm detachment from the mind.

This "detachment from the mind" refers to the aforementioned contemplation that can empty [all things]. If one were to further cling to this contemplation that can empty [all things], it would become a medicine... [of the mind].

This again becomes an illness; therefore, one must remain far removed from it. This refers to the dualistic relationship of subject and object. The scattering of ashes is a metaphor for the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Originally, the medicine is able to cure the illness; once the illness is gone, the medicine perishes. Yet, if one continues to cling to this medicine, the medicine itself becomes an illness.
The clinging to both medicine and illness is like the ashes; it is also called the "illness of clinging to emptiness. Having already emptied all phenomena, to then cling to [emptiness]...
"Emptiness. This is what is called the "sickness of emptiness. Guifeng said: "Smoke comes first and ashes come later;
this is an error by the translator. I say this is not so; it is precisely ashes first and smoke later. Why? This is the relationship between medicine and sickness.

The ash still possesses form and appearance; this serves as a metaphor for distancing oneself from illusion. Since this illusion is still coarse, it is compared to the ash. This is not an error on the part of the translator.
This "medicine" and "sickness" must also be distanced from one another. This is the third level of the relationship between subject and object, like the anvil and the hammer.

As for the extinction of smoke, it serves as a metaphor for the aforementioned medicine and sickness; it further implies that a new medicine is applied to treat the sickness caused by the previous medicine.
This is the disease of a new medicine; it is the disease of emptiness upon emptiness. Thus it is said: "Departing from and further departing from illusion.
Regarding the two instances of the character for "departing" (li), one immediately perceives the disease of the superior medicine—the disease of emptiness upon emptiness.

The Patriarch said, "Wisdom itself becomes an obstruction," which is also what this scripture means by the Bodhisattva "resolving obstructions. It may be said that before a person of great intelligence, there are indeed three feet [of distance].

Because it is dark, it is said that one must "further distance oneself" from it. These four [delusions] are distinct from the four illusions; they are merely differentiated by their coarseness and subtlety.
These four delusions are like locks made of iron, copper, silver, and gold: although they differ in value, the nature of being a lock is the same, and all must be removed.
If one were to give rise to further conceptual attachments beyond these four, how could this be? They too must be severed. Now...
Furthermore, regarding the statement that there are "four," the actualities do not exceed three (this concludes the four and leaves the four illusions; this is also the integration with the Dharma).
Cultivating illusion by means of illusion is likewise so (until): leaving illusion is itself awakening, and there is no gradual progression.
To cultivate illusion with illusion is like the joining of two pieces of wood that depend upon one another. Although all illusions are separated, they do not enter into annihilation.

When the fire arises from their union and the wood is exhausted, one knows that illusion is itself separation; no further expedient means are required. When the ashes fly away upon separation, illusion is itself awakening;
there is likewise no gradual progression. This concludes the section on the separation of illusion (the subsequent summary of the separation of illusion).
"From 'All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age' (up to) 'in this way one can forever leave all illusions.

This summarizes the three questions of Samantabhadra. If one can practice according to these four [precepts] to leave the four illusions, one will therefore attain the permanent departure from all illusions."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Samantabhadra, you should know: All sentient beings, From beginningless illusory ignorance, Are all established from the Tathāgatas’ Perfectly Awakened Mind, Just like flowers in the empty sky."
Phenomena exist by depending on emptiness; if the flowers in the sky were to cease, empty space itself would never move.

And for sentient beings in the final age, they should always remain far removed from illusions;

when all illusions are completely abandoned, (this answers the third question: "If one never practices cultivation, how can one attain liberation? Subsequently, he provides a general analogy through four points on abandoning four types of illusions):

just as fire arises within wood and the fire is extinguished once the wood is exhausted (the wood, fire, ash, and smoke—these four are all extinguished together), so too, upon awakening, there is no gradual progression.

Chapter on the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (Puyan):
I have heard that Bodhi is the ultimate state; it is divinely wondrous, quiescent, and pervasive. Perfect wisdom is profoundly illuminating; its Way transcends form and consciousness.

To establish the boundaries of the realm of birth and extinction and to treat the beginningless illness of sentient beings—which arises from the four great elements, the five aggregates, and the six sense organs—is comparable to a person’s two feet: with feet one can walk; without feet one cannot move.
Therefore, the Sage perceived that moving the feet causes the will to be lost, and lifting the feet causes one to lose their proper direction. At this point—
This is to cease and contemplate, to still and clarify, so that movement may become stillness and stillness may become clarity.

Seeing universally that sentient beings are in motion and have not yet attained stillness, and wishing to bring rest to their affliction of "empty flowers," he extensively expounds the Dharma-gate of illusion;
such is the underlying intent for the arrival of this chapter.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, amidst the great assembly, knelt with his right knee on the ground and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha,
requesting the ritual procedures and protocols as previously explained (this marks the formal request).
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, we pray that for the sake of this assembly, you will expound upon the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s practice.

As for these bodhisattvas: although they have heard of the 'illusory transformation' and the 'empty flowers,' as well as the 'illusion-like samādhi,' though they have heard them, they do not yet know how to contemplate them;

By regulating the mind in a single place, one now enters into meditative repose.
Sit upright, dwelling with the body restrained. When the body dwells in restraint, the mind is at peace; when the mind is at ease, the environment becomes tranquil.
Therefore, those who restrain both body and mind must necessarily stay in a quiet room. One must understand that although the Way has no fixed location, it necessarily arises by means of conditions.
Thus, those of old who cultivated the Way mostly stayed in mountain forests, beneath trees, or in *āraṇya*—solitary and silent places—to clear away the weeds.
They thatched their dwellings with rushes; they ate from the trees and drank from the mountain streams. Some took refuge in fragrant cliffs, while others befriended monkeys and cranes.

Some withered their bodies and minds like dry wood; some concealed their brilliance and hid their traces. Some caused springs to gush forth as they struck their staffs, while others dwelt in tranquil stillness amidst verdant peaks. Such were the sages of this tradition.
When the Way is lofty, dragons and tigers respond; when virtue is profound, ghosts and spirits are moved. How can this be compared to those of the present age who bind their emotions to fine titles?
When the Buddha was in the world, there was a śramaṇa who committed an offense and was sent away to live outside. He was utterly destitute of food and clothing.

It happened that he encountered a spirit from beneath the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings who had also committed an offense and been sent down to the human realm. They met and spoke together of food and clothing.
The ghost said, "Although I have committed transgressions, my supernatural power still remains. You may climb onto my shoulders and travel through the world;
when people see you, they will say you are an Arhat, and so you will obtain food every day. Thus, we both shall rejoice.
One day, however, the divine generals dispatched by the Four Heavenly Kings captured this ghost. The ghost fled in haste, but the śramaṇa on his shoulder could not escape.
Falling to the ground, one must suffer the consequences oneself. Furthermore, consider the retribution of the pañcāstikāya; how could one not fear it? Reflect on this!

When the ancients attained their aspirations, they nurtured the "sacred embryo" in cloud-shrouded chambers and mountain caves, or by the yellow scrolls and blue lamps, never forsaking their profound resolve.
Thinking thus, I speak these words of lament for those in this world who die in vain and live in emptiness.
Furthermore, [this next section clarifies the two objects of emptiness: first, the object of the emptiness of arising].
One should constantly maintain this thought: "This body of mine, [extending] to its appearance as a composite, is in reality identical to a magical illusion."
This clarifies the objective realm of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*). Regarding this emptiness of arising, one constantly maintains this reflection:
by means of the wisdom of emptiness, one contemplates and perceives that this body arises from falsehood. Its original single nature is of the same essence as primordial awakening (*mūla-bodhi*);

yet, suddenly perfumed by the karma of ignorance, it fails to maintain its own nature and undergoes retribution according to karma. Sustained by the elements of wind and fire, this conscious nature enters the mother’s womb.

In the interim, one mistakenly identifies what has been cast away as one's own dwelling, giving rise to a mind of attachment and delight; regarding it as one's own body, one gives rise to the notion of "mine.
Grasping this impurity, one consolidates it into a single mass to form the physical body (*rūpakāya*); this is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Experiencing this body and giving rise to perceptions of suffering and pleasure is called the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). Conceptualizing suffering and pleasure is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).
Because of this formation, it is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Consciousness abiding therein is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Just as five fingers joined together form the appearance of a fist, this is called the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), also called the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), and also called a sentient being (*sattva*).

By grasping these four great elements and five aggregates, this physical body is formed; therefore, it is called the objective sphere of the emptiness of beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). When its fundamental basis is investigated, it is non-existent.

This clarifies the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). It arises dependently upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The two elements of wind and fire cause the consciousness to coalesce and enter the mother’s womb.

The two drops of red and white [semen and blood] are called the water element (*ab-dhātu*). Just as water produces bubbles that aggregate to form a body, this is called the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).

These four great elements possess no real nature; because they are mistakenly perceived as a body, they are termed the "substantial dharmas" of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). These four great elements...
Although it lacks substantial reality, it arises through the conjunction of conditions; because it exists through the harmony of causes and conditions, it is called "dependently arisen.
"Conditions" refers to causal conditions. Having a slight causal connection with one's parents, one comes to be born into their family.
When consciousness departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) follows it, and warmth likewise follows. Since the two great elements of earth and water are no longer sustained by fire and wind, therefore—
Earth and water naturally disperse and vanish. Because past wholesome karma serves as the cause, it is called "birth. "Birth" means "to come into being.
When that karma expires, this physical body—the fruit thereof—perishes; because the four great elements disperse, it is called "death.
"Death" means "to exhaust. The soul-consciousness is scattered and dispersed; once the presiding master has departed, causes and conditions are exhausted. [The hair...]
Body hair is the sprout of blood. Nails and teeth are the sprouts of marrow. Skin, flesh, and head hair are the substrata upon which [the body] relies;
they increase when moistened by blood. Tendons and bones are the substrata upon which nails and teeth rely.
Moistened by the marrow, it then undergoes growth. There are three hundred and sixty joints and nine thousand nine hundred pores in total, as well as eighty-four thousand families of worms;
all of these, as mentioned above, ultimately return to the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, excrement, and urine belong to the water element (*ap-dhātu*).
Warmth belongs to the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*). Movement and transformation belong to the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). It is formed from the union of the vital energies of the father and mother.
The body, from birth through growth to old age and death, is entirely termed "defiled form. Earth, water, fire, and wind each return to their own source; thus it is said they are "separated.
Once the four great elements have dispersed, the delusory body immediately ceases. Upon death, when the body is cremated, the ashes fly away and the smoke vanishes;
hence it is asked: "Where now does this delusory body reside? To conclude the preceding passage, it says: "One thereby knows."
This body is ultimately without substance; it exists as a manifestation of conditioned aggregation and is truly like a magical illusion, being but a hollow realm produced by the linking of rebirth.
When the Buddha was in the world, there was a man who stayed overnight in an empty pavilion.
In the dead of night, he saw a hungry ghost carrying a corpse, followed closely by another ghost. The two ghosts contended for this corpse, [striking] one another...
They disputed over who was right and who was wrong without ceasing, and eventually asked the person in the empty pavilion, "Who brought you here?
The person in the empty pavilion, fearing that those on either side might fail to find him and would surely come to harm him, felt he had no choice but to speak the truth: "A great ghost brought me."
A small ghost in an empty pavilion plucked off the man's hand; a large ghost took the corpse's hand and grafted it onto him.
In this manner, his entire body was completely replaced. The two ghosts devoured the corpse, wiped their mouths, and departed.
This man perceived these events with perfect clarity. When dawn broke, he sat in silent contemplation: "Now, regarding this body of mine..."
Having been completely transformed by a ghost, he himself no longer possessed a body. He went about asking everyone he met, "Do I now have a body, or am I bodiless?
Eventually, he arrived at the Jetavana Monastery and questioned the arhats, "Does this body of mine exist, or does it not?
The sages said, "This person is capable of being delivered. Thereupon, they replied, "Your body has always been non-existent."
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, that which is conventionally designated as a "body" is realized as the path, whereby one realizes arhatship.

Is this not the meaning intended when the Sūtras state that all things are truly like illusions and transformations? (Next, the sense organs and their objects are called the realm of the emptiness of phenomena.)
The four conditions combine provisionally to give rise to the false existence of the six sense organs (up to: appearing as the marks of objects, which are falsely named "mind").
The four conditions are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). When these four combine provisionally, like a bubble arising from water, it is called the body.
This body possesses the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, which constitute the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*). For example, the eye conditions the dust of form, and so forth. Five.

The sense faculties (*indriya*) are also called "possessing objects of perception" (*sālambana*). As stated in the "Chapter on Emptiness": "Each [faculty] individually perceives its own sensory realm;

when these internal and external elements combine, within that combination, the accumulation of the six internal consciousnesses manifests as if there were a characteristic of perceiving. This is conventionally designated as 'mind.

One erroneously mistakes the perceived reflection for the characteristic of one's own mind. It further states: "This empty, delusory, and floating mind possesses many clever views. (From the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*)
The "Chapter on the Virtuous King" states: Suppose there were a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single basket and ordered a man to look after them.
He warned him, "If even one snake should give rise to anger, I shall execute you according to the law in the marketplace. The man was terrified;
he abandoned the basket and fled. The king then dispatched five *caṇḍālas* following him with drawn swords, yet one of them concealed his blade.
Pretending to be a close friend, he led the man to a village, intending for him to hide there. Once the man had entered the village, he saw no people;
however, he heard a voice from the air saying, "Tonight, six great bandits will come here.
Terrified, the man abandoned his hiding place and fled. On the road, he encountered a river with swift, surging waters, so he gathered bamboo and wood.
He constructs a raft to cross the torrent. Having reached the other shore, he is secure and free from affliction. The Bodhisattva is likewise:

hearing the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he contemplates the body as a chest, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as snakes, the five *caṇḍālas* as the five aggregates (*skandha*), and craving as a deceptive friend;
the six sense bases (*āyatana*) as an empty village, and the six thieves as the six external objects (*viṣaya*). The river is [the river of] affliction...

"Affliction. By means of the raft of the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), one reaches the other shore of the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*. The subsequent scriptural passage concludes the preceding discussion on the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*).
The mind that conditions these objects likewise concludes the preceding discussion on the realm of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

This is identical to the "Chapter on Emptiness," which clarifies the realms of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Previous masters were unaware of this and did not provide such an interpretation (this concludes the contemplation of the realm of the emptiness of phenomena).
Good son, if this deluded mind were not present, there would ultimately be no perceivable mind that takes objects as its conditions.
You should know that while still in the mother’s womb before birth, the four great elements form a body, which serves as the basis for the arising of empty objects.

After emerging from the womb, the sense organs grasp external forms and take the reflections of the six objects as their conditions; these are then termed the "six faculties" and the "six objects," and only then are they called "dharmas."

The sphere of emptiness. Because the six faculties, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses together constitute the eighteen realms—referred to as "all phenomena" (dharmas)—it is called the sphere of the emptiness of dharmas.
The present passage formally concludes this discussion of the sphere of the emptiness of dharmas.

Taking the reflections of the faculties, conditions, and objects to be the mind, it is therefore called "this deluded mind. If the six objects did not exist, this mind could not exist; thus, this concludes the emptiness of dharmas.
Therefore it is said that there is no conditioned mind to be perceived (next, the explanation of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons).
Good son, because the illusory body of those sentient beings is extinguished... [up to] ...because the extinction of illusion is itself extinguished, that which is not illusion is not extinguished.
This clarifies the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Contemplation must have an object; therefore, it is called the "object of the emptiness of persons.

If the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) combine to form this physical body, that is termed the "object. Furthermore, employing the contemplation of illusion (*māyā-darśana*), one contemplates this physical body of the four great elements.

Since the four great elements are subject to dispersal and cessation, it is said: "Because the illusory body ceases, the illusory mind—which fundamentally relies upon the physical body of the four great elements—[also ceases]."

When one dwells thus, once the body has perished, there is no body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Since this mind has no place of reliance, it is said that "the illusory mind also ceases.
Once this illusory mind has ceased, there is no longer anyone who grasps at sense objects; therefore, it is said that "illusory objects also cease.
This illusion that ceases the objects is itself without substance; its nature is fundamentally empty from the beginning. Therefore, it is said that "even the cessation of the illusion ceases."

The wisdom that extinguishes illusion becomes an obstruction to wisdom itself; thus, this wisdom is also extinguished. Therefore it is said: "Because illusion is extinguished, [wisdom] is extinguished.
It is like a fire-drill: it burns itself. Just as when the shavings emerge from the shavings, the shavings also emerge all at once, so too do the mind and body both cease.

When both object and contemplation are simultaneously extinguished, the beginning and the source merge as one. Since there is no agent who performs this merging, it is said that "what is not illusion does not perish";
only the wisdom of True Suchness (tathatā) remains. This wisdom is like a reflection in a mirror: when there is an image, it appears; when there is no image, it is empty.
Cultivation is entirely the nature, and the nature fully constitutes cultivation. The nature does not shift, yet cultivation remains ever-vivid.
(Below, an analogy is cited):
It is like polishing a mirror; when the impurities are exhausted, its brilliance appears.

This analogy refers to the contemplation of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). To remove the impurities of the physical body composed of the four great elements, one must rely on the power of the contemplation of universal illumination (*pariniṣpanna-pratyavekṣaṇa*). [This is] an illusion.

The body is about to perish. It is like a mirror that has become dim; it requires medicinal polishing. When the grime is removed, its clarity appears. Yet, the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti’s *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) cannot be polished.
Furthermore, one must realize that defilement is itself clarity, and clarity is itself defilement. Ignorance (*avidyā*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—these two are not two.
This can be understood through the analogy of ice and water. (Next, the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena is explained.)
"Good son, you should know that both body and mind are illusory defilements; when the characteristics of these defilements are eternally extinguished, the ten directions are pure.

This clarifies the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). "You should know that 'body and mind' refers to the body as the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) and the mind as the reflection of conditions upon sensory objects."
The three wisdoms within a single mind sweep away all marks. They do not go beyond the eighteen realms—the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses.
These organs and consciousnesses pair with their respective objects; using the攀緣心 (parāmarśa-citta, the攀缘心 or "clinging mind"), they grasp the five sense objects through the five roots of craving.
These five sensory realms are like dew upon a flower: they vanish when the sun rises. This is not the contemplation of the principle of True Suchness (tathatā).

How can the characteristics of defilement be eternally extinguished? One should know that Perfect Enlightenment is quiescent and illuminating; it is like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace—how could it endure for even a moment?

The ten directions are the ten realms: when hell is transformed, it becomes heaven; when a defiled land is transformed, it becomes a pure land. The environment and its inhabitants do not obstruct one another;
form and mind are without hindrance. (Below follows an analogy: the five sensory faculties grasp the objects of the five desires.)
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel (up to) seeing that the maṇi actually possesses five colors.

This passage precisely uses the analogy of the five sense faculties taking up the objects of the five desires. The jewel represents the single nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

Perfect Enlightenment does not abide in its own nature, but follows the five desire-faculties to take up the realms of the five sensory objects; it is like a jewel reflecting colors, manifesting according to the direction [it faces].
Manifestation. When the ignorant see forms, ordinary people relish them; those of the Two Vehicles distance themselves from them—like ghosts, tigers, dragons, and snakes.
When Bodhisattvas see forms, they are entirely Perfect Enlightenment; form is itself the Dharma-realm. When Buddhas see forms, they are neither identical to nor different from [the mind].
Yongjia said: "The mind is the root; dharmas are the dust. These two are like blemishes upon a mirror. When the stains of these blemishes are completely removed,"

When light first appears, both mind and phenomena vanish, and their nature is immediately the Truth. The sages laboriously employ provisional designations as skillful means, like gathering flowers to produce honey.
(This concludes the Contemplation on the Emptiness of Dharmas.)
"Good son, the pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment manifests as body and mind... (up to)... the self-characteristics of body and mind are likewise so.
This is the method for contemplating the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*dharmas*). As Perfect Enlightenment follows conditions to produce all phenomena:

when it is in the body, the entire nature of enlightenment becomes the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind; when the nature of enlightenment is in the mind, the eyes form into color-form (*rūpa*), and the ears form into sound (*śabda*).
Sound, the nose bound as fragrance, the tongue bound as flavor, and the body bound as touch—these attainments do not correspond to their respective categories.
The deluded are ignorant; they claim that the pure, perfect nature of *bodhi* truly possesses the characteristics of body and mind.
Recognizing these as the self, they give rise to the four types of views; clinging to them as the self, they falsely perceive arising and ceasing. Therefore, it is said: "It is also like this."
(Concluding the preceding section on the objective spheres and contemplations of the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena and of persons:
Because of this, one cannot remain far removed from illusions (up to) that which is without opposition, defilement, and even a name.
The meaning of this section of the sutra is to summarize the two kinds of emptiness regarding the aforementioned arising of dharmas.

Whether in terms of the object or the contemplation, when a sentient being comes to receive conception in the initial intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is solely due to delusion in ignorance (*avidyā*).

Beginning with ignorance as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and ending with old age and death, among the twelve links of dependent origination, one first recognizes ignorance as the beginning of erroneous application. [This concerns] the four great elements and the five aggregates.
The emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) refers to the shadows of conditions formed by the six sense objects; the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) refers to these same shadows.

These two types of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—are the objects of the deluded attachments of sentient beings. Now, employing *śamatha*—the perfect, quiescent illumination of *bodhi*—this is termed the "Contemplation of the Two Emptinesses.

Through this, one empties these four elements, five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen realms, finding them to have no fundamental root. One realizes that they are like the appearance of flowers in the sky, a manifestation of illusory transformation.

Dust is transformed into enlightened clarity. This nature of perfect enlightenment is itself fundamentally empty. When the defilement of ignorance is exhausted, there is no longer any opposing defilement.
Once the defilements are exhausted, the practice of the six perfections is perfected; it is only by conventional designation that one is called a "Bodhisattva.

Within the state of equality, even the names of "sentient beings" and "Buddhas" do not exist. Therefore, it is said that as for those who speak of names, these are the empty characteristics of all phenomena—neither arising nor...
Cessation. Neither defiled nor pure. Furthermore, there is no old age and death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death. There is no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path;

there are no Four Noble Truths. There is neither wisdom nor attainment. Only then can one be called a Bodhisattva. (This next section clarifies the Dharma realized; only then does one see that Perfect Enlightenment possesses the power to shatter delusion and open the way to awakening.)
"Good son, this Bodhisattva and the sentient beings of the final age... [up to] 'are manifested by the awakening within boundless empty space.

This clarifies the assembly of those who are the primary recipients of the teaching. As for "sentient beings of the final age," it refers to those far into the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, specifically during the latter five hundred years.

Those who thus cultivate Perfect Enlightenment (Vajraśekhara) will achieve success in their contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Although sentient beings are immersed in delusion, they are like an ancient mirror.
When unpolished, the nature of awakening is not manifest. Now, by employing perfect contemplation to illuminate the aspect of awakening, the object and the contemplation operate in tandem;

it is like a mirror becoming bright when its grime is removed. Thus, the ten realms and three thousand worlds appear simultaneously. Furthermore, one must know that the mirror of the mind is fundamentally luminous.

The three thousandfold nature-virtues are fundamentally complete; it is simply that perfect enlightenment has not yet been manifested, as they are shrouded by the dust and grime of the three delusions.
Now that the dust has been removed, both [the subject and object] vanish together, and the illusory samādhi manifests before one. This arises entirely from the inherent nature.
Upon reaching this state, all dharmas are pure in every respect; what location or direction could there be? Therefore, it is called "pure and without direction. Thus said the Buddha.

The *Zhengzong Ding* (Topical Outline) states: "The empty space of the ten directions arises within my mind; therefore, it is called 'boundless empty space. Because object and wisdom are fused as one, it is called 'that which is manifested by awakening.
'Awakening' refers to contemplation (*guan*); 'that which' refers to the object (*jing*). 'Manifested' means the mutual resonance of the Way between subject and object.
The *Zhiyao* (Essential Points) states: "The three thousand worlds of every stage are without separation; they are all perfectly complete with a single thought-moment. [This is] the Buddha..."

Since the three thousand worlds have already been fused, they are fully present within every single atom; how much more so for the Buddha within the mind that generates [sentient beings], and the sentient beings within the mind to which the Buddha responds?
If the essence of this resonance and response is identical, how could there be any distinction between the provisional and the ultimate benefits?
Therefore, it is said: "He transforms only Bodhisattvas and not those of the Two Vehicles. Yet, among those who hear the Dharma, there is not one who does not become a Buddha. This is because...

The principle of the perfected realization has been revealed above. Now, turning to the subsequent text, it further takes the three thousand subtle dharmas thus revealed and applies them one by one to form and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, sentient beings and Buddhas, the hundreds of thousands of samādhis, and the immeasurable gates of practice;
each and every one of these is none other than the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhicitta*). In this way, all sentient beings are the very body of Vairocana. One.

All lands are eternally the Land of Constant Quiescent Light; mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction (as clarified below in the section on "Contemplation Perfected through Traversing Dharmas").
Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the purity of the mind is revealed (up to: the nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise).
The wisdom of initial awakening is called "perfectly luminous awakening. When this awakening-wisdom merges with original awakening, it gives rise to the wondrous luminosity of original awakening;
this is called "Perfect Awakening" (*yuanjue*). Perfect Awakening is itself the Buddha. Having already attained Buddhahood, Vairocana...
Vairocana pervades all places. Taking this Vairocana and passing through all phenomena (*dharmas*), one immediately encompasses all phenomena within one's own consciousness-mind.
Looking back at all phenomena, one sees they are created solely by the mind. This present investigation of phenomena is intended to reveal that the mind is all-encompassing.

This "all-encompassing" nature has no separate existence; it is entirely born of conditions. This "arising from conditions" has no separate arising; it is entirely the mind’s all-encompassing nature. Mind...
The mind is inherently complete; as all phenomena are pure, it is said that the mind is revealed as pure. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In the three realms there are no separate dharmas;
they are created solely by this one mind. When the mind is pure, one perceives the purity of objects.

Many sūtras state that "mind-seeing" refers simply to the mind and the eye, as explained previously. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* investigates the location of the mind in seven ways and analyzes its functions in eight ways.

Discriminating views. This sutra also states: "The false and floating mind gives rise to many clever views. The objects of these views belong to form (*rūpa*), and form is itself the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Because the objects are pure, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is pure. The 'floating-dust faculty' refers precisely to the eye."

When practicing the Dharma-cloud [samādhi], the eyes gradually perceive external objects; is this not purity? Since the faculties (*indriya*) are thus purified, how could consciousness (*vijñāna*) not also be pure?
Therefore it is said: "Consciousness is pure. This consciousness is the seventh consciousness, also called the "transmitting consciousness" (*saṃprāpaka-vijñāna*).
This is as the worldly tradition says regarding the transmission of messages. This refers to the pair of mind and sight; therefore, they are explained first.

"The object of hearing" refers to the ear faculty (*śrotra-indriya*); these three factors—the faculty, the object, and consciousness—are pure. "The object of sensation" refers to the body faculty (*kāya-indriya*);

likewise, these three factors—the object, consciousness, and faculty—are pure. The nose, tongue, body, and mind are also all pure; hence it is said, "it is also thus. In the sutra, [this] comes first.

First it speaks of the mind (*citta*), and later it speaks of the intellect (*manas*); mind and intellect are one and the same. To perceive touch is the body (*kāya*). These two [faculties] appear together;
the Buddha’s compassion is thus earnest and profound. As above, the enumeration of the six sense organs is completed (next follows the enumeration of the purity of the six sense objects).

"Good son, because the faculties (*indriya*) are pure, the objects of form (*rūpa*) are pure; [this extends] up to and including odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*), which are likewise so.
These six objects are also called the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), because they are the domains traversed by consciousness. They are also named the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*);
'object' (*viṣaya*) takes the sense of defiling, for they are able to defile the emotional consciousnesses. Thus, they are collectively termed 'objects. When they are in the eye, they are called..."
Form [is perceived] by the eye; what is in the ear is called sound; in the nose, smell; in the tongue, taste; in the body, touch; and in the mind, phenomena (*dharma*).
Phenomena are the mind itself, for it takes all dharmas as its objects through conceptualization. These six sensory objects have the great power to lead people into the evil realms.
Great practitioners, whether monastics or laypeople, must guard against them with vigilance, just as one would guard against a domestic thief—namely, greed.
As for those whose desire is intense, one should for the time being allow them to follow their inclination. It is like a wheel used for fishing:
if the fish is strong and the line is weak, one must not pull it forcibly. Once the bait has entered its mouth, whether the fish is near or far, it will be caught before long.
Cultivating contemplation amidst the defilements is also like this. For example, when the Buddha was in the world, even laypeople all attained the fruits of the Path, such as Aṅgulimāla.
Māra, Miśrakēśī, Queen Māllikā—these took only the abstinence from alcohol as their precept. Vāsukī practiced celibacy while engaging in sexual intercourse;
Devadatta transformed his wrong views into right ones. One should know that evil does not obstruct the Path, provided it is employed with the proper method.
The Patriarch said: "Those who revile the five desires do so because they view them as obstacles to the Path. Now, this sutra examines each of these cases one by one.
These six sensory objects are all Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). Brothels, taverns, willow-lined alleys, and flower-strewn streets are all the nature of awakening.
Form itself is not delusive; it is only that people are themselves deluded by it. Wine has no intention to intoxicate people; it is people who intoxicate themselves with it.
Sages view such things as venomous snakes—Sūyī washed his ears, and Cháo Fù used them to water his oxen. Even the former sages held them in such disdain.
"I fear sounds and forms; why should I alone not fear them? Thus the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
'One who is not attached to form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena'—how excellent those words are! (Next, he proceeds through the four great elements.)
"Good son, because the six sense objects are pure... (up to) the fire element and wind element are likewise so.

This refers to the statement that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of one person pervade all places, as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. In the households of Western India, it is said: [text continues].
At noon, there was no fire. He took fire using a *yangsui* (a sun-stone or fire-mirror). First, he held the mirror in his hand and placed tinder before it, facing the sun.
In a short while, fire spontaneously emerged. Now, investigating the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is also like this:
does the fire descend from the sky, arise from the tinder, or emerge from the mirror?
If it had descended from heaven, there would have to have been a trail of fire leading from the palace. If it had been produced from tinder, tinder is a thing of the wild paths;
one does not see fire being produced in the wilderness. If it had emerged from a mirror, before the fire was taken [from it], [the mirror] would have been hot.
The mirror is on the stand; the fire is not seen arising. Thus it exists through the combination of causes and conditions.
When the mirror, the tinder, and the sun—these three—are each separate and not in combination, the fire does not arise. "Condition" refers to dependent origination; within this dependent origination:

It possesses the nature of fire. Regarding the three—mirror, moxa, and sun—if there is a distinction between them, although each possesses its own inherent nature, fire will not be produced when the conditions do not coincide.
By this analogy, if the power of the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*) is absent, the dust [of afflictions] will never be eliminated.

When one employs the illumination of Perfect Enlightenment, this is what is meant by "arising through conditions. Through the harmony of causes and conditions, the dust is eliminated and enlightenment becomes perfect; thus, it arises.
The passions of death are exhausted (next, one traverses the dharmas of sentient beings; this concerns the primary and secondary bodies, and applies to many people).
Good son, because the four great elements are pure, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the twenty-five states of existence are pure.

This sequence of sentient beings’ phenomena—the four great elements, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the twenty-five states of existence—consists of the four continents, the four evil destinies, the six heavens of the desire realm, the Brahma heavens, the heavens of the four dhyānas, the heavens of the four formless attainments, the heaven of non-conceptualization, and the heaven of the non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
Each possesses its own realms, bases, faculties, and objects. Yet, the deluded consciousness of a single person enters like a moth into a painted bottle.
The "Chapter on Emptiness" states: "That mind dwells everywhere, constantly residing within the various sense faculties. It is like a bird cast into a net.

For example, in the time of the Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who sat in meditation beneath a tree for twelve years; yet his mind remained attached to the six sensory objects, and he was unable to attain awakening.
The Buddha manifested as a monk and stayed with him under the same tree that evening. Suddenly, a turtle emerged from the river.
Gradually they reached the side of the road, where a wild dog was attacking a tortoise. The tortoise had withdrawn its six limbs into its shell, so the dog could find no opening and departed.
The tortoise then entered the water. The Buddha asked the bhikṣu, "Did you see that? He replied, "I saw it. "What did you see? "I saw the tortoise withdraw its six limbs to preserve its life.
The Buddha said, "For twelve years, you have been greedily attached to odors, flavors, and tactile sensations, clinging to objects of perception."
"Dust-like sensory objects cannot lead one into the Way; rather, they are not even like the tortoise, which is able to hide its limbs. To realize one's nature is to transcend the ordinary.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu attained the fruit of Arhatship. (Next, the purity of the Buddha-dharma’s phenomenal and noumenal environments is elucidated.)
Because they are pure, the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and so forth, up to the doors of dhāraṇī, are all completely pure.

As for the ten powers: first, the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*); second, the power of karma; third, the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); fourth, the power of the faculties (*indriya*);

fifth, the power of inclinations (*adhimukti*); sixth, the power of dispositions (*dhātu*); seventh, the power of the path leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*); eighth, the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*); ninth, the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-jñānabala*); tenth, the power regarding the [exhaustion of] outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñānabala*).

Exerting one's full effort. The four fearlessnesses are: first, fearlessness regarding knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of obstacles to the path;
and fourth, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of the path leading to the end of suffering. The four unhindered knowledges are: first, the unhindered knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*);

second, the unhindered knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); third, the unhindered knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and fourth, the unhindered knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of wisdom: first, no failure in physical action; second, no failure in verbal expression; third, no failure in mindfulness;
fourth, no divergent thoughts; fifth, no lack of concentration; sixth, no relinquishing without full awareness; seventh, no decline in aspiration.
Eight, no decrease in vigor; nine, no decrease in mindfulness; ten, no decrease in wisdom; eleven, no decrease in liberation;
twelve, no decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation; thirteen, all bodily actions follow wisdom;
fourteen, all verbal actions follow wisdom; fifteen, all mental actions follow wisdom.
Sixteenth, wisdom that knows the past without obstruction. Seventeenth, wisdom that knows the future without obstruction.

Eighteenth, wisdom that knows the present without obstruction. As for the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), they are the categories according to the depth of one’s entry into the Path.

The four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*): (1) mindfulness of the body; (2) mindfulness of sensation; (3) mindfulness of the mind; (4) mindfulness of phenomena. The four right [efforts]...

Diligence: (1) diligence and exertion to eliminate unwholesome states that have already arisen; (2) diligence and exertion to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising; (3) diligence and exertion to produce wholesome states that have not yet arisen; (4) diligence and exertion to increase wholesome states that have already arisen.

The Four Bases of Psychic Power (*ṛddhipāda*): (1) the base of psychic power consisting of desire; (2) the base of psychic power consisting of energy; (3) the base of psychic power consisting of mind;

(4) the base of psychic power consisting of investigation. The Five Faculties (*indriya*): (1) the faculty of faith; (2) the faculty of energy; (3) the faculty of mindfulness; (4) the faculty of concentration; (5) the faculty of wisdom. The Five Powers (*bala*): These are the aforementioned five faculties when they have increased to the point where they can overcome wrong beliefs and afflictions, and overcome laziness.

It is called "power" because it destroys wrong thoughts, destroys distracted conceptions, and obstructs the afflictions of views and mental objects. (7) The Seven Factors of Enlightenment: (1) the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena; (2) the factor of enlightenment of energy; (3) the factor of enlightenment of joy; (4) the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; [5] the factor of enlightenment of concentration; [6] the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; [7] the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.

5. The awakening factor of equanimity; 6. The awakening factor of concentration; 7. The awakening factor of mindfulness. 8. The Noble Eightfold Path: (1) Right View; (2) Right Intention; (3) Right Speech; (4) Right Action; (5) Right Livelihood; (6) Right Effort.

(7) Right Mindfulness; (8) Right Concentration). There are eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates in their full extent. (Guifeng said: "Since there are eighty-four thousand afflictions, each has its corresponding antidote, which is a pure dharma.
Thus, the number of defilements and purities neither increases nor decreases. In the intermediate exposition, there are five hundred; in the abbreviated exposition, there are three kinds.
There is the *āvartadhāraṇī*; there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *āvartadhāraṇīs*; and there is the *dharmaghoṣopāyāvartadhāraṇī*.
All these have the meaning of "obstructing and upholding": they obstruct evil and uphold the good, just as a complete vessel holds water without leaking.

This Dharma-gate enters into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) all at once and is purified. (Next, having clarified the realization of the true mark [dharmatā], one ascends to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva in Perfect Enlightenment.

One manifests as a Buddha in a hundred worlds and traverses all phenomena, which are entirely pure. How much more so for the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). It is like a person entering the ocean: they enter gradually and become increasingly deep. Only at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) is the Way exhausted and the position ultimate.

One manifests as a Buddha in four thousand two hundred worlds and traverses inexhaustible phenomena. The various intermediate positions are realized in succession; these may be understood from what follows).
"Good son, because the nature of all true marks (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is pure, [it extends] to the perfect enlightenment and purity of sentient beings in the ten directions.

This refers first to a Bodhisattva who has ascended to the first stage of the Perfect [Enlightenment] (*yuanju*), having shattered one grade of ignorance and realized one portion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
These three virtues are precisely the true mark. Having realized the true mark, this Bodhisattva manifests a hundred bodies throughout a hundred worlds to act as Buddhas.
How could it be limited to one body or many bodies? Even all sentient beings throughout the ten directions enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
Being perfectly pure and luminous, they proceed through the forty-two stages up to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-avabodha*). Their emanated bodies cannot be conceived by the mind;

these are the Buddha’s primary retribution (*pradhāna-vipāka*), for this is the body of primary retribution. This is because the body experiences all phenomena. (The following clarifies that Bodhisattvas experience the secondary retribution (*upādāya-vipāka*), namely mountains, rivers, and so forth.)
The great earth, grasses, trees, and the myriad phenomena of the universe—all these are dharmas.
Son of good family, because one world is pure, [it extends] until all things are equally pure and immovable.
A Bodhisattva in the first stage manifests as a Buddha in a hundred worlds; how could he merely encompass the three periods of time?
Such is the power and function of this Sage: when a fire breaks out across a trichiliocosm, he can extinguish it with a single spittle;
when a trichiliocosm is swept away into emptiness, he can restore it with a single breath. He casts the great chiliocosm beyond the four quarters and swallows the myriad phenomena within his breast.
To swallow the waters of the great ocean with a single hair-tip without disturbing the dragons and fish, and to hide Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed without harming the trees—thus it is said:

"Pure and unmoving. (Below this, the intermediate stages are further clarified: from the stage of practice through the forty-one levels up to Equal Enlightenment, where ignorance is not yet exhausted;

as the positions gradually deepen and the traversed dharmas increasingly expand, one proceeds until reaching Subtle Enlightenment, where one universally pervades the Dharma-realm. This cannot be fathomed by the mind.)
"Good son, just as space is thus equal and immovable... (up to) you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable.

This is the ultimate consummation of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]. Originally there are no stages or positions; it is only in accordance with the shallowness or depth of what is realized that its gradations are established.

For now, we shall follow the Perfect Teaching from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the forty-one intermediate stages, wherein the contemplation is perfected and one traverses the dharmas, encompassing all things."
The Dharma leaves nothing out; it does not arise from outside the mind. Regarding the equality and immovability of the nature of space and the nature of awakening, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The space of the ten directions arises within your own mind, like a single cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky.
Since the Buddha-lands and worlds of the ten directions exist within space, and space itself resides within my mind, how much more so the Buddha-lands?
The world—how could it not reside within my mind? My mind is unmoving; the nature of empty space is also unmoving.
As empty space is unmoving, the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are also unmoving. The body is unmoving, the mind is unmoving, and both the primary and secondary retributions are unmoving.
This non-movement is eternal abiding, without transition or change; every dharma is suchness. It is said:
The quiescent mark of all these dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words. This nature of immovability is not made immovable through artificial effort;
rather, the nature of awakening is inherently and naturally unmoving. Within the emptiness of its original nature, there is spontaneously no mark of movement.

The four great elements are immovable and do not emerge as the retributive environment. Constantly knowing this nature of awakening is precisely the nature of Perfect Awakening—it is neither moving nor non-moving.

Movement: it is the movement of non-movement; it is movement for the sake of [the unmoving]. This nature of non-movement encompasses the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates, all of which return to the nature of non-movement.
It is neither expansive nor narrow; it is eternally abiding and profoundly still. Its nature is inherently pure;
it is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). (Next, the wondrous enlightenment of ultimate realization is clarified by traversing all phenomena.)
"Good son, the nature of awakening is all-pervading, pure, and immovable... (up to) the dharani-gates pervade the Dharma-realm.
This is wondrous awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the ultimate fruition-awakening. Because it traverses all dharmas, it is said to be 'all-pervading.
Furthermore, as the forty-one intermediate stages have not yet reached completion, they are not called 'full. Wondrous awakening is like the moon on the fifteenth night; its orb is already—"

It is completely filled; there is no longer any false radiance. This is what all Buddhas have realized: they realize the faculties and sense objects of all sentient beings, as well as their seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
The Buddha is precisely the sentient being, and the sentient being is precisely the Buddha. How much more so for the gateway of dhāraṇī—how could it not be all-pervasive?
One must know that the eighty-four thousand afflictions are themselves the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma, and are also the eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence.
The dependent appears within the absolute, and the absolute appears within the dependent. Upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests a jewel-king land;
seated within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Wheel of Dharma. Is this not the Great Sage traversing all dharmas? Or...

If you say this is not so, the following passage states: "That wondrous enlightened nature. Since it refers to "that," it points back to the preceding scriptural text concerning the passage through the stages of wondrous enlightenment.
Beyond the word "passing" (*guò*), there is no character for "tea" (*chá*). Upon entering the stage of wondrous enlightenment from the final mind of the *Vajra* [stage], what is realized is ultimate;
all is pure. The Dharma-realm encompasses all, being fundamentally devoid of form or appearance. What further existence could there be for coming and going?

Therefore, the subsequent passage explicitly states "wondrous enlightenment" (and explains it again later): the wondrously enlightened sage has realized the ultimate limit and, by tracing back to the source, exhausts the characteristics of self-nature; these are precisely the nature and characteristics of the world, which are neither destroyed nor mixed.
It is a single dharma.
Good son, because that wondrous enlightened nature is all-pervasive, [it extends] to the gates of *dhāraṇī*, which are indestructible and unmixed.

What is called "wondrous enlightenment" (*myōkaku*) is precisely "original enlightenment" (*honkaku*). Original enlightenment is what was seen previously: the nature-virtue (*shōtoku*) within a single thought-moment of sentient beings. This...
The nature is precisely the nature of original enlightenment, like ice and water; these two are non-dual.

This nature is perfectly interfused and pervades within the faculties and objects of all sentient beings, being neither destroyed nor mixed. As for "neither destroyed," how could one destroy one faculty and separately grasp another?
It is only because people today have emotions that obstruct their wisdom and fail to achieve integration; thus they perceive birth and death.
For a Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths, the six sense organs are already pure, and this unfabricated physical body is itself the Dharma-body. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"The eyes born of one's parents see the three thousandfold world system; the ears born of one's parents hear the sounds of the three thousand great thousandfold world systems."
The Dragon Girl was none other than this very physical body born of her parents, yet she immediately went on to attain Buddhahood.

When the Great Master Zhiyi awakened to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he beheld Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as if it were still present and had not dispersed; these were all instances of the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), which can thus be considered indestructible.
As for those that are "unmixed," they are like the human eye and ear, which do not exceed one or two inches in size and each maintains its own distinct domain; the eye alone...
The eye can see, but cannot hear; the ear can hear, but cannot see. It is the same for the nose, tongue, body, and mind, each being thus.

Although they are interconnected internally, they are always separated externally; this may be called "non-intermixture. Just as pine trees are straight and thorns are curved, or crows are black and cranes are white, these too do not intermingle.
While one must understand that they are neither destroyed nor intermingled, one must also know that they are both destroyed and intermingled. This is because the Buddha...
Within the Dharma, that which is non-characteristic is taken as the characteristic; therefore, all that possesses characteristics is entirely false and illusory.
One should know that the gate of dhāraṇī both obstructs evil and maintains goodness. Now, in discussing good and evil, they are neither destroyed nor mixed.
Evil is indestructible because it is the nature of evil. The nature of evil is like water; the nature of good is like ice.
If the nature of evil were removed, from what would the universal manifestation of the form-bodies of all Buddhas arise? If one removes the water, there is no ice.
By this, one knows that the nature of evil is not severed. Although the *dhāraṇī* is said to "obstruct" evil, evil is itself good; what evil could there be?
Although evil is not severed, good and evil are naturally distinct; there is neither destruction nor confusion.
Just as the spring breeze knows no high or low, yet the flower branches are naturally long or short, so too, even worldly illusions can manifest both non-existence and existence.
How much more so the true art of illusion realized by the Great Sage? When illusory existence prevails, it constitutes all phenomena; when illusory non-existence prevails, [all phenomena vanish].
All phenomena are empty of characteristics; being empty yet not empty, they are called "empty. Being existent yet not existent, they are called "existent.

One should know that when the mind arises, phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, phenomena cease. If Master Lü could even take a pinch of earth and fashion it into incense, how much more so can the Buddha?
It can melt the Five Peaks and dry up the Four Seas; it exhausts the events of immeasurable kalpas—how could this be fathomed by an ordinary mind?
(The following provides an analogy:
It is like hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminating a single room; their light fills the space entirely, neither obstructed nor intermingled.

In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, an altar is established, surrounded by ten mirrors with a single lamp burning at its center. The forms of the lamps interpenetrate one another such that their orientations cannot be distinguished;
how much more so when the light of hundreds or thousands of lamps illuminates a single room? Although there are hundreds or thousands of lamps, their light returns to oneness.
Just as the light from those ten mirrors returns to oneness, so too does the nature of wondrous enlightenment pervade the sense organs and their objects; the nature of the sense organs...
The nature of the sense objects is entirely the nature of awakening. Because the nature of awakening is all-pervasive, the natures of the faculties and the sense objects are likewise pervasive.
Since the gates of *dhāraṇī* are neither destroyed nor confused, it is said, "it is also thus. An ancient said: "The mirror and the lamp—the lamp and the mirror are fundamentally without difference.
The great earth, mountains, and rivers are flowers before the eyes; yellow leaves flutter, filling the courtyard, yet one does not know the sound of the mortar and pestle."
In whose house does it fall? People know only that Buddha-nature is all-pervasive; they do not realize that one’s own nature (svabhāva) is all-pervasive.
Do you wish to know how one’s own nature is all-pervasive? When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. Do not go about the world discriminating between right and wrong.

(Next, it clarifies that since all phenomena are pervasive, they are equal: there is nothing to cultivate and nothing to realize; there is neither birth nor Buddha. There is a teaching, and there is an analogy.)
"Good son, because of the accomplishment of awakening... (up to) why? Because all is awakening. The accomplishment of awakening refers to the person who has attained the fruit (*phala-pudgala*).
Since that which is realized by wondrous awakening is ultimate, when one contemplates all phenomena of the world, there is neither agent nor object, neither bondage nor liberation.
One should know that 'Bodhisattva' refers to the person who is on the path (*pratipannaka-pudgala*). Although the Bodhisattva..."
Abiding in the stage of the ground, one also understands that the mind is empty and pervasive, and perceives the source of all dharmas as being neither defiled nor pure, neither bound nor liberated.
Furthermore, such a bodhisattva neither loathes birth-and-death nor craves nirvana. As the *Buddhāvatamsaka* states:
"Though not yet having attained deliverance oneself, one first desires to deliver others. This is the bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva awakens the mind, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday.

Because they are like a dream from yesterday, whether one maintains the precepts or violates them, whether one is a beginner or has practiced for a long time, one gives rise to neither hatred nor attachment. As the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā* states:
"The pure practitioner does not enter nirvāṇa; the bhikṣu who commits a grave offense does not enter hell. Why? Because all is awakened. This...
Regarding the person as cause and the person as effect, all dharmas are equal; there is neither cultivation nor realization. (The following provides an analogy:
It is like the light of the eye clearly perceiving objects before it... [until] ...because the substance of the light is non-dual and free from both aversion and affection.
This is merely taking up the light of the eyes. When it illuminates an object before one, the light simply gazes directly at that thing without yet distinguishing between aversion and affection;
for aversion and affection arise from the human mind. Now, when we take up the light as it illuminates an object, it does not distinguish between aversion and affection.
If it were to distinguish between aversion and affection, it would illuminate those things dear to me and obscure those things I loathe. Since the light is neither...
Affection. Things are also divided into two. Now I shall use light as a metaphor. The Bodhisattva’s mind is impartial;

regarding all phenomena, it is complete, neither deficient nor excessive, neither heavy nor light, neither disparaging nor praising. Maitreya said: "A single bowl for a thousand households' rice; a solitary body wandering ten thousand miles.
No one casts the 'blue or white eyes' [of disdain or favor] upon me as I ask the way at the head of the white clouds. (Next, the explanation follows.)
The realized and accomplished dharmas are beyond the four propositions and cut off the hundred negations).
Good son, for this bodhisattva and for sentient beings of the final age, [from] birth-and-death to nirvana, it is all like a dream from yesterday.

This clarifies that for the Bodhisattva, when their merit is perfected and the Way is realized, the dharmas they realize and the dharmas they accomplish are free from intrinsic nature and devoid of negation.
They see the fundamental source of nature and penetrate the dharma-realm of nature. It does not arise from the mind, nor does it enter from without;
therefore, it is neither cultivated nor realized, neither identical nor separate, neither bound nor liberated. Although Buddhas appear in the world and disappear from it...
Like sparks from stone or a flash of lightning, though possessing the Brahma-voice, their speech is like gold needles and jade thread.
The worlds of all Buddhas arise and perish in disorder, like flowers in the sky; birth-and-death and nirvana are both like a dream from yesterday.

It may be said that the Buddha is the sentient being, and the sentient being is the Buddha; how could one not realize from the beginning that one is originally a Buddha? (The following clarifies the time of realization; although it is...)
A dream: upon waking, it is ultimately non-existent. Although the events of the dream appear vividly, they leave no real trace (as will be further illustrated below).
Good son, because it is like a dream from yesterday, the nature of all phenomena is equal and indestructible.
Gautama, in the end, out of his profound and compassionate concern, attempts to exchange the Dharma he himself has realized for the contrary minds of sentient beings;
it is much like conducting a transaction within a dream, bartering gold for that person’s stubborn iron.
Although one knows the relative value of things while exchanging them, upon awakening, one realizes that both objects and persons—whether noble or base—are all matters of a dream.
One should know that regarding birth-and-death and nirvana, they may be attained through grasping, or they may be attained without grasping;

for since these exist within a dream, they are not truly subject to arising and ceasing, or coming and going. That which is realized is likewise like a dream; it is merely a point attained [within the dream].

The art of transmuting iron into gold was indeed realized within a dream; yet dream-events are not real. Gain and loss, acceptance and rejection—all are unattainable. Though unattainable, the dream-event remains vividly present. That which can realize this is precisely contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*), not calm abiding (*śamatha*). How could the sublime contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*) fail to realize it? As for the art of alchemy: [The text continues with verses: "Though the substance is transformed, the name remains as before; Though the name is changed, the substance does not perish. If one seeks the substance through the name, the substance cannot be found; If one seeks the name through the substance, the name cannot be grasped. If both substance and name are abandoned, what is there to be attained? When the mind is free from both attainment and non-attainment, This is called the 'Great Alchemical Elixir. If one practices this elixir, one will surely attain Buddhahood. The "art of transmuting iron into gold" refers to the realization that all phenomena are like dreams. Since dream-events lack inherent reality, the dualities of gain and loss, or acceptance and rejection, are ultimately ungraspable. Yet, despite their ungraspability, the appearances of the dream persist with clarity.

The capacity to witness this state is the wisdom of discernment (*vipaśyanā*), rather than mere meditative quiescence (*śamatha*). Only through the wondrous contemplation of *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*—the Perfect Enlightenment—can this be realized. Regarding the "art of alchemy": although the material is transformed, its designation remains; though the designation changes, the material itself is not destroyed. If one pursues the substance by means of the designation, the substance is not found; if one pursues the designation by means of the substance, the designation cannot be grasped. When both substance and designation are relinquished, what is there to be attained? When the mind is liberated from both attainment and non-attainment, this is termed the "Great Alchemical Elixir. By practicing this elixir, one shall certainly achieve Buddhahood.
It is not easily attained. Upon awakening, one finds oneself still within the dream; the dream is entirely empty, yet that dream remains vividly present.
Reaching this point, one may act, or one may refrain from acting; one may rest, or one may not rest.
It is the same regarding whether one follows along with it or extinguishes it. To conclude again: within this realization, there is neither subject nor object.
In the end, there is no realization. Since there is neither self nor person, there is likewise no one who realizes.

Now I ask: who is it that realizes? Who is the realizer? To speak of a dream within a dream is neither false nor real. Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*) is like a dream; the dream is itself enlightenment, and enlightenment is itself the dream.
Dream and enlightenment are empty; in emptiness, there is no mark of emptiness. Yongjia said: "Within the darkness of a dream, there is..."

"The six realms of existence—upon awakening, they are all empty, and there is no great trichiliocosm. This is what is meant by that. (This concludes the response to what was asked regarding Universal Vision.
"Good son, when those bodhisattvas practice in this way... [up to] ...they seek such a Dharma and yet do not become confused or distressed."
To conclude: that which was asked regarding contemplation and abiding is entirely the path of correct practice. While practicing, perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) is not absent;

yet after awakening, even perfect enlightenment is non-existent. At the time of realization, one speaks of sentient beings and Buddhas; yet upon realizing the truth, both beings and Buddhas are seen to be empty.
To awaken to these as flowers in the sky—wherein even these "flowers in the sky" are themselves within awakening—is to practice in such a way that one will certainly not be deluded.
[The Explanatory Verse] (The second section of verses).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

This verse truly demonstrates through non-explanation; for within the absence of combination, one seeks combination, and thus there arise the four great elements and the six sense objects—the union of the noble and the ordinary.

The Chapter of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva:

Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, in response to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the Tathāgata’s original arising and the mind of awakening on the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), sought to ensure that its essential nature corresponded with the names of the eternally abiding fruit-position (*phala-sthāna*). These are namely: bodhi, nirvāṇa, *tathatā*, buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and *amala* [consciousness].

The *ālaya-vijñāna*, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), and so forth—these are the awakening of the causal stage and the *garbha*-nature of the resultant stage.
They are mutually inclusive and mutually penetrating; ignorance (*avidyā*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are fundamentally non-dual.

Therefore, the Vajragarbha Bodhisattva uses delusion to praise awakening, uses phenomena to challenge principle, uses causes to challenge results, and uses birth to challenge Buddhahood. This is the intent of his coming.
Thus, within this great assembly, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva— from the point where [the text says] "the illusory cataracts are cleared away and the eye of wisdom is pure"—
