until the initial opening of enlightenment— must first explain the origins and the path traversed, as well as request the formal methods and rituals, just as was done previously.
Commentary:

Regarding the World-Honored One’s [teaching] from "If all sentient beings have been originally enlightened" up to "when would they again give rise to all afflictions," these three doubts arise because, upon hearing the Chapter on the Universal Eye, one first realizes that sentient beings have been originally enlightened. Out of compassion...
Master Shi said: "To become a Buddha means that 'Buddha' is awakening (*bodhi*). That 'all ignorance' refers to non-awakening (*abodhi*).
Awakening and non-awakening cannot coexist. Since sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, and a Buddha is awakening, why is it said that they again fall into non-awakening?
This is the first doubt. Furthermore, if ignorance were originally existent, there would be no..."
If clarity is non-awakening (*abodha*), how can it further be said that "sentient beings are fundamentally already Buddhas"?

Since a Buddha is awakening, to say they are "fundamentally Buddhas" and yet to say they are "fundamentally ignorant" (*avidyā*)—for ignorance and Buddhahood cannot be spoken of as coexisting—is the second doubt.
This refers, for now, to a single person who possesses both awakening and non-awakening; the subsequent doubt concerns the ten dharmas.
Regarding the sentient beings of the realms: the ten directions are themselves the ten realms.

If the various beings of the ten dharma-realms—from the Buddhas at the beginning down to those in the hells—were originally already enlightened as Buddhas, for what reason would they later again give rise to ignorance?
When would all Tathāgatas ever be born again? When would all afflictions [ever arise]? This is the third doubt. Now, this is separately excerpted from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
In the sutra, Pūrṇa also poses this question, which is largely the same as this one. The meaning is as stated in that sutra:
"World-Honored One, if all the world’s faculties, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements are the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamentally so..."
"How is it that the mountains, rivers, and great earth, along with all conditioned phenomena, suddenly arise, undergoing a sequential flux that ends only to begin again?

Pūrṇa (also known as Maitreya-putra) asked again: "If this wondrous enlightenment—the fundamentally wondrous, enlightened clarity—is neither increased nor diminished from the mind of the Tathāgata, how can it be said that these mountains, rivers, and great earth, along with all conditioned phenomena, have suddenly arisen without cause?"

[These] constitute characteristics. (Being "without state" means being without cause. Now that the Tathāgata has attained wondrous, empty, luminous awakening, when could the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena ever arise again?
If this wondrous awakening were originally wondrously luminous awakening, it would be identical to the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.
Neither increasing nor decreasing. Vajragarbha said: "The ordinary beings of the ten directions are fundamentally identical in their attainment of the Buddha-way.
Vajragarbha said: "They again give rise to ignorance. Pūrṇa said: "Without cause, they suddenly produce the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth;
these are identical. Vajragarbha replied: "When would the Tathāgata ever again give rise to all afflictions? Pūrṇa—
That [text] says: "The Tathāgata has now attained 'wondrous, empty, luminous enlightenment' and so forth. These are the same, yet there is this distinction:
that which was asked by Vajragarbha pertains solely to the cause, whereas that which was asked by Pūrṇa pertains to both cause and effect. (Next, the general explanation follows.)
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will not abandon his unconditioned great compassion" (up to) "beginning again from the end" (next, the World-Honored One instructs him to listen).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying (up to) "listen in silence" (next, the formal answer to the three doubts).
"Good son, for all worlds from their beginning to their end, through birth and cessation—up to the point that it would be impossible to escape saṃsāra.
Because of the preceding passage concerning sentient beings being originally enlightened as Buddhas, Vajragarbha then raised three doubts.

The Buddha now answers this. For the time being, he speaks from the perspective of immediate phenomena, thus saying: "From beginning to end there is arising and ceasing; before and after there is existence and non-existence; gathering and dispersing, starting and stopping.

This refers to the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), extending downward as far as the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*). The wind drives the water, the water drives the fire, and the fire drives the gold, thereby establishing the world.
As for the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), it refers to the physical bodies of worldly people, composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The five aggregates, the six sense organs, objects, and entrances, extending upward to the Buddhas and downward to the hells—all these constitute the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
These two worlds—the sentient and the insentient—are also termed the "two retributions" of the primary and the secondary. They have a beginning and an end;
they possess arising and ceasing, priority and posteriority, existence and non-existence, aggregation and dispersion, and commencement and cessation. Thus, these six pairs arise.

Regarding the realm of cessation: though moments of consciousness continue in succession with various acts of grasping and rejecting, when examined through the ultimate principle, these are all simply the beginningless ignorance and karmic consciousness of sentient beings.
As long as this ignorance has not been shattered, one follows the cycle of karma, wandering from birth to birth and death to death without respite.

If one seeks to discern Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra) by means of this incessant mind, then that Perfect Enlightenment— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content up to the point of interruption.]
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, it continues to transform without ceasing (next, using the analogy of still water, the revolving fire, the moving moon, and the shifting shore).
For example, as the movement of the eyes can cause still water to appear to shake, so too is it when a boat moves and the shore appears to shift.

The moving eyes and the fixed gaze; the rushing clouds and the sailing boat—these four are metaphors for deluded movement. Water, fire, the moon, and the shore—these four are analogies for the true nature.

The "True" refers to Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*); the "Deluded" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). As long as the karmic consciousness of ignorance has not been severed, [delusion persists].
When Perfect Enlightenment follows delusion, it turns into confusion and becomes sentient beings. To break this ignorance and the karma of consciousness constitutes awakening;
thus, the non-awakening of ignorance turns into awakening. All of these are the karma of the consciousness of ignorance, which successively alternate with one another.
"Entering the sea to count its sands—if this were not a direct approach, when would it ever be finished? (This second response clarifies the intent behind the two metaphors of Dharma and the knot.
"Good son, while the various revolutions have not yet ceased, those objects remain as they were; therefore, you have given rise to three kinds of delusion."

Regarding the claim that "those things abide from the beginning," the interpretations of various masters do not exhaust the meaning. This teaching concerns the birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
Furthermore, while the two vehicles abide in the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this *tathatā* (suchness) is like brass—it is not true gold.

Moreover, because their ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted, even Bodhisattvas who have reached the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksaṃbodhi*)—being near to the Truth and second only to the Sage—must still enter the gate of the profound mystery (*chong-hyeon*).
To practice all things in a perverted manner is like the "cloth bag" of Fenggan, Hanshan, and Shide; these were all cases of practicing all things in a perverted way.
If one were to break down the forty-two grades of ignorance stage by stage, those objects would likewise abide in their respective stages beforehand.
Since true reality is not yet fully realized, even metaphors cannot be found, let alone the delusions of view and thought possessed by ordinary sentient beings.

Without having severed even a hair’s breadth [of delusion], they constantly dwell in confusion and distress. Their ignorance and karmic consciousness are like great stones pressing down upon the grass;
yet they seek to manifest Perfect Enlightenment. Those who claim to be "good spiritual friends" today have not yet set foot on solid ground;

having attained but a small measure of knowledge and views, they give rise to arrogance, reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs—this may truly be called "creating one's own calamity. Such people are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.

It is like reeds. Those things that existed previously are also the mind’s realization of emptiness and penetration; yet, as one has not yet entered the stages of practice (*bhūmi*), it is also the Bodhisattva acting to resolve obstructions.
For example, there was once an Arhat in Western India who visited the home of a lay family.

Seeing that the father’s instruction of his son was ineffective and that he continued to beat and scold him incessantly, the Venerable One laughed aloud. The man asked, "Bhikṣu, you have compassion as your concern; why do you look at me [and laugh]?"
"Beating your child—will this not only bring you ridicule? He asked, "Why did you beat your child? He replied, "I was teaching him the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*, but he was not proficient.
[The master] asked, "Who composed that treatise? He replied, "It was composed by an ancient ṛṣi. [The master] asked, "Is the ṛṣi still here? He replied, "He is no longer here."
"Since he is not [a true disciple], what benefit is there in striking him? The Venerable One said, "This very son of yours is himself a rishi.

It was he who created him. [The other] asked, "Why do you teach him that which is not beneficial? [The Venerable One] replied, "From a mind of false conceptualization, a modicum of cleverness arises."
All belong to the realm of delusion. It is like a person living in a dark room who has not yet restored the light of a lamp;
the entire room is filled with darkness. Suddenly obtaining the light of a lamp, the interior briefly becomes bright. When the oil is exhausted and the lamp goes out, the darkness returns.
Have you not heard that long ago, on the shore of the Southern Sea, there was a withered tree in which five hundred bats lived in a hollow? Suddenly, five or six men [arrived].
He stayed overnight beneath a tree. At that time, it was the cold of winter; he gathered firewood and sat by the fire.
Among them was one man reciting the *Abhidharma* (translated as "Incomparable Dharma") with a deep and far-reaching Brahma-voice. Five hundred bats listened intently, delighting in the sound.
Suddenly, smoke and flames erupted from the treetop, and the five hundred bats were trapped and killed by the fire. Their spirits were reborn in a certain land as...
The five hundred men who left the household life and realized arhatship—the authors of the Mahāvibhāṣā Śāstra—were none other than those five hundred bats;
I, this poor monk, was among them. My learning has not reached the nature of reality, nor have I destroyed ignorance;
thus I still fall into birth and death, entering the realm of ignorance. Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a bhikṣu named Nārada who attained the four dhyānas.
This refers to those who, having claimed to have realized the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], fall into the Avīci Hell because they have deceived themselves.

Those who study the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (Complete Enlightenment) must be profoundly discerning and seek the definitive resolution of a virtuous friend; one must not rely on oneself alone. (Previously, the three doubts were answered by means of water, fire, the moon, and the shore; subsequently, the three doubts were again answered by means of two metaphors.
Thus, within each metaphor, all three doubts are addressed. The first was answered by means of the flowers seen by one with cataracts.)
"Good son, it is like an illusory cataract that falsely perceives flowers in the sky... (until) when will all such cataracts ever arise again?

Vajragarbha, [this] uses the cause to question the result, and uses delusion to question awakening; sentient beings are in the state of the cause. If they were originally awakened Buddhas, that would be the result.
Sentient beings are in the state of the cause; if they were already Buddhas, it would be like saying the flower is itself the fruit."
There is a doubt regarding the simultaneity of the garden and the fruit: if one is originally a Buddha, why would there still be all-encompassing ignorance?
Once Buddhahood has been attained, how could one become a sentient being again? Is this not a contradiction?

Furthermore, it is difficult to resolve that if the ignorance of sentient beings is inherently present, for what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further say that they have been originally enlightened as Buddhas, yet are currently sentient beings?

This is precisely the Buddha. Yet, [the practitioner] further increases their delusion. Originally there were only two doubts; because the confusion regarding the True is profound, one must untangle the stickiness and remove the bonds.
Whatever metaphors are used for what is doubted, they are merely illusory cataracts and empty flowers—two things that are alike.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like wildflowers: they do not come from the void, nor do they come from the sun. If they came from the void, since they have already come from the void..."

It returns and enters through emptiness. If there were actual entering and exiting, it would not be empty space. If emptiness were not empty, it could not naturally accommodate the arising and ceasing of these floral manifestations.
If they emerged from the eyes, then having emerged from the eyes, they must also enter back through the eyes;
since these flowers would have emerged from the eyes, they should possess the faculty of vision. If they possessed vision, then as they departed into the empty space of the flowers and returned...
This corresponds to the faculty of sight. If there were no seeing, then as [the cataract] emerges it would obscure space, and as it rotates it would obscure the eye.

Upon investigating its characteristics, there is no substance that constitutes space, nor is there any substance that constitutes the flowers. Space-flowers are fundamentally non-existent; they do not exist now either.

That they appear as space-flowers is due to the eye’s disease causing them to be seen as existing. To eliminate these space-flowers, one must remove the cataract from the eye. Once the cataract has been removed, the space...

Huá said himself: "The metaphors used to speak of the arising of Buddhas are all merely eye diseases. If the cataracts of the eyes are removed, there is neither Buddha nor arising" (this next passage clarifies that the flower and the cataract do not appear simultaneously).

Why is this? Because the two phenomena of the cataract and the flower do not exist in mutual dependence. (Up to: "The wondrous enlightenment of perfect illumination is free from flowers and cataracts.
This clarifies that the cataract arises from the eye itself, while the flower exists from within space itself; these two are each such that they know one another.

If two things were to face one another, one would say they exist in mutual dependence. These two, however, do not exist through mutual dependence. Why is this? Because the flower [arises] from space itself.

The arising [of the flower] is due to a cataract in my eye; it is not something that arises through mutual dependence. Furthermore, empty space was originally devoid of flowers, nor do they arise in dependence upon the cataract.
One may only seek the flower within the cataract; one cannot grasp it from within the empty space. For empty space has never produced a flower from the beginning;
it is only the deluded who, confused by the flower of their own cataract, grasp at the appearance of a flower in empty space.
It is like a thirsty deer that sees a mirage and, thinking it to be water, rushes toward it; in the end, it is not water at all.

Furthermore, one only knows that the flower has vanished, yet fails to recognize that the cataract has been cleared away. Then, regarding the place where the flower vanished, one asks: "After this flower has perished, when will it arise again?
Previously one was merely ignorant; now one’s ignorance is even more profound. Thus one asks: "When will these empty flowers arise again? This is the cataract.
It is within the eye; one need only remove the cataracts of the eye and need not ask about the flower.

One need only destroy ignorance and exhaust karmic deeds, and the Buddha-way will manifest before you and Perfect Enlightenment will naturally appear—there is likewise no need to ask. Now that you have already attained Buddhahood, when will you ever again become a sentient being?

Ignorance arises again; as the flower blooms and the flower withers, it merely obscures that which is within, yet does not exist in empty space. Empty space originally lacks the appearance of flowers, nor does it undergo arising or ceasing.
One should know that the birth-and-death of ordinary beings and the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles—these two are identical to the flower and the visual impairment.
If a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva cultivates the practice of the Perfect and Sudden, using their intrinsic nature to subsume their cultivation, this is called "non-existence."

All such practices are dharma-gates of inherent evil, directly pointing to the flower-like veils. Birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, which is none other than Great Perfect Enlightenment.
It may be said: "A hot griddle leaves no room for the feet of mosquitoes; how could a red furnace tolerate a single flake of snow remaining?
Is this not what is meant? (2. This answers the third doubt with the analogy of gold ore.)
"Good son, you should know that space is not something that exists only momentarily (until) it becomes the equal, fundamental nature of space.

This refers to the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). It has no arising or ceasing; no coming or going; it is neither new nor old, neither delusion nor awakening; neither empty nor substantial.
It spans all time from antiquity to the present without shifting or changing. Although one uses space to illustrate emptiness..."
The meaning of the boundlessness of space is the meaning of inexhaustibility; it is not the awakened nature itself, but is equal to empty space. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The empty space of the ten directions arises within your mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity.

This "mind of mine" refers to the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha-citta*). It encompasses the ten directions, such that empty space exists within this wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment. How could it [otherwise] be so?

Can it be said that there is temporary existence and temporary non-existence? The birth-and-death of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is called "existence," while the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles is called "non-existence.

The nature of Great Perfect Enlightenment is neither existent nor non-existent, neither empty nor real. Therefore, it does not enter the birth-and-death of ordinary beings, nor does it abide in the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in tranquil illumination, it encompasses emptiness."

This is largely the same as [the previous discussion on] emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, it says: "How much more so for the Tathāgata’s nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), which is equal and universal, yet is taken to be empty space!

One must understand that the 'empty space' of perfect enlightenment is not the empty space of the present moment. The empty space of the present belongs to the category of manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*);
it is not true emptiness (*bhūtakoṭi*). (The following provides an analogy.)
Good son, it is like refining gold ore; the gold does not exist because of the refining [itself]. (Up to: The *tathāgata*’s perfect enlightenment is also like this.
The gold within the ore is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature existing within delusion. The gold formed through refining is a metaphor for the Buddha-body within awakening.
These two aspects of Buddha-nature, though appearing as two in essence, are non-dual. While in delusion, this nature is not deluded; while in...
To awaken to this nature is also not awakening; for this nature has never been subject to delusion or awakening from the very beginning.

Thus, while it exists within delusion, it is not deluded; while it exists within awakening, it is not awakened. Therefore, it is said that sentient beings are fundamentally already Buddhas. Although sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, [it remains obscured].
It is like gold within ore: only after the ore has been smelted and removed from the furnace does it return to its original, true Buddha-nature.

The fundamental Buddhahood of sentient beings and this analogy are perfectly consistent. However, while sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature as a principle (*li*), they have not yet realized it as a fact (*shi*);

they lack the two causes of *pratyaya* (conditions) and *niṣṭhā* (completion). The adornments of cultivation and realization are already perfected in the Buddhas, just as [gold] is formed through entry into the furnace and smelting.

Gold. There is cultivation and realization; it is perfected in accordance with the *dharmadhātu*. Initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti*) and original enlightenment (*mūlapratibhāsa*) merge as one, without subsequent division.

It is like gold taken from the furnace; therefore, it is said that it does not become ore again. Although the principle is possessed by all sentient beings, they are like gold within ore—still in a state of delusion.
This is called the *tathāgatagarbha* "within the bonds" (*saṃkliṣṭa-tathāgatagarbha*). A Buddha is gold free from ore; this is called...

The Tathāgatagarbha that has emerged from its entanglements and the Tathāgatagarbha [in its latent state] are not different in their essential nature; they are distinguished only by delusion and awakening.
Sentient beings are like ore, while Buddhas are already like gold. Furthermore, ice is likened to the gold within the ore, and gold is likened to the water within the ice.
It is like hot water melting ice; the ice returns to become water. One should not say that it was not originally accomplished.
A flower can produce fruit; if the flower does not open, by what means could the fruit arise? There is no fruit without a flower, and no flower without a fruit.

Now, taking the meaning of the fruit as our focus, we do not investigate the cause of the flower. Once the fruit is realized, one no longer values the flower; the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is likewise so.
(Next, it clarifies that what the Buddhas realize is perfect and ultimate, thereby verifying the Śrāvakas’ lack of perfection regarding the Dharma-realm.)
"Good son, regarding the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas... [there is] neither delusive saṃsāra nor non-saṃsāra.

In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Pūrṇa challenges the Tathāgatagarbha with the problem of arising and ceasing, asking: "If it is pure by nature, how can mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
This is similar to the doubt here concerning Vajragarbha regarding how sentient beings are fundamentally already Buddhas.
For what reason, then, is there still the same ignorance? The Tathāgata replied: "Throughout all worlds, from beginning to end, there is arising and ceasing;
yet the eternally abiding true mind, which is the Dharma realized by oneself, is neither born nor extinguished. Thus that sutra says:
"I, with my wondrous clarity—neither born nor extinguished—contain the Tathāgata-garbha; and this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity."
Perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm, therein, the one becomes the infinite and the infinite becomes the one. Within the small appears the great;
within the great appears the small. Without moving from the site of enlightenment, one pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

Containing the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions within a single body, one manifests jeweled-king lands upon the tip of a single hair and turns the Great Wheel of Dharma while seated within a mote of dust. Thus it is extinguished.

When the dust of delusion disperses, true awakening arises; thus, the wondrously awakened nature of clarity is the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind, which is neither born nor extinguished—this is precisely the meaning [of the teaching]. Now, it is said that "fundamentally there is no bodhi, nor is there nirvāṇa.

This principle is consistent throughout. Master Yue said: "One should know that although its function undergoes ten thousand transformations, its essence remains truly unchanged. This is due to Heaven.
The moving stars revolve, yet the North Star remains fixed in its place; the *xuánjǐ* (celestial sphere) wheel turns, yet the axis always maintains its central position.

One who can understand this knows that fundamentally there is no bodhi, nor is there nirvana—whether realized or not—and neither saṃsāra nor non-saṃsāra all return to the Tathāgata’s Great Perfectly Round Ocean of Enlightenment. (Next, it clarifies that the śrāvakas do not penetrate this nature and thus can never reach that direct realization.)
"Good son, the perfected realm of all śrāvakas [up to] the measurement of the Tathāgata’s perfected realm of *vimalaprabhāsa* (pure luminosity)—the intent of this passage of the sūtra is simply this:

because Vajragarbha originally expounded the wondrous mind of *bodhi*, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, nor prior or posterior existence or non-existence; yet, upon hearing the preceding text stating that 'sentient beings are originally Buddhas'..."
He raises a point of inquiry by using the phenomena of arising and ceasing to challenge the Dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing that is Perfect Enlightenment.

Our Buddha wishes to shatter these fragments—arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing, ordinary beings and Buddhas, birth-and-death and nirvana, hell and heaven—and bring them all back to the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*):
the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Within this state beyond characteristics, he brings the Bodhi to full completion.
The sky is clear yet clouds darken it; flowers smile and birds sing—all these are the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana.
Thus, that which the Vajragarbha questioned and the Pūrṇa was confused about is likewise not separate from seeing forms and hearing sounds.
To see me through form, or to seek me through sound, is indeed the path of heterodoxy. Only...
Regarding sounds and forms, even within the space between one's lips and teeth, there is nothing that is not subject to arising and ceasing; how, then, could these be ultimate?
The Tathāgata’s realm of Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra-jñāna) does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, yet it is also not separate from seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Therefore it is said: one cannot fathom it with a mind of conceptual thought, nor can one attain it with a mind devoid of conceptual thought.
Thus, the perfected realm bestowed here upon the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is restricted solely to body and mind;
the sutra states that they do not transcend the view of annihilation. Master Zhao says: "The lesser sages extinguish the body and annihilate [the mind]."
Wisdom sweeps away shadows and cuts off discursive thought; within, there is no exertion of mental illumination, and without, the root of great affliction is stilled.
One transcends and is forever parted from all phenomenal existence; merging as one with the Great Void, they depart into the profound darkness, never known where they go.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Sentient beings of the three realms of existence, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, use their minds of cognitive knowledge to measure [reality]."
The Tathāgata’s unexcelled bodhi is expressed through worldly language to lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (next, citing a metaphor):
it is like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s light; [it serves to] first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra.

The glowworm serves as a metaphor for the wisdom of the "lesser sages"—the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. Regarding the severance of delusions, they have abandoned the afflictions of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *saṃskāra* (mental formations);

they have first realized the principle of the *satyadharma* (Ultimate Truth), which is the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle. The Buddha they perceive is merely a body sixteen feet tall, even if they exhaust eighty thousand great *kalpas* [in contemplation].
Compared to the wisdom of the "supreme sages," this is no more than the light of a glowworm; moreover, the glow of a glowworm is not fire—this light is still [insufficient].
It cannot even illuminate its own body; how much less could it burn other objects? The vastness of Mount Sumeru and the minuteness of a firefly’s glow are difficult to comprehend.

Although the Lesser Sages have severed the death and rebirth of the segmented realm (*pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa*), they still possess the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), which is likewise a mind of saṃsāra.
With such a mind of birth, extinction, and saṃsāra, one can ultimately never reach the Tathāgata’s ocean of quiescent extinction. Thus it is said.
The mind after awakening consists of forty-two stages. When ignorance is completely severed, one enters the stage of Subtle Awakening (*sūkṣma-bodhi*).
It is like the moon on the fifteenth night, with no slanting light remaining. The wisdom of Great Awakening reaches its ultimate limit here.

As for that which is the root of beginningless saṃsāra, a beginning must necessarily correspond to an end. The "end" of ignorance refers to its final exhaustion. Upon reaching this stage of Subtle Awakening, the root no longer exists.
Wisdom is fully exhausted; there is forever no birth or death. Pervading the entire dharma-realm, all is realized as pure. Therefore it is said:

"The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in retributive fruit; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land. (This concludes the [discussion of] the three questions, which are not the primary point.)

"Good son, as for the notion that there is a 'thinking mind' arising from the existence of a mind (and so forth), up to the point that such successive false imaginings have no basis in reality—it is not so.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: 'This Dharma cannot be understood through thought, deliberation, or discrimination.
To have a thinking mind is precisely the discriminating mind. This discriminating mind is but a shadow conditioned by the six sense objects; Ānanda mistook it for his true mind."
The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "This is not your mind; this is a mental object (*dharmāyatana*), a matter of conceptualized reflections.
Such a 'mind-illness' resides solely in the single character 'existence. It is improper to harbor a mind that causes one to fall into discursive thought (*vitarka*).

If there is no mind, then there is no discursive thought. As it says in the *Xingfa yun*: "Contemplate the mind as being without mind; phenomena do not abide in phenomena. Furthermore, it says: "My own mind is itself..."
Emptiness is devoid of both sin and merit, for there is no master over them. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space;

it is all-pervading. The single mark of the Dharma-realm is itself the Tathāgata, the equal Dharmakāya. It is only at the point where emptiness reaches its ultimate limit that one speaks of being "free from thought.
This is not like wood or stone, which lack mind, nor is it a state of dull insentience lacking nature. One must know that this refers to the mind manifest before one.
Consciousness does not undergo even a moment’s change; there is a distinct new consciousness-mind that is free from discursive thought.
Simply within daily life, there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span—since these four views are absent, the five aggregates dissolve and the four elements are no longer bound.
Who then would perceive the shadows of the six sense-objects? Any appearance, however slight, is entirely illusory and false.

If one sees that which is not a mark (animitta), one sees the Tathāgata. That which is not a mark is neither the mark of the birth-and-death of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), nor the mark of the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas;

it is neither existent nor non-existent. This is called the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Upon reaching this, the suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the realm of the Buddha are a single suchness, without a second suchness.
Just as these empty flowers and empty fruits all return to the fruit of Buddhahood, so too does the nature of existence (dharmatā) [return to it].
No-nature. All shall equally attain the Buddha-way. An ancient said: "The spring breeze blows over the river valleys but cannot rouse them;
the partridge cries out amidst the deep flowers. In the waves of the third draw, the fish transforms into a dragon; yet the deluded person still scoops water from the wild pond.
(This next line rebukes those who remain stuck within the afflictions of emotional attachments and conceptual discrimination.)
"Good son, this empty and delusive mind possesses many clever views... (up to) such discriminations are not correct questions.
That which arises as thought in daily life right before you—this is the empty and delusive mind; this thought is unreal."
Because of this, the floating mind gives rise to arbitrary judgments of right and wrong; because of this, clever views arise.
When a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstruction open; when a single thought of bodhicitta arises, the path of Buddhahood can be accomplished.

When a Bodhisattva of the ten wholesome actions gives rise to the Great Mind, they forever part from the ocean of suffering in the three realms. When the Dragon Girl’s single thought accords with goodness, her illusion is entirely pure.
The Dharma transforms women into men and ordinary beings into sages; one proceeds to the south to attain Buddhahood.
When Śunakṣatra harbored an evil mind and slandered the Buddha, he was seen to fall alive into hell. As it has been said of old:
"The gates of heaven and hell face each other within a single thought of the human heart. If one gives rise to a perverted mind and produces clever views, one will ultimately never achieve success.
Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue). Indeed, Perfect Enlightenment is like a fine jade; flaws cannot stain it. Perfect Enlightenment is pure; defilements cannot enter it. Perfect Enlightenment is real;

falsehoods do not penetrate it. Furthermore, one must know that the nature of Perfect Enlightenment is the very nature endowed with the three thousand virtues, which also encompasses all good and evil. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: "It is the Tathāgatagarbha, originally..."
The clarity of mind is wondrous: it is mind; it is emptiness; it is earth; it is water; it is wind; it is fire; it is the ear; it is the eye, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
it is form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena; it is the eye-consciousness element, and so on, up to the mind-consciousness element;
it is clarity and ignorance, and the exhaustion of clarity and ignorance, and so on, up to old age.
Birth itself is death; birth and death themselves are exhausted. Suffering itself is its origin, its cessation, and the path. Wisdom itself is attainment.
Generosity (*dāna*) itself is ethical discipline (*śīla*). And so on, up to: permanence itself, bliss itself, self itself, and purity itself.

Because all these are "identical" (*eva*), the mundane and the supramundane are identical with the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous source of the mind, which is free from identity and free from difference. This is it.
It is neither identical nor non-identical. How can you, with a mind that is an object of knowledge, fathom the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi?

To employ worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is like the lute, the harp, the *konghou*, and the *pipa*: though they possess exquisite sounds, [they cannot produce them without strings].
If it were not for the skillful finger, one could never produce [the sound]. You and all sentient beings are likewise: the precious, awakened true mind is perfectly complete within each of you.
Just as when I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal Samādhi emits light, so too when you briefly raise your mind, the afflictions of worldly toil first arise.
For those who cannot yet accomplish the expedient means of Perfect Enlightenment, even speaking of Perfect Enlightenment serves as an expedient means.
The entire Great Canon of teachings is a gateway of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*).
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* is said to "open the gateway of skillful means and reveal the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*). Now tell me: what is the true reality of all phenomena?

An ancient master, while reciting the verse from the *Lotus Sūtra*, "All phenomena, from their very origin, are eternally in a state of quiescent extinction," suddenly attained awakening. It is said: "The spring is warm."
The flowers are red; the partridges cry upon the willows. This is not a formal question; it is precisely a summary and a refutation.
(The above prose section is called "the meaning of the flowers not yet being exhausted," restating the intent.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Vajragarbha, you should know: the Tathāgata’s nature of quiescent extinction... (until) only then seek Perfect Enlightenment."
In the prose section, he has already exhausted all principles and perfected his nature;
now, upon reaching the verses, it is as if splitting bamboo—the knots are all severed at once, blade meeting edge—so there is no need to add frost to snow.
Furthermore, Vajragarbha is a person within a dream, and Śākyamuni the Old Man likewise speaks of dreams within that dream; suddenly, a man of non-mind awakens them both from their dream at once.
It is originally always the Illusory Samādhi; it is the Buddha-work within a dream.
*The Heart-Mirror Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha-parivarta-sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
*The Heart-Mirror Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha-parivarta-sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by Shi Zhicong of Chongshan Jiaoshi on Mount Chicheng in Taizhou during the Former [Liang] Period.
Chapter on Maitreya Bodhisattva:

Regarding the discussion of all phenomena (*dharmas*), their fundamental source is pure and pristine. They transcend names and are devoid of characteristics; they do not even constitute a single unity, let alone exist as something manifold.

Sentient beings do not yet understand that they constantly dwell within saṃsāra. The Sages take pity on them and, within the realm of namelessness and signlessness, employ provisional names and signs to speak;
within non-duality, they distinguish duality. Therefore, Maitreya, you have thoroughly investigated the turning of the faculties and have earnestly posed your questions.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, amidst the great assembly—[up to]—arising from the realm of saṃsāra with views of cyclic existence.
Maitreya, the Great Being who is next in line for succession, currently resides in the Inner Court of Tuṣita, constantly preaching the wondrous Dharma.

Now present at this assembly, he requests an investigation into the root of birth and death and the beginning and end of saṃsāra. It is like a bell set upon its stand; it will not sound unless struck.
[The section on] "Not Sounding" (the latter part is the formal request):
"World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age [up to] the skillful means of teaching and transforming to deliver all sentient beings."
The Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction (*mahāśāntinirvāṇa-samudra*) refers to the ocean of *parinirvāṇa* through the practice of the Cloud of Dharma.
"Nir" signifies non-arising; "vāṇa" signifies non-extinction; thus, it is neither arising nor extinction. What is now called "quiescence" (*śānti*) is precisely that non-arising;

what is now called "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*) is precisely that non-extinction. "Ocean" implies boundlessness. The Buddha takes Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) as his nature-ocean. If...
To enter into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vajra*) yet fail to comprehend birth and death is to be a corpse in the ocean of the Buddhas or a rotten rat in a grove of flowers;
how can one not take this as a warning? Regarding the root of saṃsāra, the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) states:
"The root of birth and death begins with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), for at the time of the *kalala*, one first receives the deluded retribution of a single lifetime."
There are only two phenomena, name and form (*nāmarūpa*). One should know that name and form are the very root of all that is mundane and supramundane;
they are able to give rise to all phenomena and universally encompass all phenomena. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Within all the worlds, there are only name and form. A wise person says: "As for 'name,' it is the mind; it is merely a designation."

Therefore it is said: "Name" refers to the mind (*citta*) and its associated mental factors (*caitasika dharma*). Although they possess the function of being cognitive objects, they lack any material obstruction that can be perceived.
Since they differ from form (*rūpa*), there are various distinctions among the mind, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the various mental factors.
Second, as for "form," it refers to phenomena possessing shape and material obstruction; these are called "form. These constitute the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and...

The first category, the "small portion," consists entirely of obstructive phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*). Since these lack the function of cognitive awareness, they differ from the dharmas of mind, thought, and consciousness;

therefore, they are designated as "form" (*rūpa*). Regarding its various natures, there are: what is called mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); what are called feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*);

what are called the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*)—that is, the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*); and what is called the body (*kāya*).
Third is speech; fourth is mind. Third [category] consists of: views, afflictions (*kleśa*), *rajas* (dust-like afflictions), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
These are all the seeds of saṃsāra. In reality, the eighty-four thousand afflictions and the *Gaṅgā*-river-sand number of delusions are all subsumed within these few categories.
One cannot fathom them with the intellect, nor can they be exhausted by counting. Since they are all fundamentally the root of saṃsāra...
Fundamentally, this ought to have been posed as a single question. Those who cultivate the Bodhi of the Buddha: "Buddha" is named for awakening;
it is the awakening of sentient beings. "Bodhi" translates as the Way; that is, the mind of the Great Way, which brings sentient beings to fulfillment.

Sentient beings are like travelers lodging within the three realms, having no means of escaping the burning house solely because they are deluded regarding the path to Bodhi, their emotions being attached and remaining unawakened. Great...
The Sage awakens the mind of the Great Way, emerges from the prison of the three realms, and causes all sentient beings to roam the ocean of quiescent extinction and reach the shore of Bodhi.
By what Dharma-gate does one rely, and how many stages of practice are there? Like a person lost in a direction who has no guide, there will ultimately be no time of escape.
A wise one says: Before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, although the ten wholesome dharmas existed at that time, [they were insufficient].
This transformation constitutes ancient goodness. Previously, there was no Triple Gem to which one could take refuge.

When the Great Sage first attained Perfect Enlightenment, he first bestowed the Three Refuges upon the elder Trapusa, establishing them as the foundation for entering the Way and the primary beginning of practice.
The Three Refuges rightly shatter the three perversions, rescue those in the three miserable realms, receive those of the three vehicles, and deliver beings from the three worlds of existence.
How much more so for the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable gates of practice, which do not consist of a single path; hence they are called "differentiated.

Regarding those who turn back toward the dust and toil of the world to establish transformation and deliver sentient beings, Guifeng said: "The vow to deliver boundless sentient beings" is precisely to enter from emptiness into the provisional.
Whether it be great compassion saving all things, or because illnesses are manifold and thus prescriptions and medicines are not of one kind—if there were no such methods...
It is appropriate, like adding a little hot water to ice. Fearing that one might fall into attachment and views, I must ask out of great compassion (this concludes the words of benefit).
I only pray that you will not abandon your world-saving great compassion (up to) the perfect realization of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision.
Cishi (Compassionate Chamber) says: "The eye of wisdom" is precisely the wisdom of suchness; "the mirror of mind" is precisely the realm of suchness.
When wisdom accords with the realm, and the realm accords with wisdom, this is the chapter on Mañjuśrī, which describes the characteristic of perfect illumination and awakening.

This is not merely the merit of the tranquil illumination of Perfect Enlightenment; otherwise, the unsurpassed knowledge and vision would be lost forever. These words are also an expression of praise and entreaty.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again from the end.
Because the Noble Wisdom has compassion for all beings and acts as a model for them, he earnestly requested three times [for the subsequent praise, permission, and hearing of the precepts].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.

As for the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it is not easily attained. There are many kinds of patience: there is the patience regarding arising and the patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*).

Only the patience of non-arising is realized by a Bodhisattva at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Stage (*pariniṣpanna-avasthā*). Once a single grade of ignorance (*avidyā*) is destroyed, one part of the three [realms]..."

The aspect of virtue is manifested; he realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Whenever he encounters adverse conditions, it is like slicing through water or blowing across light.
He manifests his body throughout the hundred realms to save suffering sentient beings—how could this be anything less than lifting Mount Tai to leap over the North Sea?
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
They were like calves longing for milk, or bees relying on honey; how could they not listen? (Next, he answers regarding the root of saṃsāra.)
Good son, all sentient beings have undergone saṃsāra from beginningless time due to affectionate craving and desire.
As the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa* states: "The flow of craving becomes the seed; the reception of ideation becomes the womb; through their union, birth occurs; and they are drawn together by shared karma."
For these reasons, there is birth and death. It is further said: "Because you love my mind and I cherish your form, there is birth and death.

The five desires, greed, and anger are all termed "various. If one reaches the ultimate source of outflows within the state of equality, there is no such thing as a Buddha's name, nor is there saṃsāra, nor non-saṃsāra. Birth and death alternate, like cold and heat.
They shift and change in succession due to deluded movement, resulting in the transformation of things. For now, I shall briefly set forth the primordial beginning. Siming said:
"It is truly because the nature of sentient beings inherently possesses defilement and evil, which cannot be altered. This nature, being perfectly luminous, is called Buddha.
The nature of defilement and the nature of evil manifest as a whole; the cultivated defilement and the cultivated evil have no separate essence, being entirely [the manifestation of that nature]."
By cultivating this nature, one encounters matters of delusion and opposition; yet there is no Buddha who is not the principle.

It is precisely through this principle that one gives rise to afflictions and creates karma, transmigrating through birth and death while remaining entirely unaware that all phenomena are entirely the principle. For long eons one employs the principle, yet for long eons remains ignorant of it.

One does not become a Buddha who is not the principle simply because of this ignorance; rather, because [phenomena] are entirely [the principle], they are called "the principle itself is the Buddha" (li-ji-fo).

Now, wishing to exhaustively investigate the source: from the True arises the delusory. Since the beginning is already True, how can it transform into the delusory? This principle is difficult to clarify.
One must know that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) are of the same substance and equal. Within this nature, both good and evil are inherently present.
If the nature is good, its character is supple; if the nature is evil, its character is rigid. The capacity for rigidity and suppleness resides in the state of equilibrium.
Within the nature of equality, it is like heaven and earth. The nature of heaven is inherently firm, yet it can be supple, as in frost, snow, mist, and dew.
The nature of earth is inherently supple, yet it can also be firm, as in gold, silver, copper, and iron—all of which arise from the earth.
Within this state of equality, there is no distinction between the ordinary being and the Buddha, just as water and ice are not distinct; it is only due to deluded movement that evil arises.
The power of its nature is strong. True Suchness internally perfumes it; though its nature is evil, it gives rise to wholesome conditions and manifests pure functions.

If it becomes utterly pure, it is the Buddha. Once Buddhahood is attained, the evil, the delusions, and the karmic nature of ignorance still remain within the goodness of the nature, not severed by even a hair’s breadth.
When a gentleman is transformed by a petty person, he temporarily acts as a petty person; now—
When one encounters a virtuous person’s transformation, one remains a gentleman; this is precisely the person as they originally were. Sengzhao says:
A Brahmin left home to lead a religious life and returned with his hair white. When a neighbor saw him, he said, "Is that former man still here?
The Brahmin replied, "I am the same man as before, yet I am not the man of before. When the nature of evil afflictions is transformed into a nature of goodness, it is likewise called a "good nature."
It is also called the poison of principle (*li*). Although afflictions are fundamentally incapable of moving it by even a hair’s breadth, this is its original face.

The *Sijiao yiyao* states: "Apart from ignorance, there is differentiation. How, then, does one distinguish between the evil within this nature and the evil of the ordinary person's views and conduct?
It is like water and ice; sentient beings, due to their emotional attachments, cling to the ice and do not know [it is water].
This water is ice; therefore it is said that "sentiment creates a barrier to wisdom" and "conception transforms the substance.
Because one uses water all day long yet perceives it only as ice, there arise the distinctions between heaven and hell, and the differences between pure lands and defiled realms. For now, however—
It is essential to investigate where this present body has come from and to reach the very root of saṃsāra.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that all this arises from failing to know the two fundamental roots and practicing erroneously, like boiling sand in the hope of producing fine food;

even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it remains nothing but hot sand. The first is the root of beginningless birth and death, which is [the nature of] you now, along with all others...
If sentient beings take the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuan-xin*; mind that grasps at objects) as their self-nature, this is precisely the conditioned mind of arising and ceasing.
This mind takes illusory objects as its substance; it arises when conditions assemble and ceases when conditions disperse.

Second, as for the beginningless bodhi and nirvana—the fundamentally pure essence—it is your present *vijñāna*-essence, the fundamental luminosity, which is capable of producing all conditions and is [the source] of what is conditioned by them.

"Those who have lost it" refers to all sentient beings who have lost this fundamental luminosity; though they act throughout their entire lives, they remain unaware and thus enter the various realms of existence in vain.
"The essence of consciousness" is precisely this present, deluded, and floating mind. "Original luminosity" is the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.
If the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha does not conform to defiled conditions, it constitutes the nine dharma-realms; if it conforms to pure conditions...

To achieve the Buddha-realm; therefore, it is said that they can give rise to all conditions (*pratyaya*). Although both defiled and pure states take [the same object] as their condition, the results of gain and loss differ in two ways:
pure conditions attain true nature (*dharmatā*), while defiled conditions lose true nature. Now, referring specifically to defiled conditions, it is said:

"That which is abandoned by conditions" refers to those who enter the various realms of existence (*gati*) in vain. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also speaks of two kinds of roots: first, the root of non-existence...
First is ignorance; second is craving for present desires. The intent is the same as this sutra (which next distinguishes saṃsāra by way of rebirth).
From "all types of natures in all worlds" up to [the end], one should know that craving is the root of saṃsāra.

Regarding the distinctions of rebirth: first, let us speak of the very first moment of the cycle of the six realms. Within the nature of Great Enlightenment, delusion and falsehood are incited by habitual perfuming;
through the karma of ignorance, one follows the natures of the six realms and takes birth in various places.

Driven by the two great elements of wind and fire, my consciousness races about to repay its past debts. Those who perform similar meritorious deeds come to be born into my household; all of this is due to...

It arises from craving; craving belongs to *tṛṣṇā* (thirst). With craving as the cause and the desire for life as the fruit, one then seizes the discarded elements of the parents to form a physical body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Thus, there are the four modes of birth: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. That which is born from within a shell is called egg-born;

that which is born from a fetal sac is called womb-born; that which is born from moisture is called moisture-born; and that which comes into being where none existed before is called... [transformation-born].
The heavens and the hells are exclusively subject to miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). The asuras possess all four modes of birth; humans likewise possess all four.
In the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), there are those born from wombs and those born miraculously. Animals possess all four modes of birth. Among humans, there are those born from eggs;

for example, in the past, in the western land, the mother Viśākhā gave birth to thirty-two eggs, which became her thirty-two sons. As for those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), they are like the *nālikera* [plant].
A woman was born upon a *nālikera* tree; from within a pool of water that had formed there, a girl emerged.

Having no parents, she took the name of the tree as her clan, and thus she was called Nālikera (the "Mango Girl"). She encountered the Buddha and realized the fruits of enlightenment; she is also known as Āmrapālī.
Later, King Bimbisāra obtained her and fathered a son named Jīvaka, the celestial physician. "Lust" (*maithuna*) refers to being immersed in, stained by, and attached to sensual desire.
However, all forms of emotional defilement are collectively termed "lust. Even for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), there is initially a dependence on karma for existence.

For such beings as these, it is all due to the transmission of vital energy through mental defilement. Since their nature and destiny are received through this process, and since life itself depends on lust, and lust in turn arises from craving, it is said that "craving is the root" (the following clarifies how desire assists in forming the causes).
Because various desires assist and incite the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.

The sentient beings' mind of desire resides within; if it has not yet encountered an object, the mind of desire does not arise. It is because of objects that the mind of desire is drawn forth and aroused.
As stated in the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-sūtra*: "You love my heart; I cherish your form. By reason of these causes and conditions, [craving] arises.
Death does not sever it; it is like oil aiding a fire—how could it not blaze even more fiercely? When desire aids the heart of attachment, one creates karma and the retribution of craving. Zao said:
"The reason sentient beings have wandered in saṃsāra for so long is entirely due to their attachment to desire.
If desire ceases within the mind, then there is no birth and death. The spirit becomes hidden in profound stillness and merges with empty space. Such virtue is called Nirvāṇa."
The *Śāsanānuśāsanī* (Teaching of the Bequeathed Instructions) says: "Because those with many desires seek much profit, their suffering and affliction are also many.

Therefore, although the cauldrons of boiling water are seething, they do not cook those who are free from desire. For instance, because the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was attached to his wife, the Buddha led him to tour the celestial palaces.
There he saw a palace where the celestial maidens were most exquisite and wonderful, yet it was alone without a husband. Nanda then—"
He questioned the goddess, and the goddess replied: "The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda maintained the precepts and was born here as my husband.
Nanda maintained the precepts because he desired to be born in heaven. The Buddha then led him to tour the great hells; suddenly, one hell became empty.
Nanda also asked the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said, "Ask the hell-warden yourself. The warder replied, "It is the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda."

It was because he wished to uphold the precepts that his retribution ended and he was reborn in this hell. Reflecting on this, one sees that the five desires are impermanent, like dew upon a flower that dries at the first touch of the sun.
If one knows this yet fails to maintain the precepts, one falls into what the Bequeathed Teachings describe as "the old elephant sinking into deep mud.
(The following clarifies how things depend upon one another in succession.)
Desire has craving as its cause, and life has desire as its cause; [this extends] until: craving and desire are the cause, and craving for life is the fruit.
The *Prabhāsa* says: "This body is false and deceptive, like an empty village. This is because sentient beings initially grasp at the aggregates (*skandha*) to form a body.
'Aggregates' refers to the combination of the five aggregates, which is conventionally designated as a 'body. It is like grasping the five fingers, whereby there is a 'fist.'"

This is a name. Ordinary beings do not understand it; they cling to these provisional names and take them to be a self. Extensively, there are sixteen such views regarding a self, a person, and knowledge.

Now, the various sūtras speak briefly of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). As for "self," if one were to consider it as identical with the phenomena of the accumulated aggregates and so forth, [it would be a fallacy].

If one is free from the false conception of a real self or what belongs to a self, yet still falsely conceives of a person within the five aggregates as "I am the practitioner" or "a sentient being," then because these five [aggregates] arise together within the five aggregates, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). This refers to the "life-principle" (*jīva*).
Furthermore, regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one falsely conceives of a "self" that receives a single lifetime's retribution; this is the "view of a living being.

One also falsely conceives within the phenomena of the aggregates of a "self" whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) maintains continuity without interruption. Because of this clinging, one calculates that there is a self-body;
therefore, it is called the "view of a body" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Now, among these sixteen [views], four views are fully presented; all are false imaginings and possess no real substance.
When a male is about to enter the womb, he perceives his mother as an object of attraction and his father as an object of rivalry.
He conceives lust for his mother and anger toward his father; regarding the father’s emission as his own property, he enters the womb by virtue of this deluded thought.
Women are the reverse of this; these matters are detailed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The designations "male" and "female" originate from delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

This physical body, being of an illusory nature, is termed a "provisional name. Since it arises from delusive conceptualization and, conversely, from semen and blood, when one examines this body, it is called "false and deceptive.
Within the aforementioned two realms of emptiness, this refers to the realm of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). [This applies to] desire...
This refers to lustful desire. "Life" refers to bodily life. If there were no craving, the various conditions would not arise, and the body would likewise not exist.
One should know that desire exists because of craving, and the body arises because of desire. Once this body exists, craving arises once again;
because of craving for the body, it in turn becomes a cause for desire, which further brings about future retribution—birth and death. In this way, they continue to revolve and succeed one another.
It is inexhaustible (the following clarifies the bitter retribution of evil karma).
Because one gives rise to various feelings of aversion and compliance toward the objects of desire... [up to] ...for this reason, one is reborn again in the hells and as a hungry ghost.

As for the objects of desire, they are the five sensory realms of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch. When sentient beings encounter these five objects, they give rise to perceptions of either attraction or aversion.
For instance, regarding the object of form: if it is agreeable, it gives rise to joy; if it is contrary, it gives rise to anger.

Or, if it does not comply with one's wishes, it is called an "object that turns its back. When the heart of love turns its back, hatred and jealousy arise, and thus the mind of anger is born, leading immediately to striking [others].
Abusive speech, killing, and various other evil karmas arise because of form (*rūpa*). The same applies to the other four objects of cognition.

Regarding "favorable" and "adverse": if form is favorable to the mind, one may become attached to it, committing acts of lust, theft, drinking, gluttony, aggression, and frivolous speech, thereby creating a multitude of evil karmas.
Through these two types of karma—favorable and adverse—one invites powerful retributions and first falls into the [hells].
[They fall into] hell. Next they become animals, and finally they become hungry ghosts, receiving the retributions of the three evil realms.

Subsequently, they are born among humans, impoverished and lowly, where they again encounter their long-standing karmic enemies and begin to settle their mutual accounts (as detailed in the text of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*).
Although this scriptural passage does not explicitly mention the retribution of animals, its intent implicitly encompasses them. One should know that sensual desire can give rise to fire.
It consumes all the world, as in the case of Śukapāla in Western India. He made his living by selling fish. Upon seeing the noble princess go out once, he suddenly felt a surge of love for her.
Consequently, he fell ill for a long time. When his mother asked him the reason, he told her what had happened as described above.
From then on, his mother constantly provided the noble one with fish. When the princess asked him the purpose of providing the fish, she wished to know what he intended.
The mother then spoke to her son regarding matters of desire. The princess devised a plan and appointed a meeting at the temple of Īśvara.
They were to arrive on a fixed day. The fisherman arrived first; the deity possessed him with the demon of sleep, causing him to fall into a deep slumber.
The nobleman’s attendants searched for him but found no one. Suddenly, among a heap of paper money offerings, they saw him fast asleep. Not... [he was not there].
He awoke. Someone had left items for him and departed. Upon waking, he did not perceive any extraordinary fragrance, but seeing the objects, he knew that a person of noble status had come.
Suddenly, a thought occurred to him, and the fire of lust arose within his body. First he burned the paper money, and next the flames reached the celestial shrine.
Therefore it is said: "The fire of desire burns the celestial temple. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* [Treatise on Great Wisdom], Vol. 2, explaining the joyful retribution of wholesome karma.
Knowing that desire is to be loathed, one abandons the path of the karma of craving, renounces evil, and delights in goodness; thus one manifests again as a deva or human.

Regarding desire, there are the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), of which form (*rūpa*) is the foremost; people fear it. Yet, if one discusses the nature of desire, it is fundamentally the nature of Bodhi.

It is like entering a battle array carrying a sword: it not only protects one's body, but also secures fame and profit. A Bodhisattva employs form to contemplate the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of form;
apart from the realm of the five desires, there is no separate Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). For now, let us discuss the aversion to desire and the delight in goodness, as follows:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: There are stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) who dwell among humans and even have wives.

While they have correctly severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm, once those afflictions are completely severed, they immediately transcend desire; yet, regarding objects of desire, they are twice as superior to ordinary people. Their wives do not rejoice in this.
He was constantly worried about this. Suddenly, a sage arrived and spoke of the matter. The sage said, "I shall instruct you:
simply say, 'The fruit of Srotāpanna. Such is the nature of the Dharma. The wife followed his words and told her husband.
Her husband’s lustful mind was instantly severed, like ice melting in hot water, vanishing like ashes and smoke. His neighbor, unaware of the reason, joined in with him.
Her husband took a painted jar out; it was adorned with five colors and was very lovely. He said, "If you give this to me, I shall play with this jar.
His wife was so greedy for this painted jar that she never let go of it. Suddenly, her husband asked for the jar; his wife handed it to him.
Her husband fumbled, and the jar fell to the ground, shattering and emitting a foul stench. The husband said, "Help me pick up this [fragments]."
A painted vase was brought. The wife said, "The painted vase has broken. The husband said, "In my view of you, you are just like a painted vase.
He then spoke this verse: "When a resolute one enters meditative concentration and observes the defilements arising from body and mind, having seen them, he conceives revulsion."
It is like a painted vase; is it not that one should know desire is to be loathed?
Furthermore, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a woman who gave birth to three or four sons, all of whom died. Because she missed her children, her mind went mad and she let down her hair.
Naked, he fled. Suddenly one day, he arrived directly at Jetavana Monastery and went straight before the Buddha. Due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he was suddenly awakened to his error;
feeling shame for his lack of propriety, he crouched on the ground. The Buddha ordered Ānanda to fetch a *kāṣāya* robe and give it to him to wear.
Afterwards, she returned home. Together with her husband, she came to see the Buddha and both attained the fruit of Arhatship.
If one loathes evil and delights in good, at best one will be reborn among humans or devas. However, if one deeply reflects upon desire, one may ascend to the ranks of the noble ones (ārya).
Among the five precepts and the three refuges for humans and devas, the five precepts are primary; all such various benefits are the karmic fruits of humans and devas. Thus far.
Generally speaking, this refers to the wholesome states of humans and devas. Below [the realm of desire] are the heavens of the four *dhyānas*: the Brahmā Kings of the first *dhyāna*;

the Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) and others of the second *dhyāna*; the Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubha*) of the third *dhyāna*; and the Cloudless (*Anabhraka*), Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*), and Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heavens of the fourth *dhyāna*.
Beings in these heavens of the four *dhyānas* are all born there as a result of practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). (The following clarifies the retribution of immovable karma.)
Furthermore, one must know that all cravings are to be loathed and abandoned; because craving leads to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), it does not constitute the Noble Path.
As the gateway for entering the Path, one must first subdue sensual desire. As stated previously: "To abandon evil and delight in the good occurs among human beings."

By practicing the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, filially supporting one's parents, practicing worldly benevolence and compassion, building bridges and paving roads, copying scriptures and crafting Buddha images, sweeping stupas and plastering the ground—through such various meritorious deeds, one attains rebirth in the heavens. First, one is born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
second, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; at the very most, reaching the heavens of the Six Desires. Or else, one is born among humans as wealthy and noble. Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore."
Seeing the devas, he now says: furthermore, one knows that all cravings are to be loathed and abandoned; one casts off craving and delights in renunciation (*śama*).

This "renouncer" abandons the preceding realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), where sensual pleasures are coarse and intense; this person, having grown weary of them and abandoned them, is born in the Brahma Heaven.
If one cultivates the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) as a sovereign, "craving" refers to the Second Dhyāna Heaven; this heaven possesses the four factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*). Internally...

Regarding the factors of purity (*śuddhi-aṅga*), joy (*prīti-aṅga*), bliss (*sukha-aṅga*), and one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā-aṅga*): since both joy and bliss already exist [in this state], it is called "the dhyāna of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-dhyāna*).
As for "bliss," in the third *dhyāna* heaven, this dhyāna possesses the foremost happiness, surpassing the previous two *dhyānas*.

It also consists of the five-factored dhyāna. The state of mental serenity is termed "bliss. As for "equanimity" (*upekṣā*), it refers to the fourth *dhyāna* heaven; this heaven possesses the four-factored dhyāna, which severs [all sensation].

Because of the cessation of suffering and pleasure, and because of the disappearance of sorrow and joy, one dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly conscious, experiencing neither suffering nor pleasure;

this is the fourth dhyāna. When the practitioner wishes to leave behind the first three dhyānas, they variously rebuke and renounce the pleasure therein; once that pleasure has faded and ceased, there arises the immovable concentration.

It arises together with equanimity (*upekṣā*), free from pleasure and regret. This state of mind is called equanimity; as described above, having abandoned affection and delight, these four [feelings] are reversed, and one gives rise to the flavor of dhyāna.
Becoming attached to the concentrated mind, the medicine turns into a disease, further nourishing the root of craving.
These higher realms of the form and formless worlds are not easily ascended; it is by virtue of being detached from desire that one cultivates superior goodness and attains birth therein.

Heavenly one, although this is still within saṃsāra, it does not constitute the Noble Path. When compared to the cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment, there is a difference as vast as that between heaven and earth;
therefore, it is said that it does not constitute the Noble Path (next, the correct joy of severing).
Therefore, if sentient beings wish to escape birth and death and be exempt from the cycle of saṃsāra, they must first sever craving and eliminate thirst.
Craving and thirst—these two are the root of saṃsāra and must be eliminated. Craving is the foremost of the three poisons;
attachment arises because of it, marking the beginning of clinging to things. Because of attachment, one grasps the five aggregates as a self. As it is said:

"Scales gather and look up toward the current. This craving and attachment exists among all six classes of ordinary beings; it differs only in degree of intensity. When killing is severe, one receives retribution in the hells;
when mild, one receives the retribution of ghosts or animals. Attachment also has degrees of intensity: if superior, one is born in the heavens;

if inferior, one is born in the human realm. The essence of craving and attachment is beginningless ignorance. Those who cultivate Perfect Enlightenment are able to contemplate this craving and attachment.
All these are the Middle Way of Buddha-nature; though one indulges in craving and attachment all day long, it does not obstruct Bodhi. Mañjuśrī himself said, "I am the teacher of desire.
This is like embracing a tiger or playing with a snake; if one does not realize the principle of nature, one will be harmed by external things.

One who has thoroughly mastered their nature does not enter only as a Buddha; they can also enter as a Māra (the latter clarifying that the Bodhisattva’s use of desire is not the same as that of ordinary beings).
Good son, the Bodhisattva manifests transformations within the world, even assuming the guise of those possessed by greed and desire to enter the cycle of birth and death.

For example, Master Buzhai of Fu Dashi and the nun Hsü-mi-to; or how Avalokiteśvara became the wife of the horse-herder, and [manifested as] the pig-headed one or the *cūta* tree—all of these used the methods of desire to transform people. Yunmen, Nanquan, Deshan, and others all employed the methods of Māra to enter the Buddha-way.
The compassion of Bodhisattvas benefits sentient beings; if they were to employ only wholesome means, then amidst them there would be no instances of evil or rebellion.

Regarding the "heavy" [afflictions]: those who are well-transformed do not accept them; they manifest evil and enter into evil. To penetrate evil within evil constitutes the Dharma-gate of the nature of evil.

By means of this, those who embrace the evil are gathered. This clarifies that in the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), one is already a Buddha; having cultivated the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*) in this stage, one contemplates the objects of the three truths (*sandiji*).

As object and contemplation blend harmoniously, although one possesses the nature of afflictions, one is able to know the Tathāgata’s secret treasury (*rahasya-garbha*); this is the wisdom of principle (*lihui*).
It corresponds [to this stage]. The mind’s contemplation is luminous and clear. This is precisely the position occupied by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe: the Five-Grade Stage of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
What is now called "the permanent severance of weary deliberations" means that the afflictions are forever suppressed such that their nature does not arise.

Because this person’s understanding-mind is empty and pervasive, it is said that they have attained the purity of the Dharma-realm; this refers to that pure understanding. This pure understanding is like a worm...
Worms eat wood; by chance they form characters. Not knowing whether these are characters or not, it is said that they create obstacles for themselves.
