"Good son, these three dharma-gates are all Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue). If one attains perfect realization, one immediately becomes Perfect Enlightenment.

These three dharma-gates are precisely the three contemplations of emptiness (kong), provisional existence (jia), and the middle (zhong). Regarding these three contemplations: the three are one, and the one is the three.

When they are negated, they are all negated together; the three contemplations all manifest the negation of marks. This applies equally to the provisional and the middle. When they are established..."

They are established together; when they are sublime, they are both sublime. They establish all dharmas, they manifest all dharmas, and they empty all dharmas—this is solely because the nature of Perfect Enlightenment possesses all natures. Those who draw near to and accord with it shall become Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The attainment of Buddhahood and Bodhisattvahood, the emergence from the provisional to transform sentient beings, and the bringing of all beings to fulfillment—none of these have ever occurred without relying on this.
Therefore, it is said that they all depend upon the three kinds of activity. Regarding "perfect realization": if one does not possess the Perfect Mind, this awakening will not be perfect.

As for the "Perfect Mind," it refers to the ten thousand dharmas in a single thought-moment, the ten realms and their thousand suchnesses, and the three thousandfold world; this is the guiding principle of the Dharma.
This is the ultimate excellence. Those who rely upon this for cultivation and realization will immediately attain the Buddha-way (next, a comparative evaluation to manifest its superiority).
Good son, suppose there were someone who cultivates the noble path (until) practicing in accordance with it for even a single kṣaṇa.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are but minor sages; they cultivate only the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, entering the Way by contemplating conditions.
This is like a single drop of water. Now, those who cultivate Perfect Enlightenment are like the waters of the great ocean: they shatter all marks while embodying all marks.

They cultivate in equality with the Dharma-realm and realize in equality with the Dharma-realm. As the *Awakening of Faith* says: "That which is free from the marks of thought is equal [to the Dharma-realm]."

The realm of empty space is all-pervading. The single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharmakāya, and it is also the inherent nature and virtue possessed by all sentient beings from the very beginning.
Because the dragon girl attained Buddhahood in the South as soon as these words once reached her faculty of hearing, it is said that she "practiced in accordance" with them.
Regarding the question concerning majestic power asked above: [the text] borrows the shrimp as...

The Eye was extensively revealed by the Muni; yet this too is like relying on emptiness or echoing sounds, failing to realize that the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is fundamentally nothing other than a single nature.
To attain it is awakening; to lose it is delusion. It is but a single principle: through delusion one becomes an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and through awakening one becomes a sage (*ārya*).
The deluded create their own separation, but the principle itself is not separated. Those who lose it lose it of their own accord.

The principle is not lost. The composition of the *San guan* (Three Contemplations) distinguishes between similarities and differences to investigate the nature of the Sage, thereby enabling all sentient beings to align their true nature with the Principle.
When the true nature accords with the Principle, the path to awakening is not circuitous, and the gate of liberation is reached.
If one does not know this Dharma-gate, then into what shall study enter, and where shall effort be applied? Wisdom—
"What is it that is being brought forth? Liang Shi said: "Since the Sage passed away long ago, no sages have appeared; the masses are merely ordinary and ignorant beings.

This has allowed demonic and heterodox delusions to flourish, with various factions burning fiercely. Amidst the endless chatter of 'emptiness' and 'existence,' there are those who create pits and traps.
Some are stuck fast to the literal words and dare not move; others drift into vast, boundless vacuity and cannot..."

Regarding those who "abide" [in practice]: there are those for whom the goal is too distant and their minds do not reach it; those for whom it is too near, such that they identify with their own bodies;

those who treat a withered tree as being in meditative concentration (*samādhi*); those who take the whistling of a hollow to be wisdom (*prajñā*); those who run about on non-paths while claiming it is expedient means (*upāya*);
those who invoke ghosts and spirits while claiming to possess supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*); and those who let their minds wander while claiming it is "vastness."
There are those who speak sparingly and thus act with secrecy; there are those who transmit [the teachings] through the teeth and tongue as oral instructions (*mukha-dharma*).

All such categories establish themselves as patriarchs and, continuing the lineage, form distinct houses. They contradict the scriptures and deviate from the sages, yet the ignorant do not perceive it.
Confucius said: "I know why the Way is not clearly understood: it is because of the encumbrances of external things. This refers to the Liang family’s...
These words may truly be called the essentials for saving the world and dispelling delusions. Those who hear them cannot fail to reflect upon themselves.
Should this not yet be the case, there is nothing I can do for them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse: ...is called ultimate nirvana.

In the "Chapter on Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇa" of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, it says: "He turns the wheel of Dharma thrice throughout the great trichiliocosm; that wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure. Gods and humans..."
The attainment of the Way is the proof of this; thus, the Triple Gem appears in the world. Furthermore, it is said:

"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind. If the Buddha had not appeared in the world, from where would this Brahma-sound be heard?

Since there is no hearing, by what dharma could one practice? Since there is no practice, how can there be realization? One who realizes may escape the suffering of the burning house of the triple world;
Bianyin has already transcended suffering, yet if he does not deliver sentient beings, it would not be the mind of a Bodhisattva.
Therefore, our Buddha manifested the exhortation to realize the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma; though it was proclaimed in a single voice, within that...

Beings understand according to their own kind, each differently. Although you, Bhadrapāla, have asked about the various methods of cultivation within the gate of Perfect Enlightenment, you have troubled my Great Awakening.

To encompass the very roots of the bonds of birth and death and the source of the maladies of cultivation and realization, I shall employ three kinds of wondrous medicines, alternating them like medicinal decoctions;
in total, there are twenty-five varieties. For one who is without a [deluded] mind, these twenty-five are all merely superfluous.
The Dharma has not yet been freed from its fatal core; thus, the sages and worthies, wishing to bestow the medicine of salvation, have presented this chapter as a formal inquiry.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇa, amidst the great assembly... (up to) ...thus he made his request three times, beginning again and again.
Vibhāṣin (Discerning Sound), having heard [the Buddha’s] majestic virtue, inquired about the meaning of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

For the time being, the World-Honored One provided an exposition based solely on the three types of spiritual capacities (*indriya*), responding precisely to what was asked. However, if one considers that the capacities of sentient beings vary in depth and that their faculties range from sharp to dull, how could there be only three?
Thus, Vibhāṣin asked again: "How many kinds of cultivation are there? (The following section concerns listening to the precepts).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vimalasvara, saying: "Listen silently... (The following provides a general indication of the twenty-five wheels).
Good son, the perfect enlightenment and purity of all Tathāgatas... [constitute] the twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of meditative concentration."
If one discusses the nature of awakening, it is fundamentally and inherently perfect and harmonious. All Tathāgatas cultivate and manifest this pure, perfectly ultimate principle;
therein there is no high or low, no cultivation, and no cultivator. Both subject and object are utterly transcended. The Buddha does not deliver sentient beings.
The Great Sage’s compassion is profound and solemn. Observing the minds of sentient beings, he sees that they all possess the *tathāgatagarbha* nature;

yet, because they have been submerged in delusion for a long time, he specifically opens the gate of skillful means to reveal the nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Thus, the *Nirgrantha Sūtra* says: "There was a king named Ugra."
The great Satyaka came to enter his kingdom. The king went out to welcome him from afar, whereupon Satyaka spoke for the king’s sake:
"Great King, you should know that one contemplates the body of the Tathāgata by relying upon the body of afflictions. Why is this? Because this very body is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Within the treasury of all afflictions and impurities, the Buddha-nature is fully present, just as jade exists within stone or [oil] within wood."

Fire within wood, water within the earth, curd within milk, oil within sesame seeds, grain within the husk, gold within ore, an image within a mold, a fetus within the womb, and the sun within the clouds.
For this reason, I say that within the afflictions there is the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Now, through skillful means, the Buddha wishes to reveal to sentient beings these various natures of the treasury, extensively opening up their immeasurable dimensions; for now, we shall treat this as the middle case.
Twenty-five types are demonstrated: single cultivation, combined cultivation, and complete cultivation. Yet, in terms of substance, they do not exceed three;

they are none other than the three stops and three contemplations, the three truths and three objects. Depending on whether the faculties are sharp or dull, and the contemplation is shallow or deep, there may be one, two, or three.
These various wheels interlace like the three eyes of a celestial king or the three dots of the Brahmin syllable *I*.

Now, the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are presented. First, their differences and similarities; subsequently, they will all be easy to understand.

Regarding the first, cessation, there are two kinds: Great Cessation and Small Cessation. As for the three types of Small Cessation: first is cessation as quiescence, so named because it destroys delusions;

second is cessation as stabilization, so named because it is capable of concentration; third is cessation as non-cessation, so named because it accords with the principle of truth (*tattva*). These are derived from the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the *Sūtra on the Three Great Cessations*: these three names were established by the Tiantai master Zhiyi based on the three contemplations (*sanguan*).

First is the cessation of the true essence (*titi zhenzhi*), which destroys the delusions of views and thoughts (*jiansi huo*) and realizes the principle of the ultimate truth (*zhendi*). Second is the cessation that follows conditions through skillful means (*fangbian suiyuan zhi*), which destroys the delusions of the sands of the Ganges (*chen sha huo*) and realizes the principle of the conventional truth (*suditi).
Third is the cessation that quiets the discrimination of the two extremes (*xi erbian fenzhe zhi*), which destroys the delusion of ignorance (*wuming huo*) and realizes [the middle way].

The Middle Way principle and *śamatha* (calm abiding) constitute "stopping by realizing the essence" (*tǐ zhēn zhǐ*). Concentrating the mind and settling it within the principle is precisely ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

*Samāpatti* (meditative attainment) constitutes "stopping in accordance with conditions through skillful means" (*fāngbiàn suíyuán zhǐ*). Although it is termed "concentration" (*samādhi*), its essence belongs to the category of wisdom (*prajñā*).

When Bodhisattvas emerge from the provisional state to transform sentient beings, they employ the method of contemplation; this is also called "reversing contemplation" and "reversing wisdom. Its meaning is likewise [as follows].

It returns to cessation (*śamatha*). *Dhyāna* (meditative concentration) is the cessation of the dualistic discrimination of the two extremes. *Dhyāna* is translated as "calm contemplation" (*zhìlù*): "calm" (*zhì*) is cessation, which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
"contemplation" (*lù*) is observation, which is the provisional (*prajñapti*). To cultivate these while emptiness and the provisional are non-dual is called the Middle Way.

As for the three observations, they are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Their grand proclamation originated with the Tathāgata; their subtle realization was recently transmitted by Zhi [yi].
Within a single mind, there are clearly three functions. "Emptiness" (śūnyatā) destroys all phenomena, manifesting their characteristic of total openness.
"Provisionality" (prajñapti) establishes all phenomena, manifesting that they are not to be destroyed. "The Middle" (madhyama) wondrously integrates all phenomena.
This reveals that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. Jingxi said: "The absence of marks in a single thought is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
the fact that no dharma is not fully contained is called the provisional (*upāya*); and being neither identical nor different is called the Middle (*madhyama*).

This is as stated in the *Sutra of the Necklace of Jewels* (*Ratnakoṭa-sūtra*), where the Bodhisattva Saṃkusumita asks about the Dharma-realm of the three contemplations, the path of the self-nature purity of all Buddhas, and that which is cultivated by all Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Three Contemplations, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Of those phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I say they are empty;
they are also designated as provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. These are all clear textual proofs for the three contemplations within a single mind.

Now, these twenty-five wheels are specifically for those practicing *Perfect Enlightenment* (Circuminscience), and they are all cultivated based on the nature of awakening according to the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna.
[This section] explains the twenty-five wheels (consisting of single cultivation, combined cultivation, and complete cultivation).

First, the single cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (from among the three [initial] contemplations and the subsequent seven contemplations, the contemplation of emptiness is employed first).
If a bodhisattva takes only the state of extreme stillness—up to this point—the bodhisattva is said to be practicing śamatha alone.
As it says in the *Zhi guan*: "Because of dullness and distraction, the clarity of samādhi is obscured and disturbed; one must neither follow them nor fear them.

To follow them leads a person toward the evil realms, while to fear them hinders the cultivation of correct practice. For one who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*), first take...

It is ultimate stillness. One applies oneself exclusively to *śamatha* (calm abiding). *Śamatha* is precisely meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) is fundamentally the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because of delusion, it obscures this principle and becomes ignorance—just as cold causes water to congeal into ice, or as the eye causes the mind to give rise to dreams.

Now, by employing ultimate stillness, one realizes that the essence of ignorance is itself the nature of phenomena. Its arising is the arising of the nature; its ceasing is the ceasing of the nature. It does not arise again.
This treatise discusses the arising and ceasing of inverted delusions. It binds the dharma-nature to the dharma-nature and contemplates the dharma-nature through the dharma-nature.
This nature is eternally such; there is no time when it is not this nature. Once the realization of its essence is established, one neither attains the real nor the false.

Returning to the source and reverting to the root, the entire dharma-realm is simultaneously quiescent; this is cessation (*śamatha*). Furthermore, contemplate that ignorance is equal to the dharma-nature from the beginning.
All that comes is empty. Even unto all dharmas, there is none that is not itself emptiness. It is like the time when the kalpa ends:
from the highest reaches up to the First Dhyāna, everything is nothing but a blazing fire. Or again, it is like everything manifested by the Ākāśagarbha, which is entirely empty;

or like everything manifested by Sāgaramati, which is entirely water. When even a fleeting thought arises, that which is thought and the thinker are both without exception immediately empty—emptiness.

Furthermore, it cannot be apprehended. The dharma-realm is profoundly luminous and all-pervasively bright; this is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Contemplation is itself cessation (*śamatha*), and cessation is itself contemplation; they are non-dual and without distinction.
Yet, when the mind is dark and dull or overly swift and sharp, if one attempts to apply cessation at such times, it becomes even more restless and scattered;
if one applies contemplation at such times, it becomes even more obscure and dim. It is like a battle between a strong force and a weak one, or like the heron and the clam holding each other fast.

With no way to advance or retreat, one must employ skillful means to dispel [delusions]. If one gives rise to a resolute mind, subduing the māras through both forceful and gentle means, there will be a profound realization that is naturally quiescent.
Thus it is said: "The afflictions are forever severed; ultimate accomplishment is attained. From this point, one enters the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (the First Abode).
Entering the ground of Nirvāṇa, which is beyond arising and ceasing, one manifests as a Buddha in various bodies—how could this be anything less than a great benefit?
To practice *śamatha* alone is to practice the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) alone; it is also to practice the true essence alone.
Therefore, the conclusion states: "This is called practicing *śamatha* alone."

Second, the single cultivation of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*). If bodhisattvas contemplate only that [all things] are like illusions—[from "this bodhisattva" up to] "this bodhisattva"—this is called the single cultivation of *samāpatti*.

To contemplate only that they are like illusions means that illusion is itself a provisional dharma. First, one realizes the emptiness of *nirvāṇa* and penetrates the empty *dharmadhātu*. Having established [this],...

To establish sentient beings, one deeply contemplates the illusory nature of all things. One realizes that the myriad phenomena are as dense as a forest, and that the nature of this forest-like array entirely enters into the realm of illusory conventionality.
To manifest these transformed worlds is to act through the power of self-realized awakened nature; this is what is called "Buddha-power.
It is not the power of a resultant Buddha’s grace-bestowing. This Buddha-power is the nature of self-awakening; awakening itself is the Buddha.

The various functions of one’s own Buddha-power should be pervasive and infinite. Emerging into the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*) to transform and guide others, one does not dwell in [mere] great compassion but practices the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Although emerging into the conventional to transform and benefit others, one does not lose the thought of quiescence;

thus, one employs skillful means (*upāya*) to rest according to conditions, as well as various tranquil wisdoms. Wisdom is precisely the contemplation of the conventional; when cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are practiced together, it is called "single-practice samādhi."
Bhadrapāla. Third, as for practicing Madhyamaka alone:
if Bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions [up to] "this Bodhisattva," this is called practicing *dhyāna* alone.
This Sage has entered the stream of the noble ones. First, he extinguishes all illusions; he has not yet spoken of issuing forth from the provisional to save sentient beings.

At this stage, he employs only his solitary, abiding wisdom to perfectly illumine the single mark of the Dharma-realm. Since there is no birth to be saved, it is said that he first extinguishes all illusions and does not engage in active function.
This is like a dragon king bringing down rain: the channel itself remains unmoved, yet the function of raining is spontaneously accomplished. In the middle...

Since the Path has already brought rest to the two extremes, emptiness and the provisional return to the Middle, one thereby realizes the true mark (dharmatā). This is called practicing śamatha alone.
Regarding the fourfold combined practice: first emptiness, then the provisional.
If bodhisattvas first attain ultimate stillness—that is, first practice śamatha and subsequently practice samāpatti—then...
This first employs *śamatha*. "First attaining ultimate stillness" refers to *śamatha*. "Illuminating all illusions" employs *prajñā-vipaśyanā*; "illumination" is itself *vipaśyanā*.
These two medicines—emptiness and the provisional—are for both one's own practice and the transformation of others; hence it is said, "arising in the bodhisattva path."
The five pairs of practices: first emptiness, then the middle.
If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, [proceed]... this is called first practicing *śamatha* and subsequently practicing *dhyāna*.

Simply take the two characters "stillness" (jing) and "wisdom" (hui) to distinguish between *śamatha* (stopping) and *vipaśyanā* (contemplation). "Stillness" refers to stopping; "wisdom" refers to contemplation.
As stopping and contemplation advance further, one severs afflictions and transcends birth and death.
Sixth is the cultivation of fulfillment. First is emptiness, middle is the provisional, and last is the middle.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of quiescent wisdom, first cultivate *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivate *dhyāna*.
This Sage first employs the contemplation of emptiness to treat his internal ailments; he then employs the contemplation of the provisional to benefit beings and deliver them from birth;
finally, he severs the afflictions and realizes quiescent extinction—this is the Middle Way.
Seventh is the cultivation of fulfillment. First is emptiness, middle is the middle, and last is the provisional.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, first cultivate dhyāna and subsequently cultivate samāpatti.
This noble contemplation of emptiness is the essence of true cessation (*tattva-śamatha*). With its fierce and powerful strength, it suddenly severs the afflictions.

Once the roots of the fetters of birth and death are severed, one further employs the two contemplations of the Middle Way and provisional existence to deliver sentient beings; that is, following conditions, one brings to rest the dualistic discrimination of the two extremes through the two types of cessation, thereby together accomplishing the Buddha-realm.
The eighth is the cultivation of the three together. First one cultivates emptiness;
then one cultivates the provisional and the middle together. If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, cultivate samāpatti and dhyāna together.
The power of this noble contemplation of emptiness is potent; by means of the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ālayavijñāna*), it suddenly severs the afflictions.

Within a single thought-moment, it universally reaches all sentient beings. With a single breath, the great trichiliocosm is immediately established. Such is its efficacy; therefore, it is said that "the realm is established."
Ninth is the cultivation of fulfillment. One cultivates emptiness and the provisional simultaneously;
subsequently, one cultivates the Middle Way. If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness—that is, after shamatha and samāpatti—subsequently cultivate dhyāna.

Reaching ultimate stillness, one realizes true cessation (*bhūtasthiti*). This is also called the power of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which further incorporates the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*) to skillfully respond to conditions;

thus it is said that this "resources" give rise to transformative manifestations. Taking the Middle Way as its essence, one further cultivates *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) to shatter the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The tenfold complete cultivation consists of cultivating [the emptiness of] space equally, followed by cultivating the provisional.
If Bodhisattvas, through the power of ultimate stillness—that is, after *śamatha* and *dhyāna*—subsequently cultivate *samāpatti*.

Reaching ultimate stillness, the "True Cessation" (zhēnzhǐ) is also called the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Its power is strong; it is moistened by the "Middle Contemplation" (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) to assist in the realization of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

Subsequently, through the "Provisional Contemplation" (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), transformations manifest before one. As for "world" (*loka*), the world has spatial directions; as for "realm" (*dhātu*), a realm has its distinct divisions.
For example, Śākyamuni has a karmic affinity with the Sahā world; he comes here to save sentient beings according to their respective locations.
Eleventh, the simultaneous cultivation of both: first the provisional and subsequently the empty (from this point onward, in the latter seven contemplations, the provisional comes first).
If bodhisattvas, by means of their power of transformation, first cultivate *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivate *śamatha*.
This first employs the power of transformation to arise. According to the place of transformation, one contemplates emptiness and enters cessation.
These twelve are practiced in pairs: first the provisional, then the intermediate.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, [proceed]—this is called first practicing *samāpatti* and subsequently practicing *dhyāna*.
This first employs the contemplation of the provisional (prajñapti-darśana) to emerge from the establishment of the provisional; hence it says, "variously conforming.
Thereafter, one enters the true emptiness of nirvāṇa; hence it says, "attaining quiescent extinction. This constitutes the contemplation of the Middle Way.
Thirteenth is the cultivation of fulfillment. First, one practices with a provisional [body]; next, with an empty [body];
and finally, with a middle [body]. If various bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, cultivate śamatha first and then cultivate dhyāna in the middle.
Regarding those who perform Buddha-work through the power of transformation: these are the noble ones who emerge from the stream of reality to transform sentient beings.
Like the Great Master Fu (Fotuo Dashi), he manifested his traces at Shuanglin in Wuzhou; he had a wife and children, plowed fields, and engaged in worldly affairs.
If one observes him with a mundane eye, one feels self-reproach; yet if one observes him with the eye of the Way, everything is nothing but Buddha-work. He dwells in peace.
As for "The Tranquil One": Maitreya constantly preaches the wondrous Dharma within the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven; yet while his body remains among humans, he does not stir from that Inner Court.
An ancient saying goes: "The mad Maitreya arrives in Mingzhou, carrying his staff slung across his shoulder bag."
Even if you were to manifest a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred million transformation bodies, each single body would still possess its own sorrow.
Cultivating the fourteen [practices] in their entirety: first the provisional, then the middle-of-the-middle, and finally the empty.
If various bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, first cultivate *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and subsequently cultivate *śamatha* (calm abiding).
This Bodhisattva first uses provisional manifestations to deliver sentient beings, employing all manner of transformations and unimpeded activities.
Like the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder (Kṣitigarbha), he constantly dwells at a ferry crossing; he enters the water to carry burdens for people and performs all kinds of manual labor.
If one takes only a single coin, how could that not lead to stillness? Thus one attains the Buddha-way through fifteen years of complete cultivation.
First one cultivates the provisional, then one cultivates the empty and the middle simultaneously.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of their power of transformation, [practice] up to the simultaneous cultivation of *śamatha* and *dhyāna*.

By means of the power of transformation and skillful means, this is precisely what is called "stopping" (*śamatha*). Stopping that accords with conditions through skillful means is the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).

Provisional contemplation serves as the vanguard, while the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) serves as the central army; therefore, it is said to be "ultimate stillness and quiescent extinction. This refers to the contemplation within emptiness.
This is the realization that the essence [of reality] transcends the two extremes; it is the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) in accordance with both.
This is the complete cultivation of the sixteen [aspects], wherein one cultivates the provisional and the empty simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of the Middle Way.

If Bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation, [proceed] from *vipaśyanā* (insight) and *samāpatti-śamatha* (the meditative absorption of calm abiding), they subsequently cultivate *dhyāna* (meditative concentration).

First, the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) and the emptiness contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Both of these contemplations arise based on the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) and manifest various transformations until they reach stillness—this is emptiness.
Seventeenth, the complete cultivation: one cultivates both the provisional and the middle simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of emptiness.

If Bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bala*), cultivate *śamatha* after [the practice of] *samāpatti-dhyāna*, they employ the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) as their transformation;

this aids in extinction (*śānti*), which is the contemplation of the middle (*madhya-vipaśyanā*). The meditative concentration of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-dhyāna*) is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

The provisional and the middle are precisely essence and function. To further enter emptiness and further enter meditative concentration may be called "calculating on a chessboard within the tent," possessing the merit of securing victory a thousand li away.
Eighteenth: Cultivating both simultaneously. First *samādhi*, then *śūnyatā* (the seven subsequent contemplations employ *samādhi* first).
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation (*nirodha*), [practice] from "first cultivating *dhyāna* and later cultivating *śamatha*" [up to that point].
This Sage employs the Middle Way, which is precisely the single nature of Perfect Enlightenment. This nature does not remain fixed;
it manifests as stillness and as emptiness, shattering all marks and sweeping away all dharmas. Whenever cultivation is initiated, one uses this contemplative insight to establish all dharmas;
thus, there is no dharma that is insufficient.
Nineteen: Cultivating Both Simultaneously. First the Middle Way, then the Provisional.
If various bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation (*śamatha*), [proceed]—this is called first cultivating *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivating *samāpatti*.
This Sage employs the Middle Way; while abiding in the principle of quiescent extinction, he employs the provisional, and thus it is said that "he gives rise to functional activity.

Regarding all objects, he employs the Middle Way to illumine them, and thus it is said that "quiescence and function are in accord," accomplishing all matters such that there is no matter not accomplished.
Twenty: Cultivation through Fulfillment. First, middle, and last; middle emptiness.
Later, if bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence (*śamatha*), cultivate *samāpatti* after having cultivated *śamatha*.

From this Middle Way of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there arise the various distinctions of intrinsic nature; these also function through the application of the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā).

Just as fire becomes bright when it encounters space, and water becomes clear when it encounters space, they manifest in myriad ways and encompass all beings for their transformation—this is the power of the contemplation of the conventional (prajñapti-vipaśyanā).
Twenty-one. Cultivation in full sequence: first middle, then provisional, then empty.
If Bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation (*śamatha*), first cultivate *samāpatti* (meditative attainment) and subsequently cultivate *śamatha*.
This noble application of the Middle Way takes transcendence of all dependencies as its meaning; it is the most subtle of all dharmas, for nothing exceeds the Middle.
It is simply the eternal wisdom that is without an object; though without an object, it conditions, and this objectless great compassion is termed the unconditioned self-nature.
Although it gives rise to activity, it ultimately returns to emptiness; the activity is merely provisional. It is like a bell on its stand: when struck, it rings. The bell—

This refers to the contemplation of the Middle Way. The hollow interior within the bell is the contemplation of Emptiness (śūnyatā). Striking it so that it rings is the contemplation of the Provisional (prajñapti).
Thus, the three contemplations of Emptiness, the Provisional, and the Middle are manifested in their functional application in this manner.
Twenty-two. Cultivation by way of complete integration. First, the middle, and the simultaneous cultivation of emptiness and the provisional.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of quiescence, [proceed] until they simultaneously cultivate śamatha and samāpatti.
First, one cultivates Madhyamaka, which is the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). It encompasses all various phenomena (*dharmas*).

Within these phenomena, it is both eternally luminous and quiescent, and both quiescent and luminous; therefore, it is said that transformations arise, and this is called "attaining without falsehood."
Twenty-three. Cultivation with full endowment. Cultivating both emptiness and the middle simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of the provisional.
If Bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence (up to the point where they) subsequently cultivate samāpatti.
This Sage employs the power of the Middle Way’s quiescence to sustain ultimate stillness. The Middle Way is like water; ultimate stillness is like its clarity.
Yet from this arises transformation, like waves upon the water. The waves are inexhaustible and the ripples are endless; such is the nature of the provisional.
Twenty-four. Cultivation through completion. This refers to the provisional cultivation within the state of equilibrium. Subsequently, one cultivates emptiness;
that is, when Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*), [proceed] up to *samāpatti*, they subsequently cultivate *vipaśyanā*.

This noble stream possesses the power of the Middle Way and is further stimulated by the cultivation of provisional contemplation; it relies upon transformation to reach the contemplation of quiescent emptiness.
Like the Great Clarity Heaven—pure and luminous—one finds peace therein and encounters the source at every turn.
Twenty-five. Perfectly Cultivating the Three Contemplations and the Three Stills.

If various Bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (up to) accord with the purity of intrinsic nature—these Bodhisattvas perfectly cultivate the three contemplations and the three stills. By means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, they perfectly harmonize all things; this is "perfect."
Awakening is the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It is also called the eternally abiding true mind; it is also termed the inherently pure and luminous essence;
it is also called original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*); it is also called the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. It is also the treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
When cultivated and manifested, it possesses all names and penetrates all phenomena. Yet, when in a state of delusion, it becomes evil, it becomes foolish, it becomes ignorant, and it becomes...
The three poisons—lust, anger, and delusion—are the nature of killing, stealing, false views, Māra, and the icchantikas;
they are the nature of obscuration characterized by dullness and stupidity, and the nature of evil. They possess immeasurable names and constitute the dharma-gate of the nature of evil.

Now, to say they are the Buddha or Perfect Enlightenment is to establish names based on their manifestation through cultivation. To call them ultimate truth or conventional truth is likewise [to name them according to their manifestation].
The Two Truths: they are the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional; they are the Middle Way. Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):

all phenomena—such as the forms and sounds of ordinary beings and sages, as well as causes and effects—are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); it is not empty through investigation, but is empty from the very beginning.
This is termed the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): within the emptiness of nature, all phenomena are fully present.

There is nowhere it does not pervade; self and other are without obstruction; a single hair-tip contains all lands. This is also the contemplation of the provisional (parikalpita), which has been inherently possessed from the beginning.

Yet, regarding this truth of reality (paramārtha-satya) and the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya), these two are non-dual. Blended into one, they have never been one; separated into two, they have never been two.
One should know that this is the contemplation of the Middle Way (madhyamā-pratipad). This contemplation of the Three Truths is...
The nature of Perfect Enlightenment is quiescent yet luminous; luminous yet quiescent. It perfectly encompasses all things. Regarding these various natures and characteristics:

"nature" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and "characteristics" refer to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore, within these two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, the two truths are themselves one.
How could they be separate from the nature of enlightenment? Because the nature of enlightenment pervades the minds of all sentient beings, those very beings are Buddhas. For this reason...
The enlightened nature within the minds of sentient beings resides in the Buddha; the Buddha is precisely the sentient being, and the sentient being is precisely the Buddha.

The Buddha is precisely the sentient being, and the sentient being and the Buddha are equal. This enlightened nature exists even in hell; hell is precisely the Buddha, and the Buddha is precisely hell.
Among the realms of ghosts, animals, humans, and devas, which does not proceed from this? Regarding all phenomena, one employs the three contemplations to illuminate them.

To realize this within one's own body and mind and to be liberated from views and interpretations is not something newly awakened to now; it is because one has never been deluded from the very beginning.
Buddha and birth are one and the same. (This concludes the section establishing the primary cause.)
"Good son, these are called the twenty-five wheels of the bodhisattva; all bodhisattvas practice in this manner.
These twenty-five wheels were originally established for sentient beings to cultivate and realize.

If one discusses the entry into the Way according to karmic conditions—whether provisional or real, partial or perfect, sharp or dull—how could there be only twenty-five? As the sutra itself says: 'If..."

Regarding the various bodhisattvas, because within a single wheel there are various matters concerning its extent and degree, they are unable to exhaustively fathom its principle or fully realize its nature.
(Next, a general demonstration of the methods for practicing the precepts.)
If Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age [from] "a single thought of doubt or regret" [to] "will not achieve success.
This shows that Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age must practice according to the teachings. If one does not follow the sequence of the wheel, it will ultimately be in vain.
"Brahmacarya" (the holy life) means non-lustful desire; it is the purification of bodily action. "Tranquility" is the purification of verbal action.
Furthermore, one should contemplate and purify the mental karma. With the three karmas thus purified, one acts in accordance with wisdom and performs repentance with earnest supplication.

Regarding the phrase "for twenty-one days," this refers to a fixed period; it means to practice with diligence during these twenty-one days, which is called "breaking through obstacles by adhering to the appointed time.
One should focus the mind on cultivating the truth, employing the twenty-five wheels, each established with its respective marker, and seek [enlightenment] with a sincere heart.

Alas! These words concern ordinary people of shallow understanding whose power of contemplation has not yet taken root; they must rely upon the characteristics of phenomena, like using a borrowed boat to cross over or employing a raft to reach the shore.
One should write the twenty-five names upon slips of wood and, before the Buddha, pray with a sincere heart, seeking the empowerment of hidden spiritual forces.
Do not give rise to even the slightest doubt. Having finished the prayers and repentance, one proceeds to—
For twenty-one days, one should practice with a sincere and deeply firm resolve; this must not be done in haste. Thereafter, draw a lot from the box at random, without making any selective choices.
Following the instructions revealed by the knots—whether sudden or gradual—one should practice according to the teachings.

Since each practitioner’s own preferred path is singular, they may cultivate whichever suits them. However, as it is difficult to distinguish between superior and inferior paths and one cannot decide for oneself, one relies upon the Sage.
As for the power, one should practice according to what has been divined; one should immediately practice based on that which was determined and must not again crave other contemplations.

If one practices a single wheel alone, or practices all three contemplations in their entirety, this is called "sudden" (頓). If one practices them concurrently or alternates among them, [this is called "gradual"].

This is called "gradual. This gradualness is not the gradualness of a gradual teaching. Rather, it is identical in taking perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna*) as the beginning of contemplation, identical in taking the true aspect (*dharmatā*) as its object, and identical in taking the supreme tranquil light (*śāntaprabhā*) as the essence of contemplation.

It is merely that because faculties are either sharp or dull, realization occurs sooner or later; this constitutes "gradualness. It does not matter whether one is slow-witted or clever; it is simply when the mind harbors doubt.
"Regret" means that [the vow] is not accomplished.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Bianyin, you should know that all Bodhisattvas... will before long realize Nirvana."

The verse and the prose commentary do not differ in meaning. There are two phrases—"excluding only those of sudden awakening" and "and those whose nature does not accord with the Dharma"—that cannot avoid being explained again.
Guifeng said: "Excluding only those of superior capacity who possess complete and sudden awakening and understanding."
This also applies to all dharmas characterized by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For those who do not follow [such signs], it is not necessary to rely fully upon the twenty-five wheels, the altar practices, the probing of knots, and so forth. One who does not follow such dharmas does not grasp at signs.
Since one does not follow signs, one follows true awakening (*bhūtāvabodha*). This is the sudden entry into perfect luminosity; everything encountered meets with the Way. It cannot...

To further bind it with ropes is like having warts where there were no sores; this refers to the previous teaching that "if one realizes illusion as it is, one is immediately detached," and such passages where no expedient means are employed. Therefore, it says, "except for these."
The old Śākyamuni’s nature is prone to stumbling; A spider’s web catches the moon at the bottom of the water.
Bianyin could not understand picking up the golden ball; He cut the hanging rope to bind the wild geese at the edge of heaven.
Twenty-five wheels alternate in cultivation; Where one gains the advantage, there he drops the hook.
The scaled dragon does not dwell upon the silk line; do not seek it in the depths of the misty waves.

Chapter on the Bodhisattva Who Purifies All Karmic Obstructions:
Contemplating the teachings bequeathed by the sages and worthies, we see that the human body is the physical form inherited from one’s parents; it is truly not [to be treated lightly].
This is a ruinous injury. However, ordinary beings lack wisdom; they grasp at this as real and give rise to the notion of "mine. The *Dharaṇīśvararāja-sūtra* states:
"The birth of beings in the world all arises from attachment to a self. If one is free from attachment to a self, there will be no place for the body to be born into the world.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Within the entire world, nothing surpasses name and form (*nāma-rūpa*). If one wishes to contemplate them as they truly are..."

One should simply contemplate name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). "Name" is the mind; "form" is substance. Therefore, although one has already crossed over oneself by purifying karmic obstructions, one still desires to deliver others.
Thus, in a state free from delusion and distress, one gives rise to delusion and distress and questions the Tathāgata, Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, to apply hexagrams at the Gate of Ghosts is like gouging a sore into healthy flesh; it is for this reason that there exists [this inquiry] which exhausts the source of the four views.
This is the intent of this chapter.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhakarmāvaraṇa (up to) "we Bodhisattvas are deeply moved with joy and consolation.

This inconceivable matter is simply the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s practices during his stages of cause; for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he sought it through diligent toil and suffering.
Suo: The ancients said there was no such thing as "spontaneous Śākyamuni" (this is the formal question).
World-Honored One, if the nature of this awakened mind is inherently pure [up to] why it causes all sentient beings to be deluded and distressed, failing to enter [it].
Regarding this question, both the Gui-feng and Ci-shi schools maintain that it does not mean one is entirely ignorant or utterly deluded.

Their intention is to clarify that although one already knows the perfect luminosity of the awakened nature (*jue-xing*), one merely suspects that the ordinary mind still persists and is incompatible with the source of awakening. Now, I say:

this is precisely for the sake of the ordinary person who is deluded regarding perfect awakening and has not yet found a path for cultivation and entry; what does it have to do with a sage who already knows?
If [the truth] is already known, why must one ask the Buddha? If the fruit has already been realized by the Buddha, yet the person remains deluded, as it is said in a sutra:

"To cause all sentient beings to fall into confusion and fail to enter [the path]—how could such a person toward whom all sentient beings are treated thus be considered a sage? (Next, the vow to speak forth with sincerity.)
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively explain this for us... [repeated] thus three times, beginning again from the end.
Guifeng said: "If one speaks directly of the fundamental substance, it is called the awakened nature (bodhi-svabhāva); if one investigates the differentiated phenomena, [it is called the dharmas]."

All lack intrinsic nature and are identical to all phenomena; this is precisely what is called *dharmatā*. Now it is said: the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are one essence and not two.
However, when referring to those who have attained the fruit, that which is cultivated and manifested by them is called the nature of awakening.

When referring to ordinary beings who are deluded, that which is cultivated and manifested within their state of confusion is called the nature of phenomena. This *dharmatā* pervades all dharmas. (Next, permission was granted for the exposition and listening of the precepts.)
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions and the great assembly, saying: "Listen in silence.
The entire treasury of the teachings, the hundreds of thousands of samādhis, and the immeasurable gates of practice are all the skillful means of the Buddha. He opens the gate of ambrosia;
yet if one investigates the original source, the living being and the Buddha are equal. All dharmas are, without exception, the Buddha-dharma."
The Buddha-dharma is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); the true mark is all phenomena (*dharmas*).

It is only because sentient beings are lost in delusion that the Sages lay out the path and fashion rafts to ferry people across; this is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). (Next, the formal exposition.)
"Good son, all sentient beings from time immemorial [until now] have taken the four inversions to be their real self-substance.

Tiantai says: "The divine self (*ātman*) is fundamentally unobtainable; yet those who have not yet seen the Way all falsely reckon a 'self' and 'what belongs to the self' within the dharmas of mind and form, the four great elements, the five aggregates, the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses. This is the mind that reckons a self."
There are many conditions to be traversed; now, I shall briefly distinguish four views (from the *Fajie Cidi*).
It is said here that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have only engaged in worldly activities, all of which have a beginning—such as the building of houses or the construction of dwellings.
All things have a beginning; only this single thought-mind has no point of origin in time. We merely speak of it as revolving in birth and death.
Now that this present body exists, one must know where one was before one's parents were born, and what constitutes the beginning.
Therefore, it is said: "From the beginningless past. For now, let us follow how the wind and fire seize my consciousness-spirit and cause it to enter [the womb].
In the mother’s womb, one takes up two drops [of semen and blood] to form a body; this is precisely what is called deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). These drops were originally not mine;
they were cast off by my parents, yet I falsely claim them as my own. Thus, I falsely reckon the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This conjunction of the five is like dew upon a blade of grass, gathering for only a brief moment, or like the five fingers forming the appearance of a single fist.
The five aggregates constitute the body; it is likewise so. How much more so for ordinary people who, failing to understand this, cling to these provisional names as being "self" and "mine.
As the sutra says: "As for 'self,' it is either identical to or separate from the five aggregates, the four great elements, the sense organs, the objects, and consciousness."

To falsely calculate "I" and "what belongs to me" is truly what is called the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). As for "persons," they also falsely calculate that within the dharmas such as the five aggregates there is a "practitioner," and they falsely calculate their own physical appearance to be a "person.
Jingxi says: "The 'self' is calculated with respect to the internal; the 'person' is calculated with respect to the external.
As for "sentient beings," they also [falsely calculate] within the various dharmas such as the five aggregates and form that these things are collectively formed into this [being].
Regarding the body, to calculate that there is a self born is called the "view of a sentient being" (*sattvadrṣṭi*).

Regarding the "life-span" (*jīva*), one also calculates within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) a single period of retributive life, whether long or short—such as a person wishing for a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years.

These are all the "view of a life-span" (*jīvadrṣṭi*). Jingxi said: "Sentient beings take 'continuing the previous' as their meaning; the life-span takes 'proceeding toward the subsequent' as its function."

Ordinary beings, having already clung to a self and recognized the four inversions as the actual substance of that self, are taught the Dharma of non-self by the Buddha in order to shatter the deluded attachments of sentient beings and those of the Two Vehicles.
Having abandoned the notion of self, the followers of the Two Vehicles become Arhats. (Next, hatred and love arise from the self.)
From this, there arise the two objects of aversion and attraction (extending to) the mindfulness of breathing, all of which lead to confusion and delusion.

Due to these aforementioned false attachments, one reckons that there is a self-body; this is called the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Once the view of a self-body has arisen, views of attachment and aversion immediately follow:
one hates that which opposes the self and loves that which accords with it. Such love and hate both stem from the clinging to a self; therefore, it is said:

Based on these two objects, there arise aversion and attachment. Aversion, when it pertains to views, constitutes the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), namely the five sharp-faculties (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-śraddhā*).
It is the state where the mind observes principles with a distorted intent, becoming deluded and inverted. Attachment refers to the heart of greedy defilement; it is called "attachment" (*tṛṣṇā*).

If one becomes deluded regarding the physical forms of men and women, following the mind as it pursues external objects, and the defilement becomes entangled and persistent, this is collectively termed "attachment. Attachment pertains to...
Afflictions (*kleśa*) belong to the delusions of thought; they are the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-saṃyojana*).

Because of their falsity, one mistakenly identifies with and clings to the four elements and five aggregates, taking the sense organs and their objects as a self. This is already false; upon this, one further gives rise to hatred and attachment.
This refers to the persistent clinging to falsehood. These two delusions depend upon one another like ice and water, giving rise to the paths of deluded karma.

One thus transmigrates through the three realms and enters the burning house; these paths of karma are precisely the six destinies. Due to this deluded karma, there are degrees of lightness and heaviness.
The two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—are likewise divided into light and heavy. When wholesome karma is heavy, one is born among humans or devas; then [the asuras...]
If one's evil karma is heavy, one falls into hell; next, into the realms of animals and hungry ghosts. Thus it is said that false views cause one to transmigrate.

Alternatively, among those in the human realm who weary of transmigration, there are those who cultivate the Dharma of the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, realizing the nirvana of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—the conditioned dharmas of the Lesser Vehicle. Such persons have slightly awakened to the nature of emptiness and have mastered the four [truths].
The great five aggregates are by nature empty and quiescent; they do not establish the notions of self, person, or cognitive views.

To attain the path of the Lesser Vehicle and extinguish the two truths is like staying overnight in a thatched hut or entering a conjured city—it is not ultimate extinction. This is called the "erroneous view of nirvana.
Because of this, one cannot enter pure awakening. Thus, the Great [Vehicle] refutes the Small; the wisdom of the Lesser Vehicle is like...
Fluorescence—how could it be compared to the wisdom of the Mahāyāna? It is like the bright sun shining in the sky. This awakening is perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

For those who do not enter into perfect awakening, there is still the illumination of awareness; this is the characteristic of pure awakening, and it is not a characteristic of awakening that is in opposition [to reality].

It is not that Perfect Enlightenment (Vajracchedikā-pratyutpanna-bodhi) does not allow you to enter; it is simply because those who think they can enter possess the wisdom of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which is self-secluding and self-obstructing.
It is not that Enlightenment obstructs you; therefore it is said, "There are various capacities to enter," yet it is not through Enlightenment that one enters.
The Great Perfect Enlightenment Wisdom shatters all darkness, extinguishes the minor wisdom of a firefly's glow, and reveals the lofty brilliance of the golden grain.

A single movement of thought is the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); the cessation of thought is the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Both ordinary persons and those of the two vehicles alike return to delusion and confusion.
Reaching this point, where incense and rotten onions are placed in the same vessel, one cannot help but distinguish between them (next, taking birth-and-death and ignorance as the root).

Why is this? Because there exists the primordial ignorance (*avidyā*) that has been active since beginningless time—[extending] until the nature of the body and mind and so forth are all [products of] ignorance.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "With ignorance as the cause, the three subtle states arise; with objective conditions as the condition, the six coarse states arise.

What is here called "beginningless" is precisely fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodha*), which perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness) and gives rise to the three kinds of marks: the mark of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*).
Because it manifests through successive transformations, it is called "fundamental ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*). Since this is fundamental ignorance, internal delusion serves as its cause.
The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—surround space; within this, your ignorant and deluded consciousness falsely assumes the role of the sovereign of space.
If one cannot subdue it, one will likewise be afflicted by others. Not so.
For one who is able to practice patience, these two meanings are not established, nor is a sovereign self established. Now, we discuss the harmony of the four great elements;
the mind is at the forefront of the five sense faculties and is therefore designated as the "master. The *Śāsanānuśāsanī* states: "Regarding these five faculties, the mind is their master;
it forms this physical body, and within it, one establishes a 'self,' even claiming it to be one's own sovereign. If the mind were absent...
With the eye of wisdom, one cannot differentiate between form and mind, the four great elements, the five aggregates, the sense organs, objects, and consciousness;

all are but illusory transformations, like flowers in the sky. Thus, the nature of body and mind is entirely a phenomenon of ignorance, subject to arising and ceasing, and does not transcend falsehood.
(Next, he cites a metaphor.)
For example, it is like a person who does not take their own life;
this is a metaphor for craving (*tṛṣṇā*). In the preceding text, craving is the cause and the love of life is the effect.

It is also the case that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause and ignorance is the effect. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Old age and death have an effect, which is called ignorance; [and] ignorance..."
There is a cause; it refers to old age and death. Therefore, birth and cessation both arise from ignorance (*avidyā*).
As explained above, ignorance acts as its own sovereign, giving rise to self-love (*ātma-sneha*). One loves one's own physical body; who would be willing to sever their own life?

Since it is said that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the cause and the love of life is the effect, both cause and effect consist of the nature of love, which is not relinquished and proceeds spontaneously and involuntarily.

To take life—if one were willing to take life, it would mean abandoning craving; since one does not abandon craving, one cannot escape the three realms (thus concluding that this constitutes an obstacle to the Path).
Therefore, one should know that those who possess craving—even those who seek the Way in continuous succession—will all fail to achieve success.

"Craving" refers precisely to the affliction of attachment (*dṛṣṭi-rāga*). It is solely because sentient beings are deluded by afflictions—that "affliction" (*fan*) being defined as clamor and agitation, and "disturbance" (*nǎo*) as oppression and confusion—that they vex and disorder the body and mind, thereby preventing true illumination from arising. What is now termed "craving" is precisely greed (*lobha*).
The mind that is stained, characterized by attachment and entanglement, is collectively termed "craving. This craving loves that which accords with the self and hates that which opposes it.
Both this hatred and this love exist within my empty, deluded, and floating mind. The substance of this deluded mind is fundamentally non-awakening;
it is the active manifestation of ignorance and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), wherein neither good nor evil has yet arisen.
At that time, there was originally nothing; it is merely within the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that one gives rise to feelings of aversion and attachment.
Because of the false conceptualization that "I am able to nourish others," and because of the conceptualization that "since birth I have been nourished by my parents," this is called "nourishing.
Now, through these feelings of aversion and attachment, one nourishes ignorance within the internal mind.

If one suddenly encounters circumstances that are either adverse or favorable and immediately gives rise to aversion or attachment, this is the sixth "view of nurturing" (*poṣadṛṣṭi*) among the sixteen views of self and person (*ātmapudgaladṛṣṭi*).

(From the *Fajie Cidi*). If one harbors aversion and attachment in the mind—aversion leading to resentment and attachment leading to delight—then resentment and hatred, as well as seeing and loving, are all merely emotional conceptions.
To seek the Way by means of these is to move further and further away from the Way; therefore it is said:
None of these are established. (Next, the inquiry is raised; the four marks are indicated. First, the mark of self.
"Good son, what is the mark of self? It refers to that which is realized by the minds of all sentient beings."
Guifeng’s intention was that the "one who realizes" refers to an Arhat; he held that such a person still possesses the mark of self (*ātman*).
However, I maintain this is not the case. This "self" is the first of the sixteen views, namely the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

It arises solely from a failure to clearly understand name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), and the elements (*dhātu*), leading to the false calculation of a real self and what belongs to a self. Our Buddha feared that people would fail to recognize this view; therefore—
The seeing resides latently within the mind, making its characteristics difficult to discern; hence it is said that "it is realized by the mind.
Although it is said to be realized by the mind, what is the appearance of that which is realized? Below there is a simile to clarify this (the following section explains by means of a simile).
Good son, it is like a person whose hundred joints are in perfect harmony (until) for this reason, the essence of the self manifests only when it is perceived through experience.
It is like a person who is normally healthy and free from any sensation of pain or itching; yet, when suddenly feeling slightly unwell, they apply needles or moxa.
Only when the needle or moxa touches the body do they say there is ache and pain. Once they know the pain, they first realize that there is a self. Therefore it is said:
Regarding that which is realized by the mind: for the time being, this refers to sentient beings manifesting the "self," rather than an Arhat. As the Sūtra says:

"As for all sentient beings—if they were truly sentient beings, why would one need to apply needles and moxibustion? Therefore, it is said that [the self] manifests only upon realization. (The following provides examples:
even at the final moment of the Equal Enlightenment stage, there remains one grade of ignorance that has not yet been destroyed, and the mark of selfhood is not yet exhausted.)
Good son, even the mind that realizes the Tathāgata’s pure nirvāṇa is still the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
This example of the mark of selfhood applies not only to ordinary sentient beings, but extends even to the Buddha; therefore, it says "even its mind.
As for "realizing the Tathāgata," this refers to a Buddha of partial realization (*vibhāga-satya-buddha*), not the ultimate Buddha of wondrous enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Buddha also refers to me as "I," yet this is the "I" of the non-substantial Dharma. This "I" that possesses [the Dharma] is not the "I" of the deluded mind of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
As long as one has not realized the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), being cut by a blade or smeared with fire is entirely suffering.

When a sage encounters such adversity, it is like cutting through water or blowing upon light; what difficulty could there be? It is because ordinary beings have not yet destroyed ignorance (*avidyā*) that they suffer from this ailment.
It is entirely present. If you know the Buddha-ground, you will clearly realize that the "I" which realizes nirvana is itself the mind that realizes it;

this continues until the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). When the forty-two grades of ignorance are completely shattered, the hundred negations are fully revealed, and the myriad delusions have all vanished—like the moon on the fifteenth night. Upon reaching this state, there is neither you nor me, neither this nor that.
There is neither ordinary person nor sage; neither good nor evil; neither heaven nor hell; neither pure lands nor defiled realms.
All are forged into a single whole; therefore it is said: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally manifesting within all classes of living beings" (next, the two aspects of human form).
"Good son, what is the mark of a person (pudgala-nimitta)? [From here until] 'all things' are entirely the mark of a person.
The *Jizhe fajie cidi* states: 'The mark of a person refers to [the perception of a self] within the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, and so forth.'"
One falsely conceives that "I" am a practitioner, distinct from those who are not practitioners; therefore, one is called a "human.

One also conceives that "I" have been born into the human realm, distinct from other realms; therefore, one is called a "human. The *Cishi* (Compassionate Chamber) states: "One must understand the latter three characteristics."
All [notions] rely upon the mark of self (*ātman*) and are established from the root. Jingxi says: "When people calculate based on what is external, they form the mark of a person (*pudgala*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: 'Because one grasps at marks within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one calculates that there is a mark of a person, and thus gives rise to the mind of self (*ātmacitta*).
Because of this mind of self, there arises the notion of 'mine' (*mamakāra*). Once the mind of 'mine' arises, for those things that benefit the self, greed and desire arise."
To give rise to anger toward those who oppose me is a fetter (*saṃyojana*); it does not arise from wisdom, but arises from deception and delusion—this is called ignorance (*moha*).

The three poisons are the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*). Now, when it is said that sentient beings awaken to and realize [the truth], one fears that people might mistakenly take this to mean the awakening to the Way and the realization of the Way; therefore, it is said that this is not so. This is the intended meaning.

He said: "If I am compared to other species and am considered a human, then regarding the characteristics of being human—such as noble status, benefit, or opposition—I may claim that the human path is superior;
yet in reality, this is merely establishing the mark of 'human' based solely upon one's own body."
"Awakening" (wu) refers to awakening to that person; "realization" (zheng) refers to realizing one's own appearance, status, and wealth.
Therefore, it is said: "Having awakened, one has already transcended all who realize. The meaning is: I have already surpassed all people; none are equal to me. What I can do, others cannot;
what I understand, they do not. Such instances are all forms of transcendence; this is not yet the realization of a sage.

The realm is called "transcendence. Therefore it is said that all are characterized by the mark of a person (referring to ordinary people and not the sages; even for those who have not yet eliminated the mark of a person).
Good son, from the mind’s ultimate realization of nirvana down to the exhaustive mastery of the realization of principle—all such states are termed the mark of a person.
"His mind" refers here to the minds of all sentient beings. The dragon girl possesses the mind of an animal; Devadatta possesses the mind of a hell-being;
King Miaozhuangyan possesses the mind of wrong views. Thus, across the ten dharma realms, it is said that "his mind" [is present].
Excluding the ultimate Buddha, there is nothing that is not mind. Since the mind exists, there is a mind that is born as a deva, a mind that becomes a human, and a mind that becomes a Buddha;
even the mind that realizes nirvāṇa exists. Therefore, it is said that "all are the self.

When the mind harbors even a slight awakening, one awakens to being a human, but this is not awakening to becoming a Buddha. "Exhausted" (殫) means "to the end. To speak according to the fullness of its principle, [the notion of] error...
One recognizes one's own body and falsely establishes a sovereign self; therefore, it is called the mark of a person (the next three are the marks of sentient beings).
Good son, what is the mark of a sentient being? [From here until] "to maintain that which is apprehended is called the mark of a sentient being."

Tiantai said: "Within the combination of dharmas such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), one falsely calculates that there is a self arising;

therefore, this is called the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*). Now I say: at the initial moment of conception, one gathers the discarded remains of the father and mother, resulting in five factors:

first, form (*rūpa*); second, sensation (*vedanā*); third, perception (*saṃjñā*); fourth, mental formations (*saṃskāra*); and fifth, consciousness (*vijñāna*). These five all gather the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to be collectively formed.

As for its substance, at that time there is the harmony of the four great elements and the harmony of the five aggregates; it is conventionally designated as a "physical body" and established with the characteristic of "mine.
As for "sentient beings," they are born from a collective gathering; thus, sentient beings are born from the harmony of the five aggregates.
It is like five fingers joined together to form a fist: because these five constitute a fist, the name "fist" exists. [It is the same with] the five aggregates.
The formation of the body is conventionally designated as a "sentient being. It is also called the "view of sentient beings" or the "view of a person.
This name exists even within the mother's womb; it is entirely a false conceptualization and lacks any real substance.

That which cannot be reached by the mind’s own self-realization arises from the knowledge and views of "self" and "person," leading one to be haughty and arrogant, thinking, "I am a sentient being; others are not sentient beings."
"This is me" gives rise to self-exaltation; "he is not me" gives rise to pride toward others. Thus, there are two kinds of inferiority: first, others being inferior to oneself;
second, oneself being inferior to others. The term "inferior" (下) applies to both self and others.
Therefore, an analogy is established below: "I am a sentient being. From this, one knows that what the person calls a "sentient being" is neither me nor him.
The text further explains this itself, saying: "Why is it not the self? 'I' refers to sentient beings; therefore, it is not the [true] self.

This is 'I,' yet since it is not another, it is sentient beings. Since that other is also not 'I' because it is sentient beings, that which is not the self is not the self. Why is it not that [other]? 'I' refers to sentient beings; since 'I' is already not that other, that other is likewise..."
It is not the self; it is the sentient being. To summarize: because it is not that self, it is neither "that" nor "self. It is the self, yet not that;
even as that, it is not the self. Yet sentient beings, through their deluded attachments, distinguish between "that" and "this," claiming there is awakening and realization.
All such things belong to the realm of the self and persons, whereas that which is beyond this realm of self and persons— [End of excerpt]
To maintain the notion that there is something to be understood, and to establish [theories of] awakening and realization—all these are the deluded thoughts of "self" and "others.
They do not depart from these five aggregates (*skandhas*), which gather together to form a body; this is called the mark of a sentient being (next, the four marks of life and longevity).
"Good son, what is the characteristic of the lifespan? (Up to: the conceiving of a self and the awareness of a self are likewise thus.
Regarding 'lifespan' (*āyuṣka*): the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks only of the 'clinger to lifespan' (*ātmabhāvagrāha*) and does not mention 'life-force' (*jīvita*).

Now, when we speak of 'lifespan,' the 'clinger to lifespan' refers to the false conceptualization that there is length or brevity within the five aggregates of form and mind; this is what is called 'lifespan.'"

Regarding form and mind, within the aggregates and the dharma-realm, one calculates that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is established as a continuous, uninterrupted connection; this is called "life.

Life and longevity are essentially one, though the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* divides them into two. Because one calculates that the life-faculty is a continuous, uninterrupted connection and clings to this, one calculates that there is a self-body;
this is termed the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). As for "the mind illuminating purity," the mind is itself...
Life (*jīvitendriya*) is merely the breath of inhalation and exhalation; this breath is simply the wind-element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*).
If this breath-wind is not pure, it becomes obstructed and stagnant, all of which arises from this mind. To know all phenomena is "knowledge" (*jñāna*); knowledge is illumination.
To illuminate all phenomena is called "awakening" (*bodhi*). As for "all-encompassing wisdom of karma" (*sarvakarmajñāna*), this karma is itself wisdom.
This wisdom is itself karma. By the karmic power of this ignorance, one knows all phenomena. This wisdom is not the wisdom of the omniscient one (sarvajñajñāna);
rather, it is a wisdom that arises upon the basis of karma. At that time, people called it the "spiritual platform" (lingtai).
That which this wisdom does not perceive is like the life-faculty (jīvitendriya). It is said that those who know the life-faculty in the world are few; this refers to that very point. If the mind...

One knows that life has its long and short spans, and that it is an illusory transformation (*māyā*). As the "Chapter on Emptiness" states: "The mind is like an illusory transformation. Therefore, it says:
"If the mind illuminates and perceives, all is awakened. Here, "illumination" (*zhào*) means knowing. Thus, one immediately knows and perceives all phenomena (*dharma*).
All of these are false and illusory; therefore, it is said that the character "one" (*yi*) following the word "awakened" (*jue*) includes the wisdom of awakening as well.

Both the subject that awakens and its objects are defilements. These defilements consist of the four great elements, the five aggregates, the sense organs, their objects, and consciousness—all of which are afflictions.

Both the subject that awakens and the object awakened, the subject that knows and the object known, are equally defilements. The subject that awakens is like boiling water, while the object awakened is like ice. Therefore, it is said:
It is like hot water melting ice. One who knows that the ice is melting—who is it? Both the knower and the known are entirely without substantiality; therefore, the word "who" (*ye*) is used.
