If one were to maintain a self that possesses the knowledge of knowing, this would be merely perceiving the objects of which one is aware—just like the hot water and the ice, where both the agent of melting and the object melted are devoid of characteristics. Therefore, it is said, "it is also thus. (Next, the general indication of the error of maintaining a self.)
The Way). Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks [of existence]; for this reason, it is called the "final age of the True Dharma.

The divine self (*puruṣa*) is originally the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). This nature does not maintain itself independently; following the influence of perfuming (*vāsanā*), it enters into a state of harmonious integration within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and gives rise to delusion.

If one calculates that there is a self and fails to comprehend the four marks [of existence], then even if one practices for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, one will ultimately not attain sainthood.
This is because the self has not been eliminated; since the nature of the fire [of affliction] has not been severed, the elimination of the self is the essential gateway for entering the Way.

Whether in the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, if one does not eliminate the self, one will never be a sage. Even when the Buddha was in the world, there were those like this; therefore, it is said: "In the final age of the True Dharma."
In the five hundred years hereafter, while this Dharma is indeed the True Dharma, those who propagate it will for the most part mislead people with false teachings.

They will revile the Buddhas and curse the Patriarchs; all such occurrences take place during the final age of the True Dharma. Although the Dharma itself remains correct, its propagators are called "heretical.
This is what is meant by the "final age" (the reason for which is now being investigated).
Why is this? Because they take all notions of self to be nirvana, there is what is called "realization" and "awakening," which constitutes their accomplishment.
Now, in this world, there is a certain class who studies the art of non-arising; desiring that nothing arise or perish, they give rise to this mind.
Having already fallen into birth and extinction, those who seek [enlightenment] by turning back from this move further and further away from the Way.

To say, "I am an Arhat," "I am without mind," or "I have reached my destination," is like leading the blind with the blind; such blindness will continue without end. As for *nirvāṇa*: what dharma is called *nirvāṇa*?
You do not recognize the True Principle. The *nirvāṇa* of the Two Vehicles and the Small Vehicle within the Three Realms merely transcends the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).

Birth and death; *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. In the Mahāyāna, one shatters ignorance and ascends to the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjue chuzhu*), realizing a portion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*);

this is Mahāyāna *nirvāṇa*. The Buddha is ultimate *nirvāṇa*. How could there be anyone who is purely an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) whose three poisons (*triviṣa*) are not severed even in the slightest degree, and whose natures of lust, anger, and delusion remain entirely intact? What kind of *nirvāṇa* could such a person realize? If one were to take [this state] as having attained...

Supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are also [aspects of] nirvāṇa; yet even demonic enchantments possess the five supernatural powers resulting from karmic retribution—how could these be taken as proof of attaining nirvāṇa?
Furthermore, the Great Teaching (Mahāyāna) disparages the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), referring to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas as "heterodox persons. Kāśyapa himself said:
"Before hearing the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, I was still possessed of heterodox views; how much more so when one mistakenly identifies with the conceptualizations of self and person (*ātman-pudgala*)."
This is like mistaking fish eyes for pearls and considering it reaching one's destination; it is called awakening, it is called realization, and one even says, "I have already achieved it.
An ancient said: "This is discernment; this is clarity. If one does not choose virtuous friends and excellent companions...

To distinguish between the correctness and error of one's views is not merely to avoid self-deception; it is also to avoid misleading others. How could the gravity of such an offense be fully described?
(Next, an analogy is cited:
It is like a person who mistakes a thief for his own son; the family’s wealth and treasures will never be secured.

"Robbers" refers to the six robbers of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Amidst forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*), they plunder the family treasures of their own accord;
how could they ever gather together again? This specifically refers to the "robbers" as the *karmic consciousness* of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since beginningless time, this robber has harmed me greatly, yet I simply fail to reflect upon it. This is the karmic consciousness of ignorance.
Consciousness is also called the "paternal nature" between father and son. The father is the paternal nature—the originally awakened Buddha-nature.

After wandering through the cycle of birth and death, father and son have lost one another. Today, by practicing Perfect Enlightenment, one reunites with this paternal nature and establishes the relationship between father and son.

Ignorance and the Dharma-nature are of one essence; the father is the son, and the son is the father. The thief is the leader, and the leader is the thief. If you mistake them, [you will fall into error].
One cannot avoid being harmed by others. (The next question: "If you ultimately admit this and take it as proof, how does that hinder the Path?
Why is this? Because those who possess self-love also love *nirvāṇa*. (Up to: How should one know that phenomena are not liberated?
The Buddha-dharma cannot be sought with a mind that possesses attachment; nor can it be attained by a mind devoid of attainment.
One must employ the mind that possesses attachment as the functioning of a non-attached mind. As the present text says: "For those who possess self-love, the love of the heart is not severed.

For those who seek nirvana, this love of the heart is ignorance (*avidyā*). If ignorance is not destroyed, and if one seeks the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) with a loving heart, one is far removed from the Way."

Those who merely suppress the root of craving are like a tree from which the branches and twigs have been removed; they will grow back again. If one cuts the root of the tree, it can never again take root.
To sever the root and realize true nirvana is different from merely suppressing the root of craving, which is like pressing down grass with a stone.
To be reborn again upon encountering conditions is not ultimate. Outsiders and ordinary people take suppression to be cessation and mistake it for the mark of Nirvana;
though they use medicine to treat illness, they cling to the medicine as the illness itself, and thus the root of their disease becomes even deeper.

Therefore, it is said that this is true birth and death, and thus they are not liberated. It is not that the Dharma is not subtle, nor that they cannot escape birth and death; it is simply you who do not understand.
Because this Dharma cannot be employed [without wisdom], the Sūtra says: "That the blind do not see is not the fault of the sun and moon. This Dharma is like entering the midst of a battle;

one who skillfully employs weapons moves with ease and remains unhurt. One who does not employ them skillfully may brandish a halberd and stab their own mouth—not only will they injure their hand, but their life itself will be difficult to preserve.
(Next, it clarifies that the mark of selfhood (*ātman*) is not yet exhausted.)
"Good son, those sentient beings in the final age (up to) will have their faculties playing freely without interruption.
'The final age' refers to the latter five hundred years, when strife is firmly entrenched. For those who study the Bodhi—that is, the Way—at this present time, their view of self is not eliminated;
even if they possess a slight degree of knowledge and insight, they immediately claim to have realized and attained it. Such as these..."
People, simply because they do not recognize the true path of Bodhi, mistakenly enter heterodox paths and deviant regions, taking them for the true Way.
Not having realized, they claim realization; not having attained, they claim attainment. Thus it is said that they take their own slight realizations to be self-purification.
During the time of the Buddha, the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners were all among those of deviant views, yet some of them also possessed supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Such individuals already belong to the category of those with wrong views; how much more so now, when they use only their verbal karma to deceive and delude sentient beings?

The world lacks the discernment of "blue and white eyes" (the ability to distinguish the wise from the foolish), so they follow one another into the lands of the heterodox. Like leading the blind by the blind, they enter together into the fiery pit.
The Buddha, out of compassion for these people, uses words of urgent admonition to uproot their wrong views and cause them to return to right view; therefore, he praises that Dharma.

They immediately give rise to joy and desire to deliver others through false teachings. Those who receive them believe they have already attained that person’s true path and can transcend birth and death;
yet how could they know that birth and death are accumulating ever more heavily? In truth, they are lost within delusion—people who are doubly deluded.
Both disciple and teacher fall together into ruin. Only one with clear vision can properly distinguish between the virtuous and the depraved.
When they expose their faults and point out their delusions, this person immediately gives rise to anger and resentment; throughout their entire life, they remain bound by enmity.
Such a person is simply because they have not eliminated the notion of a self (*ātman*); because they stubbornly cling to the self, their very essence is ignorance (*avidyā*).
The eighth consciousness is also called the *ālaya-vijñāna*. This self-consciousness is only exhausted upon reaching the stage of ultimate Buddhahood;

even Bodhisattvas at the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) have not yet exhausted this subtle consciousness of mine. Therefore, it is said to "grasp and maintain," lying latent within the inner mind in the field of the eight consciousnesses.
Since it lies latent within, it "plays" among the various faculties—that is, the six sense organs. When present in the eye, it is called "seeing. In... [text truncated]
The ear is called "hearing. At the gateway of the six sense organs, when one encounters sensory objects such as forms and sounds, one feels joy if they are favorable and anger if they are adverse.

In both cases, the grasping of a self-identity remains uninterrupted. This is why the view of a self is said to occupy the foremost position; it is for this reason that [the following] concludes by establishing the obstruction to awakening.
Good son, that practitioner who does not eliminate the mark of self cannot enter pure awakening.
Awakening is perfect awakening; it is the principle of the purity of nature. It is like a white jade disk that cannot tolerate even the slightest flaw;
if there is even a small blemish, it is not pure. This "blemish" is precisely the grasping at a self. If one retains this grasping at a self, the nature is not pure, just as [a flawed jade].
"A solitary crane does not enter among a flock of chickens" (this second line correctly explains why it is not so).
"Good son, if you know that the self is empty, there is no one who can destroy the self" (up to: "the life-span of sentient beings is also like this."
If one knows that the self is empty, this emptiness is primordial emptiness; it is not an emptiness produced by effort. It is also called the emptiness of inherent virtue.
This emptiness of emptiness transcends all marks while encompassing all marks; it is the emptiness of non-emptiness, the existence of non-existence.
This emptiness and existence are inherently present within the fundamental nature. Seeing joy, one does not rejoice; seeing anger, one does not become angry.

Since these are originally present, why indulge in anger or joy? What I am saying now has not yet reached that level of realization. It is because of my speaking that people may revile me, yet I do not give rise to anger.
Although I do not direct anger toward others, my internal thoughts do not cease; I merely suppress them for a moment. Only...
It does not manifest on the countenance, yet it still persists within the mind; therefore it is said: "If one knows that the self is empty, there is no one who can destroy it. Yongjia said:
"When the body is in accord with emptiness, whether it is cut by a blade or smeared with incense, what suffering is there? What joy?
When the mind is in accord with emptiness, whether it is reviled or praised, what anxiety is there? What delight? However, to establish a "self" capable of speaking is...

Because of non-anger. If one gives rise to such a thought, both the subject and object have not yet been eliminated; that there is "that" and "I" is entirely because the mark of self (*ātman*) has not been severed.
For example, during the time of the Buddha, there were two people who stole someone's lotus flowers and plotted together, saying:
Another suddenly woke up and called out, "Who has stolen my flowers? The thief ought to have imitated the cry of a mandarin duck to leave no doubt.

Indeed, one person entered the pond to steal the flowers; when the owner asked, "Who has stolen my flowers?", he did not imitate the cry, but instead replied, "I am a mandarin duck," and was thus caught by the master. This is fundamentally due to that single word, "I."
It has not been eliminated at all; who is there who does not suffer from this? This is what is harmed by my illness.
Therefore, because the view of a self and the view of a life-span have not been severed in sentient beings, it is said: "it is likewise so" (next, the illness is explained as a dharma).
Good son, sentient beings in the final age mistake illness for the Dharma (up to) "therefore they cannot enter pure awakening.

It is like a person who has an illness and must take various medicines; once the medicine reaches the illness and it is eliminated, one should also abandon the medicine. Or, there may be some people who...
Because one clings to and does not relinquish medicine for the sake of curing illness, the medicine instead becomes the illness itself.

How could one know that while the disease is easy to treat, the medicine-induced illness is difficult to cure? Even diligent cultivation and the person who can preach it are both termed the root of illness.
It is solely because they do not recognize that true nature is fundamentally empty that they mistake the medicine for the disease.
Although they exert themselves with diligence in seeking the Way, they fail to realize that the self and human nature are empty; thus, they give rise once more to false conceptions.

The original purpose of studying the Buddha is to cure illness, yet after a long time, they instead turn the medicine into a disease and their arduous practices become mere toil. This is like a woman in the Buddha’s time who, loathing her body, set it on fire.
Just as you were about to enter the fire, you suddenly encountered a spiritual friend who said: "By burning your body and loathing your body, you still do not escape suffering;

that suffering is further compounded by suffering, for you have not realized the emptiness of nature. Even if you were to burn a thousand bodies, you would still not be free from suffering. It is like a broken donkey-cart:
the donkey loathes the cart and destroys the old one, yet although the old cart is destroyed, a new cart comes along again; he does not realize this."
There is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span. It is like a bird cast into a net; there is no place from which it can escape.
Although the mind wishes to escape in every thought-moment, alas, there is no way out. Yet one seeks a way out. An ancient said: "When the mind roams the Dharma-realm, all thoughts are stilled;
like the sun resting upon the sky, it does not dwell in the sky. (Next, this clarifies how the ordinary is confused with the sagely.)
Good son, the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age do not understand these four marks; for this reason, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
These four views are originally the true suchness (tathatā) and Buddha-nature; however, because false conceptualization arises, they regard this physical body as already being substantially existent.
Furthermore, they reckon that their own capacity to understand the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is their own mind, as well as the four samādhis.

This is the gateway to the Path. I am one who practices what I have attained; my false conceptualization of what I understand is the "superior person's dharma" that I practice. Such understanding and practice are all merely false conceptualizations.

There is no non-self or non-person within the nature of Perfect Enlightenment, yet because of the view of self, one acts as a sovereign master; therefore, one will ultimately not achieve realization. Furthermore, there is...
There is a type of person with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) who, not having attained [realization], claims to have attained it; not having realized it, claims to have realized it.

Deceitfully calling themselves a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend), they manifest themselves for the sake of gain and offerings. As the Sūtra says: "In the past, there was a poor man who fled to another country and falsely claimed to be a prince.
The people of that country did not recognize him, so they gave him their princess as a wife. When this man encountered food and drink, he would constantly give rise to anger."
He was rebuked. Later, a man from that country happened to see the princess and recounted the aforementioned events. The guest said, "I shall teach you a verse.
When he gives rise to anger, simply recite this verse and his anger will subside of its own accord. The verse says:
Fleeing to another country to evade his debts, he falsely claimed to be a person of noble status. Coarse food was his constant diet; why then should he trouble himself with anger?
This man’s heart of anger has indeed been subdued, yet now this arrogant person increases his pride, falsely claiming to have attained realization, and seeking fame and profit.
To envy those who are virtuous and capable is to create the causes for the hells; yet one remains unaware of this oneself.

Therefore it is said that because one has not severed self-love (*ātmasneha*), one cannot enter pure awakening (*viśuddhabodhi*). Is this not deception? (Next: delusion regarding the cause while pursuing the fruit).
Good son, when sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age hope to achieve the Way, they cannot enter the ocean of pure awakening.

Even when those seeking the Way apply their minds with such hope, it is because their pride (*māna*) has not been extinguished. If they apply their minds to seek enlightenment, this too is the notion of self and person (*ātman-pudgala*).
Even if they should attain a fragmentary understanding, they will again fall back into the realm of the self. True Way does not reside in much hearing (*bahu-śruta*).

It does not lie in powerful memory. The *Buddhāvatamsaka* (or *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*) says: "Ānanda, though you may memorize and uphold the twelve divisions of the sutras of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, with their pure and wondrous principles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is not equal to cultivating untainted karma for even a single thought-moment. It further says:

"Ānanda, even if you possess powerful memory, you cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts. If the outflows of desire are not first eliminated, your accumulation of learning will result in [the burden of]..."
This is an error. Thus, the Sūtra says: "It only increases one's learning and causes the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to grow.

If you wish to cultivate the True Way, you must employ the quiescent illumination of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). When the mind is distracted, bring it to rest; when it is dull, clarify it.

With courageous and diligent effort, subdue both the stiff and the soft [states of mind] to extinguish afflictions, and give rise to the Four Great Vows (the vow to deliver sentient beings, the vow to sever delusions, the vow to study the Dharma-gates, and the vow to attain Buddhahood). Contemplate thus.

As the mind advances further, anger, attachment, and sycophancy will no longer arise in response to objects. Furthermore, one should regard every perceived object as being entirely *pariṇata-ālaya-vijñāna* (perfectly enlightened awareness);
by illuminating them with this awareness, the objects encountered will vanish like ice dissolving in hot water.

Should there be times when obstructions are heavy and the [delusory] state does not recede, one must seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to gain clear discernment, so as not to become lost in false views.
If one harbors feelings of love or hatred toward the teacher sought, one will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Pure Karma, you should know that for all sentient beings [up to] they ultimately do not achieve it.
○ "In the Chapter of Bodhisattva Pujue, it says:
'Dhyāna is fundamentally without illness; that which is ill is not dhyāna. Illness is one's own illness; non-illness is dhyāna. (From the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra Commentary*)
It is said: "Chan is the Buddha-mind; its wisdom-mirror is perfectly bright and clear. It is also translated as "the abandonment of evil.
The Tathāgata’s pure and immaculate wisdom is fundamentally free from evil; evil is itself a sickness. The Sage takes Chan as medicine to treat the sicknesses of sentient beings.
How could one use a sickness to treat another's sickness? Now, when Pujue speaks so freely of "Chan-sickness," it is because Chan is capable of treating [it].
This is called a "dhyāna-illness. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "A good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is a great causal condition;
it is through their guidance and instruction that one now attains Buddhahood. Those currently seeking a good spiritual friend are those who act as teachers and models for others.

Yet, in these final ages, their own insight is not clear; they are like one blind person leading another blind person, blinding the eyes of others by proclaiming what is false to be true. Themselves...
Deceiving those who deceive others—our Buddha, foreseeing the future, urgently taught the methods for saving those from illness. He briefly spoke of four illnesses;
in reality, however, illnesses are immeasurable. Yet these four illnesses fundamentally arise from the body, the body arises from the mind, and the root of illness lies in the mind.
Meditation has no other path; it is simply that the human mind has many facets, and because compassion and wisdom differ, they consequently form four [types].

Regarding illness: if one seeks illness within the mind, which mind is the illness and which mind is not the illness? It can be understood by comparing them through the four states of activity, cessation, spontaneity, and extinction (the following is the formal request).
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Pujue (Universal Awakening), amidst the great assembly, made this request three times, beginning again from the end after each repetition.
The essence of dhyāna is stillness; the essence of vipaśyanā is clarity. Through dhyāna, the mind is stilled and does not scatter; through vipaśyanā, the mind is illuminated and does not grow dark.
Entering the Way of the Mahāyāna takes dhyāna and vipaśyanā as its tent and pavilion, employing samādhi and prajñā as its vanguard to shatter hindrances and destroy demons.

It is precisely because of this that it is now said, "Speak clearly of the illnesses of dhyāna. Since the Buddha has long been distant and the sages have vanished, false teachings flourish while Māra is powerful and the Dharma is weak.
Gold and brass cannot be distinguished; the Jing and Wei rivers cannot be told apart. Illnesses are preached as medicines, and the false is taken for the true.
One uses raw jade as if it were refined jade; though the names are the same, their natures differ. Without right view, all is in vain.
Because it involves arduous practice, one asks, "What kind of person is sought? and thereby corrects [the inquiry]. Furthermore, dharmas are of many kinds:
there are false dharmas and true dharmas, evil dharmas and wholesome dharmas. By means of which dharma is the model established? Practices are also of many kinds; some are correct and some are false.
Among the ninety-six types [of non-Buddhist paths], all are false practices. This was seen by a Brahmin who had gone to gather flowers.
The body of the Kṣatriya [Kāśyapa] developed an itchy rash, so he cauterized it with fire. When the non-Buddhists saw this, they took cauterizing the body with fire to be the Way;
thus, there arose the practice of "five-fold heat-cauterization. A bhikṣu, unable to endure his life coming to an end, threw himself from a cliff; the non-Buddhists imitated him.

Therefore, there are those who throw themselves off cliffs or leap into fire, and some even go naked or observe precepts such as those regarding chickens and dogs; these are all heterodox teachings. Now you ask:

"In reliance upon what practices should one cultivate this? Furthermore, illnesses are of many kinds: the illnesses of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), and the illnesses of the *dharmas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
There is the disease of ignorance and the disease of the body; there is the disease of the mind. Those of the Two Vehicles do not recognize these true diseases;
going to impoverished neighborhoods and dwelling in thatched huts are both diseases within the Buddha-dharma. By what method should one eliminate these two diseases?
There are also many kinds of generating the resolve [for enlightenment]. Now, for one who seeks Perfect Enlightenment, how should they generate the bodhicitta? Thus, one deeply understands...
The Inconceivable Realm: For example, when meeting the fifty-three virtuous spiritual friends, they all say, "I have already first resolved upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;

I do not yet know how you, O Benevolent One, have resolved your mind. These five matters all pertain to the Final Dharma Age, a time when dragons and tigers have vanished, the Right has declined and the Deviant flourishes. Universal Awakening is like a spark struck from flint; thus it was said by the Sugata.
Like an echo following a sound (the subsequent precept permitting the discourse).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying (until): "Together with the great assembly, listen in silence."

To cultivate the practice after generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one must first seek out those who possess correct knowledge and vision (the definitive resolution). [The Buddha] replied correctly:
"Good son, when sentient beings of the final age are about to generate the Great Mind, they should seek out all those who possess correct knowledge and vision."
The "great mind" refers to the bodhicitta. For one who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment, if they do not take the Great Way as their mind, who could possibly fulfill such a great resolve?
Those who give rise to the great mind are many, but those who attain Buddhahood are few. As the Sūtra says: "Like fish eggs, like the flowers of the *āmra* tree..."
When a bodhisattva first resolves their mind [on enlightenment], there are many causes for the three matters, yet those who reach the fruition are few.

It is like fish that produce many offspring, but few become fish themselves; though struck by wind, waves, and currents, many are lost and few survive. Or like the *āmra* flower, which blooms profusely, but few bear fruit.
The generation of the bodhicitta is likewise: even if a hundred people resolve their minds, it is not certain that they will succeed.
One person attains Buddhahood. For example, the Buddha and Ānanda, during the time of the past Buddha Śūnyarāja, both gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment together.
Ānanda delighted in much learning, while Śākyamuni was diligent in vigor. Now that the World-Honored One has attained Buddhahood, Ānanda, known as "Joyful," serves as his attendant.
An Shigao practiced the path alongside one person; although this person practiced, he possessed much anger. The world...
Kang Senghui said: "You resemble me; you are not beneath me. If you do not restrain your anger, I fear you will sink into ruin.
After death, you will become a great python at Hongting Lake, possessing a majestic presence that extends for a thousand li.

You will be able to part the winds to aid passing boats and receive offerings of animal sacrifices from people. Later, you will encounter Kang Senghui, who will manifest himself to meet you and fully recount these matters."
He took all the gold and silk accumulated in the temple and gave it to Śrīmitra to build a monastery; subsequently, he was reborn in heaven.

Thus, to maintain the precepts within one's mind is something difficult for people to achieve. Now, having resolved to cultivate *yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment), using the contemplation of stillness and illumination to observe the mind, you must likewise seek out those with correct knowledge and vision to decisively determine how to apply your mind. If the very first step is wrong, it will remain so for the rest of your life.
Regarding the retinue of Māra and those who seek right knowledge and vision, some say: "One sees with the Buddha-eye; that which resides in the mind is called 'knowledge'. One may only say:

first study the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and thereafter employ the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to receive and transform sentient beings. This is not something that belongs to the Buddha alone;
O Good Friends, it pervades both ordinary people and sages. An ordinary person is a teacher of men. During the Buddha's lifetime, there were the four levels of faith.

After his extinction, there were five classes of people. Pu-jue (Universally Awakened) was one who skillfully employed knowledge and vision; he directly questioned the people of the present day: "They cannot distinguish beans from wheat.

When encountering others, they first take whoever enters as their master. They avoid heterodox teachers as they would snakes or tigers, like entering a region of contagious poison where not even a drop of water can touch their lips.
As the ancients said: "It is better to break the precepts as much as Mount Sumeru than..."

One may be perfumed by a false teacher for even a single thought-moment, causing [the seeds] to flow into the *ālayavijñāna* from which they cannot be extracted for kalpas on end. (Next, the transcendence of virtues:
The mind does not dwell upon signs and does not cling to the stages of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas... up to... not causing sentient beings to enter into non-discipline (*asaṃvara*).
One who possesses the mind of the Great Way will certainly not dwell in signs (*nimitta*), will not cling to existence or non-existence, and will not become intoxicated by sounds or forms.
*The Diamond Sutra* says: "They do not cling to form, sound, smell, taste, or touch. The mind of such a person is like empty space; like a bird flying through the sky, it does not dwell in the sky.
If the mind dwells in signs, that is the mind of an ordinary person, the mind of the Two Vehicles, or a stubborn, biased, and limited state.
The deluded mind is but a narrow path, a track traversed by swallows and sparrows.
If it were the Great Path of the Mind, it would be the realm of the Buddhas and the realm of the Bodhisattvas, like the tracks left by a great elephant. Therefore it is said:

"When a Bodhisattva of the Ten Good Deeds gives rise to the Great Mind, they forever part from the ocean of suffering in the three realms. The Śrāvakas merely sever the afflictions of views and thought; [the Pratyekabuddhas] rely on...
Awakening further invades habitual tendencies; lacking a heart of compassion, one does not deliver sentient beings, like a deer leaping alone without looking back at the herd.
One with right knowledge and vision is like fine jade dwelling among mountain rocks; though mixed within the human world, they may manifest the realms of worldly toil and coarse, evil conditions.
This is not like a tiger wearing a sheepskin—its substance remains that of a sheep—or like bait used for catching fish.

The hook cannot avoid the fragrant bait; without bait, the fish will not swallow the hook. Spiritual teachers use fragrant bait as a Buddhist practice to net the fish that are the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm.
It is like the Great Master Fu, who had a wife, children, and kin, and engaged in worldly affairs.
Did Emperor Wu of Liang fail to recognize this? Layman Pang possessed a fortune of a hundred thousand households, yet he sank it in the Xiang River.
Jiang: "How could this be grasping at wealth? At the moment of death, he said: 'I only wish to empty all that exists; be careful not to reify what does not exist.

These two great beings—[Hui]tan and [Zhi]yi—grasped at wealth, wives, and children, yet they still praised the cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment. For those who were laypeople, they taught them to sever desire;

for those who remained in the secular world, they taught them not to entangle themselves in desire. Both were skillful means. Furthermore, they entered the Vinaya discipline. — *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* (淨名).
It is said: "He manifests the experience of the five desires, yet is also seen practicing dhyāna; furthermore, it is said he manifests having a wife and children, yet always delights in seclusion.
These are all manifestations of the faults [of worldly life]. (Next, it clarifies that those who have attained the four reliances and the four fruits may serve as teachers and models.)
One who seeks such a person will immediately attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such a person is the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*). Their "eye of the path" is upright. The nine characters beginning with "Anuttara" (無上) are translated as "Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.
They are a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who shows people through right contemplation and guards against what is non-virtuous through the precepts of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*). This...
The person immediately attains the sphere of right mental conduct, which is the unsurpassed state. Relying on this, they give rise to the bodhicitta and all enter the ocean of sarvajñā (omniscience).
(The following clarifies those who have entered Māra’s realm; though they possess correct knowledge and vision themselves, they must not fail to make offerings.)
When sentient beings of the末法 (mòfǎ) age encounter such a person, they shall remain free from pride and arrogance despite various afflictions.
In the past, Śākyamuni was a king who abdicated his throne to seek the Dharma under the Rishi Asita.

For a thousand years, he offered his own body as a bed and seat for the Rishi to rise and sit upon; furthermore, for a thousand years, he gathered firewood and drew water for him. Thus did he practice the Way.
His mind did not retreat, and he has now attained Buddhahood. Is this not indeed the act of not begrudging one's own body or life?

Furthermore, in the past, there was a wild fox who, being pursued by a lion, fell into a pit while fleeing for its life; having no means of escape, the fox remained at the bottom of the deep pit and reflected, speaking these verses:
"It is a pity that this body is not fed to the lion; had it been fed to the lion, [it would have served a purpose]."
"I have gained merit for myself, yet I am now dying in vain; this body is lost to no purpose, and it profits nothing.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard the fox reciting these verses from afar, he descended to see him and asked from atop the pit: "Do you not cherish your own life?"
He possessed right knowledge and vision and said, "I now wish to hear your Dharma; you may speak it.

The fox replied, "How can a Dharma Master remain below while his disciple remains above, and yet the essential points of the Dharma be preached? Śakra, by means of his supernatural power, raised him up.
Even after being raised, the fox was still unwilling to speak. Śakra folded his robe to form a seat and requested him to preach. This was during the Buddha’s stage as a bodhisattva, such as this.
These and other such examples are all mirrors for reflection. How could sentient beings of the final age who seek Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra) allow their own arbitrary whims to prevail?
When Śatānīka pounded his son’s bones to extract the marrow in order to seek Prajñā, how could there have been any lingering sense of fault or pride?
(Next, he again uses worldly dharmas as analogies.)
How much more so when one gathers wealth, wife, children, and kinsmen [until] the mind’s flower illuminates and shines upon the lands of the ten directions.
Worldly people know only how to employ phenomena (*dharma*), but do not know how to employ principle (*li*). Phenomena are precisely the natures of lust, anger, and ignorance—unwholesome dharmas.
When one employs principle, then lust, anger, and ignorance are themselves the gates of great liberation. For the sake of ordinary beings, the Buddha...
For those of the Two Vehicles, it is taught that one must distance oneself from lust, anger, and delusion.
For Bodhisattvas, however, it is taught that lust, anger, and delusion are themselves the Buddha-dharma. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Upasunda used the dharma of lust to guide people;
those who merely made the sound "um" or "cup" all attained samādhi. Aṅgulimāla, in his rage toward the Buddha, brandished a sword to kill him and shouted at the Buddha, "Gautama, stop!"
"You stay," [the Buddha] said. "You do not stay," the Buddha replied. "Instead, you are teaching me to stay. Upon these words, Aṅgulimālya awakened to his true nature;
he cast down his sword and realized arhatship. Those who skillfully employ evil dharmas to enter the Way are said to have "entered Māra.
Yet Māra and the Buddha are identical—suchness is one and not two. Anāthapiṇḍika, the Elder, spread gold over the ground to purchase a grove for the construction of a monastery.
How could a temple, for the sake of accumulating wealth, harm its status as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?

When the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was still a layman, he loved his wife so much that they would not part from one another. When the Buddha went out to beg for alms, his brother Nanda brought a bowl of rice to offer him;
meanwhile, his wife took a drop of saliva and smeared it on her husband’s nose, saying, "Do not let this saliva dry before you return," as she led him away.
In Jeta’s Grove, [Nanda] was forcibly made to shave his hair. The Buddha had him hold the corner of his *kāṣāya* robe as they traveled to the celestial palaces.

There, Nanda saw the beauty of the heavenly maidens and asked one of them, "Why do you have no husband? The maiden replied, "The Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda, maintains the precepts here to become a husband.
Subsequently, Nanda maintained the precepts for the sake of desire; later, he became an Arhat and received a prophecy that he would become a Buddha.
How can one, with a mind attached to appearances, deceive others into failing to achieve the realization of sainthood?

When King Asoka killed five hundred Brahmin seers, the king was reborn in heaven while the five hundred fell into hell. Such scriptures and treatises take delusion and transgression as the work of the Buddha;
it may be said that the lotus grows from the mud and does not arise on dry land. If, within delusion, there is indeed...
Aspect: Ice is simply water. Evil possesses all wholesome dharmas; this dharma-gate of the inherently evil nature is also a principle of toxic harm.
This is like a physician who thoroughly understands all diseases: if it is a "wholesome" illness, one may treat it with ginseng and *fuling*;
yet for a distinct feverish illness, it must be treated with Yellow Dragon Decoction. [The essence of] the Yellow Dragon’s excrement is clear.
It is because they seek to cure their illness that they do not loathe the impurity of the medicine; this can be understood by reflection.

As soon as the flower of the mind brightens, the Buddha-lands of the ten directions naturally appear before one, like the moon shining brightly upon a clear pool. (Next, the good spiritual friend is explained; there are four illnesses.)
Good son, the sublime Dharma realized by that spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) should be free from the four illnesses.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "A spiritual friend is a great causal condition; that is to say, they transform and guide others, enabling them to see the Buddha."

The *Dhyāna Sūtra* states: "Although all conditions may be fully present, guidance depends upon a good teacher. Regarding the contemplation performed by a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Buddhas and bodhisattvas are spiritual friends; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are spiritual friends."

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* also states: "The factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); through them, one achieves perfect enlightenment. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:

"There are demons of spiritual friends, demons of samādhi, and demons of the bodhicitta. Demons can cause people to abandon the good and follow evil, and they can also transform people so that they fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
The *Māratantra* states: "Apart from the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), everything else is Māra."

How could such matters not be distinguished? If one does not recognize a person of right knowledge and vision as someone worthy of reliance and refuge, then with turbid waters and obscured pearls, what leisure is there to rest the mind, and what leisure is there to cultivate contemplation?
Therefore, it is said that this is a "great causal condition. Now, it is said that one should avoid the four illnesses; these are the four illnesses of one who acts as a teacher for others.
They are not his disciples; they suffer from four maladies. Now, those who act as teachers for others claim that what they have attained is profound and subtle, beyond the reach of others like you.
This is truly the teaching of Māra. If it were the realm realized by a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), [it would be otherwise].
Like a bird flying through the sky, it does not abide in the sky, yet it traverses the sky by itself;

it delivers sentient beings who need no delivering, cuts off afflictions that need no cutting off, studies dharma-gates that need no studying, and accomplishes the Buddha-way that needs no accomplishing. (Next, the four illnesses [or one illness] are presented.)
First, regarding "produced illness": if there is a person [who, from] ... because it is not produced but is obtained, it is therefore called "illness.

The wise teach *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* specifically for the sake of sentient beings to treat these various illnesses. It is said: "Recently, many have attached themselves to non-Buddhist teachings (*tīrthika*).
It is further said: "This person gives rise to views based on the Dharma; although such [views] are also what is attained, they are likewise non-existent."
If one is not meticulous and thorough, it is difficult to distinguish between right and wrong; errors and deviations, the heterodox and the orthodox, will become intermingled.
To err by even a hair’s breadth is to lose oneself by billions. If the true Dharma cannot be discerned, jade and stone remain undifferentiated;

thus one brings ruin upon oneself and others alike, and both fall into perdition. Moreover, as for the views of outsiders, they too claim to speak of the sublime. Even when outsiders observe these appearances...
One should assume the physical form of a Buddha. This is like the two fruits, *ciñcā* and *kālaka*, which are identical in color;
yet one can kill a person while the other can restore life. The *ciñcā* is like a persimmon; those who do not recognize it may mistakenly consume it, resulting in extreme harm.

Even if one follows the instructions of a teacher, there is fear of falling into the two vehicles, the state of externalists, or the realm of Māra; the notion of a "divine self" (*ātman*) is entirely [false].

These are the dharmas of bondage; they are not a self or a master. They are mutually contradictory, and taking what is merely a limited realization as *nirvāṇa*, one sinks further into birth and death.
Where there is attachment, attachment arises; where there is aversion, aversion arises. Though one possesses compassion, it results only in views of craving.

Though one mimics the cutting away [of defilements], it is ultimately nothing but forced endurance. Though one possesses all-knowledge, it does not transcend mere conceptual calculation. Though one is a spirit...

All these are merely transformations of outflows (*āsrava*). The four Vedas studied are not the power of *dhāraṇī*. Although the dull afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) may be severed, one is like a crawling insect;
the treatments of worldly physicians, once the illness has subsided, cause it to flare up again.

The eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) gather into a vast ocean, and the net of suffering within the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) is boundless. How can such things as these be regarded as true?
Regarding the Dharma: for instance, when the Buddhas teach the Dharma of emptiness, it is for the sake of delivering those who cling to existence.

If there are those who cling to emptiness, they cannot be transformed by the Buddhas. To act as if one were creating illness, to create such fabrications, and to act with this body—this body is false and deceptive.
The body is merely a provisional designation. Even if one can manifest the body of a Buddha, it still cannot be regarded as the true Buddha;

to cherish it is an error, for one will then follow false followers. For example, when the Venerable Kūṭadanta transformed an outsider, that outsider was able to manifest the thirty-two marks of a Buddha, indistinguishable from the actual Buddha. It is like the fox with supernatural powers who could manifest the body of a Buddha.
If one engages in conditioned activity—creating birth, creating a Buddha, creating a human, creating a deva, or creating a māra—one must carefully discern this.
"I, within my fundamental mind, perform various deeds"—this mind is illusory and floating, full of many clever views.

How can one trust such illusion and thereby grasp at perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*)? Moreover, perfect enlightenment does not belong to the realm of illusion, nor is it something produced through conditioned activity.
Therefore, it is said that it is not attained through effort. If one relies on the true and perfect [nature], this is the real mark (*dharmatā*).
The real mark is itself the wholesome dharma. It is collectively termed "Dharma" and is also called the "Dharmakāya. If one relies upon and cultivates this Dharmakāya and real mark, [one attains it].
At the time of cultivation, one also perceives the Dharma-body of the true mark; yet there is no "I" who can cultivate Perfect Enlightenment, nor is it that others cannot cultivate it.
One does not give rise to the notion of "mine. Furthermore, one must know that the mind capable of cultivation is by nature empty and quiescent;

my own mind is itself empty, and neither sin nor merit has a master. Although one does not seek to create Perfect Enlightenment, Perfect Enlightenment arrives of its own accord, like [the reflection] in a mirror.
It is like an image: once the grime on the mirror is exhausted, what need is there to worry about the image within the mirror?
(2. Relinquishing Illness) Second, regarding relinquishing illness: if there is another person... [up to] ...it is called "illness" because it does not exist through relinquishment.
These four are all called "sicknesses. Sickness refers to the sickness of views. Loving the Buddha and loving non-Buddhist paths both belong entirely to the sickness of views.
This is what is meant by "taking [them] as sickness," which is here termed "the sickness of indulging in views. This sickness is difficult to cure.

If one says, "I do not seek birth-and-death," this is the deluded view and deluded sickness of an ordinary person. While they do not seek birth-and-death, birth-and-death arrives of its own accord, and they fall to the ground.
The prison of the six realms of rebirth and the twenty-five states of existence are all instances of birth and death;

if one does not seek liberation from them, and since birth and death have no end, is this not indeed a sickness? *Nirvāṇa* is that which is realized by the followers of the Two Vehicles; yet if one does not seek *nirvāṇa*, one will not escape the triple world.
To crave *nirvāṇa* is likewise a sickness of views. Perfect Enlightenment does not reside within the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle. If this is so...
The birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa that one perceives are not the Buddha-nature. If one seeks by clinging to these two extremes, it is already a sickness;
how much more so for one who does not seek at all? This sickness is even more severe. Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa—these two dharmas fall into the two extremes and will never achieve Buddhahood;
therefore, they are said to be a sickness. Nowadays, those who study the Buddha and study the dharma of emptiness... [must...]
To perceive the nature [of emptiness] is, in fact, not to realize it at all. Emptiness is the primary illness; this illness of emptiness is difficult to cure.
One hears only that emptiness can destroy all phenomena, yet one does not see that all phenomena can destroy that emptiness. Because fire obtains emptiness, it burns and destroys everything.
Because water obtains emptiness, it washes away and disperses everything. Because earth obtains emptiness, it gives birth to and supports everything. Because wind obtains...
Because it is empty, it establishes all phenomena and destroys all phenomena. How much more so when the human mind becomes attached to emptiness—is that not a sickness?
It is not that emptiness cannot be used; rather, it is because one cannot employ the Dharma.

It is like a person who takes medicine to cure an illness, but the medicine itself becomes the illness—this is simply because sentient beings do not recognize the empty stillness of their own fundamental nature and do not penetrate that nature.
Emptiness. To fall into the error of [viewing emptiness] as having existence is a mistake. The nature of emptiness is originally empty; it is not something made empty through deliberate action.
If one does not sever birth and death, nor seek nirvana, one falls into the sickness of the two extreme views.

If one wishes to depart from the sickness of the two extremes, one must rely upon the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). If one relies upon and practices this, then one cultivates various merits. One cultivates...
It is the practice of non-action. It is where the path of speech is severed and the sphere of mental activity ceases. It shatters all inversions;

mind after mind is stilled, flowing spontaneously into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Therefore, it is said that allowing the mind to follow its own inclinations constitutes a sickness (the third sickness of cessation).
Third, regarding "stopping and abiding": if there is another person [who... because it is not in accord with stopping, it is called "sickness.
As for stopping the sickness: if the deluded mind is scattered, one should stop it by means of stopping; that scattering will then cease. This is a superior and excellent medicine.
Who would not submit to this? All Tathāgatas of the ten directions rely upon *śamatha* (calm abiding). That it is now said to be a "sickness" is because you do not skillfully employ *śamatha*;
therefore, it is called a sickness. When ordinary beings employ *śamatha*, although their mental scattering is stilled, [it is not yet true cessation].
It cannot be used by those in the heavens of the four dhyānas, by Māra kings, by followers of the two vehicles, or by partial bodhisattvas;
it is like a pit or a trap. As described in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Māra led his various celestial maidens to come and delude the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Māra said to the Bodhisattva, "Noble sir, accept these twelve thousand celestial maidens to serve as your attendants.
The Bodhisattva did not recognize that he was Māra; instead, he addressed him as "Kauśika" (the Lord Śakra).
He said, "Do not offer such unrighteous things to me, a śramaṇa son of the Śākya. This is not appropriate for me. Before he had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti appeared.
It was previously stated: "This is not Śakra; it is Māra who has come to harass and obstruct you.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas, realizing that Vimalakīrti could not be disturbed by him, wished to vanish and depart, but he could not. Even though he exerted all his supernatural powers, he still could not leave.
He heard a voice from the sky saying, "Only by giving these women to him can you depart. Out of fear, Māra...
With a humble and respectful air, Vimalakīrti said to the sisters, "Sisters, Māra has given you all to me;
you must all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, he preached the Dharma of detachment to the women.
The women experienced what they had never known before. Then Māra came again and said to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, 'Householder, you have relinquished everything.'"
"Such a person is a bodhisattva. [Vimalakīrti] said, "I have already renounced them; you may take them back to the celestial palace.
The women said, "In the presence of the householder, we find the joy of the Dharma with which we delight ourselves."
"I no longer take pleasure in the delights of the five desires. I am now returning to my palace with Māra.
Layman, what Dharma do you teach me so that I may dwell within Māra’s palace? The layman replied, "There is the Dharma of the Inexhaustible Lamp; you should study it. As for the Inexhaustible Lamp:
it is to delight in constantly revering the Buddha, to delight in making offerings to the Saṅgha, to delight in firmly upholding the precepts, and to delight in extensively practicing giving."
A single Bodhisattva inspires hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is like a single lamp that lights hundreds of thousands of other lamps, yet its own light is never exhausted.

By means of this dharma, one shall dwell within the palace of Māra until the path of Buddhahood is accomplished in the future. If one takes the inexhaustible lamp as the standard, the lamp is able to...
It destroys darkness. When one is in darkness, by applying *śamatha* (calm abiding), it becomes light. When one is in distraction, by applying *śamatha*, one attains concentration.

When one is in stinginess, by applying *śamatha*, one practices relinquishment. When one is an ordinary person, by applying *śamatha*, one becomes a sage. It is simply that using it skillfully is not a disease, whereas being unable to apply *śamatha* is.

Even non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) employ *śamatha*; they transform it into ninety-five kinds [of paths], all of which are heterodox. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also employ *śamatha*, yet they possess only...
The *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* is employed exclusively by Bodhisattvas, like the moon beyond the clouds or a flower emerging from the water; these are all methods for quelling afflictions.

Now, in practicing *Perfect Enlightenment*, one takes the Middle Way, the Buddha-nature, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and the principle of suchness as the object of contemplation and the basis for subduing [delusions].
Whether walking or sitting, there is meditation; whether speaking or remaining silent, one rests within the cessation of the two extremes.

Birth and death, nirvana; ordinary beings and sages, sounds and forms; cause and effect, the environment and its inhabitants; fame, profit, wealth, and honor—all such various dharmas are dual extremes.

Not to cling to these two extremes, yet not to cling to the Middle Way or to the attachment to dharmas (dharma-love), is like traveling across a great ocean without relying on a boat, without employing oars or paddles, and naturally reaching the shore. To study in any other way is called [the path of duality].
As for illness: if one practices the sublime *śamatha* of the Middle Way, which empties all signs and destroys all delusions, it is called "stopping by realizing the true nature" (*tǐzhēnzhǐ*).

This stopping is itself contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); when object and contemplation are in suchness (*tathatā*), one proceeds directly until the final moment of the vajra-like mind, at which point it does not become an illness. (Next: Reducing Illness)
Fourth, regarding the cessation of illness: if there are people who—[omitted]—do not realize that cessation itself is not attained, they speak of it as "illness.
To regard cessation as illness is entirely due to failing to penetrate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and instead grasping at the mere appearance of emptiness while practicing good and evil.
As for those who abide in the principle of emptiness, there are four types of persons who grasp this emptiness differently. The Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna contemplate cessation.

The Śrāvaka analyzes and exhausts [defilements] as extinction; the Pratyekabuddha contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination—whereby the cessation of ignorance leads to the cessation of volitional formations—and attains the realization of a Pratyekabuddha through reaching the ultimate principle.
The Bodhisattva employs the six perfections to reach the principle of quiescence as extinction. The extinction of the Small Vehicle does not reach Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue).
The person of universal capacity (tongren) takes illusion as extinction; the person of distinct capacity (biere) takes the single principle following conditions as extinction.
"To bring about cessation"—this view held by these three types of people is entirely unreasonable. All of them seek cessation while remaining within the logic of quiescence;

therefore, what they now describe is identified as a "defect. Failing to realize the nature of cessation—the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha* and the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)—they remain outside the gate, lodging in a thatched hut.
What is clarified here regarding cessation is that it is "ceasing yet not ceasing," wherein saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are [non-dual].
Extinction. Sentient beings do not extinguish; Buddhas do not extinguish. The six classes of ordinary beings and the four classes of noble ones do not extinguish.
Form and mind do not extinguish. The two retributions of the environment and its inhabitants do not extinguish. Heaven and hell do not extinguish. Afflictions and ignorance do not extinguish.
Views and attachments do not extinguish. The eighty thousand dust-like defilements do not extinguish. All *dhāraṇī* gates do not extinguish. Water and fire...

It is not extinguished. Evil Māras are not extinguished. All phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds—the teachings of the Buddha and the phenomena of sentient beings—are entirely unextinguished.
Thus, it is called the "ever-abiding mark of the world. It is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). It is the myriad phenomena of the universe.
It is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. It is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*. It is the eternally abiding true mind. It is the essence of intrinsic purity and luminosity. It is...

Vairocana manifests perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) in all things. All phenomena are the essence of perfect enlightenment; the roaring of the ten thousand apertures is the function of perfect enlightenment.
Perfect enlightenment exists within the birth and death of sentient beings, within the *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvakas*, and likewise within all daily activities.
One is perfect enlightenment all day long, yet never perceives it as such—just as one who speaks of fire cannot [perceive it].
This burns the mouth. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal emits light; when you briefly raise your mind, the dust of affliction first arises.
This refers to employing the cycle of arising and ceasing, where cessation is fundamentally not cessation. If one cannot employ it, then arising and ceasing are themselves extinguished.

Now, it is said that failing to realize the nature of cessation, one dwells within arising and ceasing, taking the finger-pointing as cessation and the pitfall as cessation—just as [the previous passage] refuted.
A clod of earth falls into a deep valley. Now, taking up the nature of Great Perfect Enlightenment, it is fundamentally without cessation;

why then need one discuss cessation? That which is fundamentally ceased is fundamentally empty; why then need one further empty it? Using the nature to subsume cultivation, one points directly to the twelve links of dependent origination:
suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path; birth-and-death and ignorance—all are fundamentally unceasing. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One does not sever the fetters."
"Subdue and purify the sense faculties. He further said, "Do not dwell in the ocean of afflictions; with the eyes born of one's parents, see the entirety of the three thousandfold world-system.
Layman Pang said, "Difficult, difficult! To spread out a hundred loads of sesame seeds upon a tree. Laywoman Pang responded, "Easy, easy!
The meaning of the Patriarchs is at the tips of the hundred grasses. Lingzhao said, "Neither difficult nor easy."
When hunger comes, one eats; when weary, one sleeps. Now it is said: "The difficult is not difficult; the easy is not easy. When hunger comes, one does not eat;
when weariness comes, one does not sleep. Whether acting, ceasing, following, or extinguishing—throughout the entire world, all ultimately return to the primary meaning.
(This concludes the four illnesses.)
To be free from the four illnesses is to be pure. (Up to: If one observes otherwise, it is called false observation.
To have a mind is called false; to be without mind is called correct. The *Xingfa* says: "Observe that the mind is no-mind; phenomena do not abide in phenomena."
The Truth of Cessation is quiescent. Yongjia said: "The mind is the root; dharmas are the dust. These two are like blemishes upon a mirror.

When the stains of these blemishes are completely removed, the light finally appears. When both mind and dharmas are simultaneously extinguished, the nature is itself the Real. Whether it be right contemplation or wrong contemplation—"
"Form a single mass. If you wish to subdue dragons and tame tigers, do not learn the methods of handling snakes. Vajrapāṇi said: 'Even dharmas should be relinquished;
how much more so non-dharmas. How can one not relinquish them? (Next, instruct him to serve a spiritual friend.)"
"Good son, those sentient beings in the final age who wish to practice [the path]—[up to]—by practicing in this manner, they will enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Sentient beings employ their emotions and establish a mind of discrimination; the Buddhas employ principle (*li*) and are free from discriminatory thought. As the Sūtra says:
'Toward all people, one should maintain the perception that they are Buddhas. And as the Precept Sūtra says: 'All men are my fathers; all..."

Women have been my mothers throughout all my successive births; there is no birth I have not undergone. Those who study the Buddha’s Way employ compassion and do not establish the duality of self and others.

Therefore, it is said that those practicing in the末法 (dharma-ending age) should, for the remainder of their lives, make offerings to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and serve spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Virtuous friends possess the power of refinement and polishing, while spiritual teachers possess the virtue of pointing out the way from delusion. One should draw near to them...
Consciousness. Furthermore, one must sever arrogance. Those who come to associate with you should not be treated with pride; those who act as teachers to others should not be conceited.

When instructing disciples, whether they are close or distant, do not give rise to anger or resentment. Whenever you encounter such circumstances—whether favorable or adverse—contemplate them as being like empty space.
Space is devoid of discrimination; since there is neither intimacy nor distance, there is no pride or arrogance. There is no...
Whether in body or mind, hatred is naturally equalized. This nature of Perfect Enlightenment exists within all sentient beings; it is of one and the same substance.
You possess this Perfect Enlightenment, and I likewise possess this Perfect Enlightenment. There is but one Perfect Enlightenment; there are no two Perfect Enlightenments.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. By means of this pure mind and this mind of equality...
With a mind free from hindrance, one enters Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). It is as if walking in the era of the Xi family; in Perfect Enlightenment, there is no private concealment.
(Next, the precept against hatred and attachment:
"Good son, sentient beings in the final age shall not attain the Way" [up to] "hatred and attachment toward self and others are likewise so."
This sutra has already eliminated ignorance and the karmic consciousness as the ultimate teaching. When there is ignorance, the view of self arises;

this is precisely self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*). When there is self-clinging, there are immediately aversion and attachment, joy and anger. If one can sever self-clinging, hatred and love will not arise.
Since there is neither hatred nor love, there are no enemies. If one sees an enemy, one should regard them as a parent;
one should not give rise to thoughts of hostility or harm toward one's parents. When I have eliminated hatred and love for others within myself, others likewise will harbor no hatred or love for me.
Thus it is said that hatred and love for self and others are likewise the same. With impartial compassion, one does not seek *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment).
Since [even these] come naturally, how much more so when one seeks Perfect Enlightenment with this wondrous mind? It is like adding flowers upon brocade;
how could it not be harmonious? (Next, he resolves his aspiration to deliver all sentient beings.)
"Good son, when sentient beings in the final age seek Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue), [they should]—up to the point where—'thus resolve their minds so as not to fall into false views.
To cause all sentient beings to enter ultimate Perfect Enlightenment is the first of the Four Great Vows:
'Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them. When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind, they vow to deliver sentient beings as vast as space."

To raise one vow, the other three vows follow accordingly. Furthermore, it is said that there is no "awakened one" who thinks, "I am the one capable of awakening," "others are incapable of awakening," "they are capable of awakening," or "I am incapable of awakening.
Upon reaching this state where there is neither "self" nor "other," one does not grasp at awakening, nor does one grasp at non-awakening.
There is no distinction between those who have crossed over and those who have not, between the severed and the unsevered, or between the awakened and the unawakened. There is nothing.

That which is the characteristic of self and other—such a mind is the mind of equality, the mind of the *dharmadhātu*, the mind of emptiness, the mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) that is quiescent and illuminating, and it is the mind of sentient beings. To arouse the mind in this way is not to fall into false views.
The Sages have thus earnestly exhorted us to praise perfect enlightenment; by means of this, one should examine whether one’s own mind accords with it or not. If it accords, then cultivate it.
"Join the *tāla* [palms]. If you do not join them, it is called deluded thought; if a person does not act accordingly, there is nothing I can do for them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Pujue, you should know that for all sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age... [until] they realize awakening and enter parinirvāṇa.
Once the four illnesses have left the body, the lotus of the mind naturally manifests its brilliance. Last night at the third watch, for whom was the moon ultimately clear?
